subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Introduction
question: (a) Define mental health and mental health nursing. (3 marks) (b) Trace the evolution of mental health services, treatments and nursing practices in the world and in India. (8 marks) (c) Explain the present scenario of mental health care in India. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Timeline of mental health care
labels: ancient demonology and trephining – Hippocrates' humoral theory – Middle Ages witch-hunts – Pinel unchains patients (1793) – Tuke's York Retreat (1796) – Kraepelin's classification – Freud's psychoanalysis – ECT (1938) – lithium (1949) – chlorpromazine (1952) – Peplau (1952) – community mental health and deinstitutionalisation (1960s) – India: Lunacy Act 1912

answer_html:
(a) Definitions (3 marks)

  • Mental health (WHO) – "a state of mental well-being that enables people to cope with the stresses of life, realise their abilities, learn well and work well, and contribute to their community." It is more than the absence of mental disorders and is an integral part of health.
  • Mental illness (mental disorder) – a clinically significant disturbance in a person's thinking, emotion regulation or behaviour, usually associated with distress or impairment in important areas of functioning.
  • Mental health (psychiatric) nursing – the specialised area of nursing that promotes mental health, prevents mental illness and cares for people with mental disorders, using the theories of human behaviour as its science and the purposeful use of self as its art (therapeutic use of self), in hospital and community settings.

(b) Evolution of mental health services, treatment and nursing (8 marks) A. In the world

  1. Ancient period – mental illness was believed to be caused by evil spirits, gods or sorcery; treatments were magic, prayers, exorcism and trephining (making holes in the skull to let spirits escape).
  2. Greek and Roman period – Hippocrates (460–377 BC) gave a natural explanation: an imbalance of the four body humours; he described melancholia, mania and phrenitis and advised rest, diet and exercise. Temples of Aesculapius offered rest and pleasant surroundings.
  3. Middle Ages – return of demonology; mentally ill people were branded witches, tortured or burnt; others were chained in asylums (e.g. Bethlem – "Bedlam" – in London), often shown to the public for money.
  4. Renaissance and the humanitarian era
    • Philippe Pinel (1793) removed the chains of patients at Bicêtre and Salpêtrière in Paris – the beginning of humane, "moral" treatment.
    • William Tuke (1796) founded the York Retreat in England, with kindness, work and religious support.
    • Dorothea Dix (USA, 1840s) campaigned for state mental hospitals and better care.
  5. Scientific era (19th–20th century)
    • Emil Kraepelin classified mental disorders (dementia praecox and manic-depressive psychosis); Eugen Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia (1911).
    • Sigmund Freud developed psychoanalysis – the role of the unconscious and early experiences.
    • Physical treatments – insulin coma therapy, electroconvulsive therapy (Cerletti and Bini, 1938), psychosurgery.
  6. Psychopharmacological revolution – lithium for mania (John Cade, 1949), chlorpromazine (1952), then antidepressants (imipramine, MAO inhibitors) and benzodiazepines – patients could be treated and discharged.
  7. Community mental health movement (1960s onwards) – deinstitutionalisation, community mental health centres, rehabilitation, crisis intervention, and later the rights-based approach (UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, 2006) and WHO's Mental Health Action Plan.
  8. Psychiatric nursing
    • Early attendants were untrained "keepers".
    • Linda Richards, often called the first American psychiatric nurse, organised nursing care and training in mental hospitals in the 1880s; the first school for psychiatric nurses opened at McLean Hospital (USA, 1882).
    • Hildegard Peplau published Interpersonal Relations in Nursing (1952), describing the nurse–patient relationship as therapeutic – she is called the "mother of psychiatric nursing".
    • Psychiatric nursing became part of basic nursing curricula, with post-graduate specialisation, nurse therapists and advanced practice roles.

B. In India

  1. Ancient India – the Charaka Samhita described unmada (insanity) and its causes and treatment; Ayurveda and Yoga stressed the unity of mind and body; temples and dargahs served as places of healing.
  2. British period – mental asylums were set up in Bombay, Calcutta, Madras and other cities in the 18th–19th centuries mainly for custody; the Indian Lunacy Act (1912) governed admission and detention.
  3. Reforms – the European Mental Hospital at Ranchi (1918), now the Central Institute of Psychiatry, became a centre of modern psychiatry; the Indian Psychiatric Society was formed in 1947; the All India Institute of Mental Health, Bangalore (1954) grew into NIMHANS (1974).
  4. Nursing – a diploma course in psychiatric nursing was started at Bangalore in the 1950s; psychiatric nursing was later made compulsory in GNM and B.Sc. Nursing; M.Sc. and Ph.D. programmes in psychiatric nursing followed.
  5. Legislation and programmes
    • National Mental Health Programme (NMHP), 1982.
    • Mental Health Act, 1987 (replaced the Lunacy Act).
    • District Mental Health Programme (DMHP), 1996 – community-based care through district teams (first tried in Bellary, Karnataka).
    • National Mental Health Policy, 2014.
    • Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 – a rights-based law (in force from 2018) that guarantees access to mental health care and decriminalised attempted suicide.

(c) Present scenario of mental health care in India (4 marks)

  • Burden – the National Mental Health Survey (2015–16) found that about 10.6% of adults had a current mental disorder (lifetime 13.7%), with a treatment gap of about 70–92% for different disorders; depression, anxiety and substance use (alcohol, tobacco) are the commonest problems.
  • Shortage of professionals – very few psychiatrists, psychiatric nurses, psychologists and social workers for the population, mostly in cities.
  • Services – mental hospitals and NIMHANS-type institutes, psychiatric units in medical colleges and district hospitals, DMHP in almost all districts, mental health services at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (primary care), de-addiction centres, and NGOs.
  • Tele-mental health – Tele-MANAS (2022), a 24×7 toll-free helpline (14416) offering counselling in many Indian languages.
  • Policies – the National Suicide Prevention Strategy (2022) aims to reduce suicide deaths by 10% by 2030; mental health is part of school health (Ayushman Bharat School Health and Wellness), adolescent health (RKSK) and the national programme for the elderly.
  • Challenges – stigma and myths, belief in supernatural causes and faith healers, poor awareness, lack of rehabilitation services, homelessness of persons with mental illness, and limited funding.
  • Role of nurses – community mental health nursing, Tele-MANAS counselling, psychosocial rehabilitation, school and workplace mental health, and advocacy for the rights of persons with mental illness.

Changing trends in mental health nursing

  • From custodial to therapeutic care – from locking up and guarding patients to the therapeutic relationship, milieu therapy and active treatment.
  • From institution to community – shorter hospital stays, general hospital psychiatric units, DMHP, home care and rehabilitation in the community.
  • From illness to wellness and recovery – emphasis on mental health promotion, prevention, strengths and the recovery model.
  • From paternalism to rights – informed consent, advance directives and nominated representatives (MHCA 2017), least restrictive care, patient and family participation.
  • From generalist to specialist – post-basic, M.Sc. and Ph.D. programmes, nurse counsellors, nurse psychotherapists and community mental health nurse specialists.
  • Evidence-based and technology-supported practice – tele-psychiatry, Tele-MANAS, electronic records, digital mental health tools.
  • Focus on special groups – children and adolescents, women (perinatal mental health), the elderly, persons with substance use, the homeless and disaster survivors.

Nursing importance

  • Knowing how care moved from chains and custody to humane, scientific and community-based, rights-based care helps the nurse respect patients' dignity and work against the stigma that still delays treatment.

Conclusion Mental health is a state of well-being that lets people cope, work and contribute, and mental health nursing promotes it and cares for people with mental disorders. Care has evolved from demonology and chains, through Pinel's moral treatment, Kraepelin and Freud, ECT and the drug revolution, to community and rights-based care; nursing evolved from custodial attendants to Peplau's therapeutic relationship. In India, from Charaka and the Lunacy Act to NIMHANS, NMHP, DMHP, the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and Tele-MANAS, services have grown, but a large treatment gap, shortage of staff and stigma remain challenges for nurses to address.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Introduction
question: (a) Explain the nature and scope of mental health nursing. (4 marks) (b) Describe the mental health team. (3 marks) (c) Discuss the roles and functions of the mental health nurse in various settings and the factors affecting the level of nursing practice. (8 marks)
tags: factors affecting level of nursing practice

diagram.caption: The mental health team
labels: patient and family at the centre
peer support worker and community health workers (ASHA)

answer_html:
(a) Nature and scope of mental health nursing (4 marks) Nature

  • Holistic – it considers the biological, psychological, social and spiritual needs of the person, not only the diagnosis.
  • Interpersonal – the nurse–patient relationship and the therapeutic use of self are the main tools of care.
  • Based on behavioural sciences – psychology, sociology and psychiatry provide its scientific base.
  • Continuous and long-term – many mental disorders are chronic and relapsing, so care continues from hospital to home.
  • Team-based and rights-based – the nurse works with a multidisciplinary team and protects the dignity and rights of patients (Mental Healthcare Act 2017).
  • Preventive and promotive as well as curative – it works at all levels of prevention.

Scope

  • Hospital care – psychiatric hospitals, psychiatric units of general hospitals, emergency psychiatry, de-addiction centres, child and adolescent units, geriatric units, forensic wards.
  • Community care – DMHP, primary health care (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs), home care, day-care centres, half-way homes, rehabilitation centres, NGOs.
  • Special areas – school mental health, industrial (workplace) mental health, disaster mental health, prisons, homes for the elderly and the homeless, consultation–liaison psychiatry in general wards, tele-mental health (Tele-MANAS).
  • Education, administration and research – teaching, supervision, policy, nursing research.
  • Advanced and independent practice – nurse counsellors, nurse psychotherapists, family therapists, community mental health nurse specialists.

(b) The mental health team (3 marks) The team works together for the comprehensive care of the patient and family:

  1. Psychiatrist – diagnosis, prescribing medicines and physical treatments (ECT), leadership of the team, legal procedures.
  2. Psychiatric (mental health) nurse – 24-hour care, therapeutic relationship, observation, milieu management, medication, counselling, health education, rehabilitation and follow-up.
  3. Clinical psychologist – psychological assessment and testing, psychotherapy (behaviour therapy, CBT).
  4. Psychiatric social worker – social and family assessment, family counselling, linking with welfare schemes, rehabilitation and community resources.
  5. Occupational therapist – activities and work skills to improve functioning.
  6. Others – counsellors, recreational, art and music therapists, dietitian, special educator (for children), vocational instructor, peer support workers, ASHAs and community workers, and the family as partners in care.

(c) Roles and functions of the mental health nurse in various settings (8 marks) General roles

  • Care provider – meeting physical and psychological needs (hygiene, nutrition, sleep, safety).
  • Therapeutic agent – establishing a therapeutic nurse–patient relationship; individual counselling; group and family work.
  • Creator of a therapeutic milieu – a safe, accepting and structured ward environment.
  • Observer and recorder – accurate observation of behaviour, mood, speech, sleep and response to treatment.
  • Medication manager – safe administration, monitoring of side effects, adherence and education.
  • Health educator – patients, families and the community (illness, medicines, relapse signs, stigma).
  • Advocate – protecting patients' rights, informed consent, least restrictive care.
  • Case manager and coordinator – linking the patient with services, follow-up and rehabilitation.
  • Counsellor, consultant and liaison nurse; teacher, supervisor, manager and researcher.

Roles in specific settings

  1. Inpatient (hospital) setting – admission assessment, risk assessment (suicide, violence, absconding), observation levels, care during ECT, management of aggression with de-escalation and least restrictive methods, activity scheduling, discharge planning.
  2. Outpatient and emergency – triage, crisis intervention, brief counselling, depot injection clinics.
  3. Community setting (DMHP, primary care) – case detection and referral, home visits, follow-up and drug distribution, family psychoeducation, rehabilitation, awareness and anti-stigma campaigns, training of ASHAs and Anganwadi workers.
  4. School mental health – identifying learning, emotional and behavioural problems, life skills education, anti-bullying and anti-substance programmes, counselling of students and parents.
  5. Industrial (workplace) setting – stress management, prevention of burnout, alcohol and drug problems, employee assistance programmes.
  6. De-addiction centres – detoxification care, motivation enhancement, relapse prevention, family work.
  7. Child guidance clinics – assessment and care of children with developmental and behavioural problems, parent training.
  8. Geriatric setting – care of elderly persons with dementia, depression and delirium; carer support.
  9. Forensic settings – care of mentally ill prisoners, assessment, legal documentation.
  10. Disaster settings – psychological first aid, identifying people at risk of PTSD and depression, referral.
  11. Tele-mental health – counselling and follow-up through Tele-MANAS and telephone services.

Factors affecting the level of nursing practice

  • Educational preparation and competence of the nurse (basic, post-basic, specialist), continuing education.
  • Personal factors – the nurse's own attitudes, beliefs and stigma towards mental illness, self-awareness, emotional maturity and stress (burnout).
  • Work setting – type of institution, philosophy of care (custodial or therapeutic), nurse–patient ratio, workload, resources and infrastructure.
  • Role clarity and team relationships – recognition of the nurse's role by other professionals, delegation, autonomy.
  • Policies and legal framework – the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, institutional policies, job descriptions and INC standards.
  • Supervision, leadership and support – clinical supervision, mentorship, staff support systems.
  • Patient-related factors – acuity of illness, risk of violence, culture and family involvement.

Qualities of a mental health nurse

  • Self-awareness – understanding one's own feelings, values and prejudices so that they do not interfere with care.
  • Empathy, warmth and genuineness – understanding the patient's feelings while remaining real and sincere.
  • Non-judgemental acceptance and respect for the patient's dignity.
  • Patience, tolerance and emotional stability – remaining calm with difficult, hostile or withdrawn patients.
  • Good observation skills – noticing small changes in behaviour, mood, speech and sleep.
  • Effective communication and listening skills.
  • Consistency, honesty and trustworthiness; keeping promises.
  • Flexibility, creativity and a sense of humour.
  • Sound knowledge of psychiatry, drugs, law and ethics, and willingness to keep learning.
  • Team spirit, leadership and advocacy; ability to look after one's own mental health.

Functions of the nurse in the nursing process

  1. Assessment – history, mental status examination, risk assessment, physical assessment and family assessment.
  2. Nursing diagnosis – e.g. disturbed thought processes, risk for self-directed violence, social isolation, self-care deficit.
  3. Planning – realistic, measurable goals set with the patient and family.
  4. Implementation – therapeutic communication, milieu management, medication, activities, psychoeducation, skills training.
  5. Evaluation – reviewing progress, changing the plan and preparing for discharge and follow-up.

Levels of mental health nursing practice

  • Basic level – the registered nurse provides direct care: assessment, therapeutic relationship, milieu management, medication, health teaching, crisis care, case management and rehabilitation.
  • Advanced level – the nurse with a master's or higher degree in psychiatric nursing functions as a clinical nurse specialist or nurse practitioner: individual, group and family psychotherapy, consultation–liaison in general hospitals, supervision, teaching, research and programme management.

Nursing importance

  • The mental health nurse spends the most time with the patient, so her skills in relationship-building, observation and advocacy decide the quality of care and influence recovery.

Conclusion Mental health nursing is a holistic, interpersonal, team-based and rights-based speciality whose scope extends from hospitals to communities, schools, workplaces, prisons, disaster areas and tele-health. Working with psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, occupational therapists and families, the nurse acts as care provider, therapeutic agent, milieu manager, educator, advocate, case manager and researcher, and her level of practice depends on her education, attitudes, work setting, policies, supervision and team support.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Introduction
question: Explain the concepts of normal and abnormal behaviour.
answer_html:
Introduction There is no sharp line between normal and abnormal behaviour – they lie on a continuum, and judgement depends on the person, the situation and the culture. Several criteria are used together to decide whether behaviour is abnormal.

Normal behaviour

  • Behaviour that is appropriate to the situation, acceptable in the person's culture, and allows the person to function effectively – work, relate to others, care for oneself and cope with stress.
  • Characteristics – realistic perception of reality, self-awareness and self-acceptance, emotional stability, ability to form satisfying relationships, productivity, autonomy and adaptability (Jahoda's criteria of positive mental health).

Abnormal behaviour Behaviour that is deviant, distressing, dysfunctional or dangerous – the "four Ds":

  1. Deviance – markedly different from what is usual or accepted in the society (e.g. talking to oneself loudly in public).
  2. Distress – causes suffering to the person (anxiety, sadness) or to others.
  3. Dysfunction – interferes with daily functioning – work, study, self-care, relationships.
  4. Danger – to self (suicide, self-neglect) or to others (violence).

Criteria (models) used to judge abnormality

  • Statistical criterion – behaviour that is rare or far from the average (but some rare traits, like high intelligence, are not abnormal).
  • Social norm criterion – behaviour that violates the norms of the society (norms differ between cultures and change over time).
  • Subjective distress criterion – the person feels unhappy or anxious (but some ill persons, e.g. in mania, feel no distress).
  • Maladaptiveness (impairment) criterion – behaviour that prevents the person from adapting to life's demands – the most useful practical criterion.
  • Ideal mental health criterion – deviation from positive mental health.
  • Medical (clinical) criterion – presence of signs and symptoms that fit a recognised diagnosis (ICD-11 or DSM-5-TR).
  • Legal criterion – unsoundness of mind as decided by courts.

Points to remember

  • Cultural context – possession states during religious festivals or hearing the voice of God in prayer may be normal in their setting.
  • Context and duration – grief after a death is normal; prolonged, disabling grief may not be.
  • Labelling someone "abnormal" carries stigma, so judgement must be careful and respectful.

Nursing importance

  • Understanding these criteria helps the nurse observe behaviour objectively, avoid judging patients by personal standards, consider culture, and recognise when a change in behaviour needs professional help.

Conclusion Normal and abnormal behaviour lie on a continuum. Behaviour is considered abnormal when it is deviant, distressing, dysfunctional or dangerous, judged by statistical, social, subjective, adaptive, ideal, medical and legal criteria, always keeping the person's culture and context in mind.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Introduction
question: Explain the myths and misconceptions about mental illness and the role of the nurse in reducing stigma.
answer_html:
Introduction Myths and misconceptions about mental illness are widespread in India and lead to stigma – negative attitudes and discrimination – which delays treatment, isolates patients and families and worsens outcomes.

Common myths and the facts

  1. Myth – Mental illness is caused by evil spirits, black magic, sins or bad karma. Fact – it results from a combination of biological (genes, brain chemistry), psychological and social factors, and it is treatable.

  2. Myth – Mentally ill people are violent and dangerous. Fact – most are not violent; they are more often victims of violence and abuse.

  3. Myth – Mental illness cannot be cured. Fact – most people improve with treatment; many recover fully and lead productive lives.

  4. Myth – Marriage will cure mental illness. Fact – marriage does not treat illness; hiding illness before marriage often causes suffering for both families.

  5. Myth – Mental illness is a sign of weakness; the person can "snap out of it". Fact – it is an illness, like diabetes, needing care and support.

  6. Myth – Psychiatric medicines are "sleeping pills", addictive and damage the brain. Fact – most (antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilisers) are not addictive and are safe when taken as prescribed and monitored.

  7. Myth – ECT is a punishment or "shock" that damages the brain. Fact – modern ECT is given under anaesthesia with muscle relaxants and is a safe, effective treatment for certain conditions.

  8. Myth – Mental illness and intellectual disability are the same. Fact – they are different conditions.

  9. Myth – Children do not have mental health problems. Fact – many mental disorders begin in childhood and adolescence.

  10. Myth – Only "mad" people go to a psychiatrist. Fact – psychiatrists treat common problems such as stress, sleep problems, anxiety and depression.

  11. Myth – Mental illness is contagious or always runs in families. Fact – it is not contagious; genes increase risk but do not decide it alone.

Effects of myths and stigma

  • Delay in seeking treatment and preference for faith healers; poor adherence to medicines.
  • Self-stigma – shame, low self-esteem, hiding illness.
  • Discrimination in jobs, marriage, housing and education; social isolation; family burden.

Role of the nurse in reducing stigma

  • Education – correct information to patients, families, schools and communities through talks, posters, street plays and media.
  • Contact – opportunities for the public to meet people who have recovered (contact is one of the most effective anti-stigma methods).
  • Model respectful behaviour – use person-first language ("a person with schizophrenia", not "a schizophrenic"), maintain confidentiality and dignity.
  • Support families – psychoeducation and support groups; reduce blame.
  • Work with faith healers and community leaders for early referral.
  • Advocacy – promote the rights given by the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (including protection from cruel treatment and discrimination); oppose chaining and abuse.
  • Integrate mental health into general health care so that it becomes part of routine services.

Conclusion Myths that mental illness is caused by spirits, is incurable, makes people violent or can be cured by marriage are common and lead to stigma, delayed treatment and discrimination. Nurses reduce stigma by educating, enabling contact, modelling respect, supporting families, working with community leaders and advocating for patients' rights.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Introduction
question: Explain the prevalence and burden of mental disorders in India.
answer_html:
Introduction Mental disorders are common in every country and are among the leading causes of disability. WHO's World Mental Health Report (2022) estimated that about 1 in 8 people worldwide (970 million in 2019) live with a mental disorder, anxiety and depression being the commonest.

Prevalence in India

  1. National Mental Health Survey (NMHS) 2015–16 (NIMHANS, 12 states)
    • Current prevalence of mental disorders in adults – about 10.6%; lifetime prevalence – about 13.7%.
    • About 150 million Indians needed active care.
    • Common mental disorders (depression, anxiety, phobias) and substance use disorders (alcohol, tobacco) were the most frequent; prevalence was higher in urban metros, among middle-aged adults, and in people with lower income and education.
    • Treatment gap – about 70–92% for different disorders.
    • Prevalence among adolescents (13–17 years) about 7%.
  2. India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative (2017 data) – about 197 million Indians (1 in 7) had a mental disorder, depressive and anxiety disorders being the commonest; the contribution of mental disorders to total disease burden doubled between 1990 and 2017.
  3. Severe mental disorders – schizophrenia, other psychoses and bipolar disorder each affect a smaller proportion (well under 1% of adults at any time) but cause the greatest disability.
  4. Suicide – India records more than 1.7 lakh suicides a year (NCRB, 2022), many linked to depression, alcohol use, family and financial problems.

Burden of mental disorders

  • Disability – mental disorders are a leading cause of years lived with disability; they begin early (half by about 14 years of age) and often last for life.
  • Mortality – suicide, and early death from physical illnesses (people with severe mental illness die years earlier).
  • Family burden – caregiving stress, financial strain, stigma.
  • Economic burden – loss of productivity and income, cost of care.
  • Social burden – homelessness, unemployment, school drop-out, crime and victimisation.
  • Comorbidity – with diabetes, heart disease, HIV, TB and substance use.

Reasons for the large treatment gap

  • Lack of awareness, stigma, belief in supernatural causes; shortage and uneven distribution of professionals and services; cost and distance; poor integration with primary care.

Implications for nursing

  • Early identification and referral in community and primary care; training of ASHAs; nurse-led counselling and follow-up (DMHP, Tele-MANAS); suicide prevention; family psychoeducation; research and advocacy for more services.

Conclusion About one in ten Indian adults has a current mental disorder (NMHS 2015–16), and about one in seven Indians was affected in 2017, mostly by depression, anxiety and substance use. With a treatment gap of 70–92%, mental disorders cause a heavy burden of disability, suicide, family stress and economic loss, which nurses can reduce through early detection, community care and awareness.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Introduction
question: Who was Philippe Pinel? State his contribution to psychiatry.
answer_html:
Philippe Pinel (1745–1826) was a French physician regarded as one of the founders of modern psychiatry.

  • In 1793 at the Bicêtre hospital (and later at the Salpêtrière) in Paris, he removed the chains from mentally ill patients and replaced cruelty with kindness, understanding and humane treatment – the beginning of "moral treatment".
  • He observed patients carefully, kept case records, classified mental disorders and wrote a treatise on insanity.
  • He believed that mental illness could be treated and that patients should be respected. His work inspired similar reforms (William Tuke's York Retreat) and laid the foundation of humane psychiatric care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Introduction
question: Write the contribution of Hildegard Peplau to psychiatric nursing.
answer_html:
Hildegard E. Peplau (1909–1999), an American nurse, is called the "mother of psychiatric nursing".

  • In 1952 she published Interpersonal Relations in Nursing, presenting nursing as a therapeutic interpersonal process.
  • She described the phases of the nurse–patient relationship – orientation, identification, exploitation and resolution.
  • She described the roles of the nurse – stranger, resource person, teacher, leader, surrogate and counsellor.
  • She explained the levels of anxiety (mild, moderate, severe, panic) and how the nurse helps patients cope.
  • She developed graduate education in psychiatric nursing and the role of the nurse psychotherapist.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Introduction
question: Write the WHO definition of mental health.
answer_html:
WHO definition – "Mental health is a state of mental well-being that enables people to cope with the stresses of life, realise their abilities, learn well and work well, and contribute to their community." It is an integral part of health and well-being and is more than the absence of mental disorders. Key features

  • It exists on a continuum from optimal well-being to severe distress.
  • It is influenced by individual (biological, psychological), social, economic and environmental factors.
  • It allows a person to make decisions, build relationships and shape the world they live in.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: (a) What is the need for classification of mental disorders? (3 marks) (b) Describe the classification of mental disorders according to ICD-11. (7 marks) (c) Explain DSM-5-TR and compare it with ICD-11. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: Main groups of ICD-11 Chapter 06 (mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders)
labels: neurodevelopmental; schizophrenia and other primary psychotic; catatonia; mood (bipolar

depressive); anxiety or fear-related; obsessive-compulsive or related; disorders specifically associated with stress; dissociative; feeding or eating; elimination; bodily distress; substance use or addictive behaviours; impulse control; disruptive or dissocial; personality; paraphilic; factitious; neurocognitive; disorders associated with pregnancy and the puerperium; secondary mental syndromes

answer_html:
(a) Need for classification (3 marks) Classification arranges mental disorders into groups on the basis of their features, using agreed diagnostic criteria. It is needed for:

  1. A common language – professionals in different places understand the same diagnosis in the same way.
  2. Diagnosis and treatment planning – each category guides treatment and indicates prognosis.
  3. Communication and record keeping – case notes, referrals, insurance and legal documents.
  4. Statistics and epidemiology – counting cases, planning services and comparing countries.
  5. Research – comparing groups of patients and evaluating treatments.
  6. Education – teaching students a systematic approach.
  7. Legal and administrative purposes – disability certification, mental health law, health insurance. The two main systems are the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) of the World Health Organization and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) of the American Psychiatric Association.

(b) ICD-11 classification (7 marks)

  • ICD-11 was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2019 and came into effect on 1 January 2022, replacing ICD-10.
  • Mental disorders are in Chapter 06 – "Mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders" (codes beginning with 6A–6E). Sleep–wake disorders and conditions related to sexual health (including gender incongruence) have been moved to separate chapters.

Main groups in Chapter 06

  1. Neurodevelopmental disorders – disorders of intellectual development, autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, developmental learning and speech disorders, tic disorders.
  2. Schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders – schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, schizotypal disorder, acute and transient psychotic disorder, delusional disorder.
  3. Catatonia – associated with another mental disorder or induced by substances.
  4. Mood disorders – bipolar or related disorders (bipolar type I, type II, cyclothymia) and depressive disorders (single episode, recurrent, dysthymic disorder, mixed depressive and anxiety disorder).
  5. Anxiety or fear-related disorders – generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder, agoraphobia, specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, separation anxiety disorder.
  6. Obsessive-compulsive or related disorders – OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hypochondriasis, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania.
  7. Disorders specifically associated with stress – post-traumatic stress disorder, complex PTSD, prolonged grief disorder, adjustment disorder.
  8. Dissociative disorders – dissociative neurological symptom disorder (conversion), dissociative amnesia, trance and possession trance disorder, dissociative identity disorder.
  9. Feeding or eating disorders – anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, pica.
  10. Elimination disorders – enuresis, encopresis.
  11. Disorders of bodily distress or bodily experience – bodily distress disorder.
  12. Disorders due to substance use or addictive behaviours – alcohol, cannabis, opioids, tobacco and others; gambling disorder and gaming disorder.
  13. Impulse control disorders – pyromania, kleptomania, intermittent explosive disorder, compulsive sexual behaviour disorder.
  14. Disruptive behaviour or dissocial disorders – oppositional defiant disorder, conduct-dissocial disorder.
  15. Personality disorders and related traits – classified by severity (mild, moderate, severe) with trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia) and a borderline pattern specifier.
  16. Paraphilic disorders.
  17. Factitious disorders.
  18. Neurocognitive disorders – delirium, mild neurocognitive disorder, amnestic disorder, dementia.
  19. Mental or behavioural disorders associated with pregnancy, childbirth or the puerperium.
  20. Secondary mental or behavioural syndromes associated with disorders or diseases classified elsewhere.

Important changes in ICD-11

  • Subtypes of schizophrenia (paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic, etc.) are removed and replaced by symptom specifiers (positive, negative, depressive, manic, psychomotor and cognitive symptoms).
  • New diagnoses – complex PTSD, prolonged grief disorder, gaming disorder, hoarding disorder, compulsive sexual behaviour disorder.
  • A dimensional approach to personality disorders.
  • Bipolar type II disorder is recognised separately; catatonia is a separate group.
  • Clinical descriptions and diagnostic requirements suitable for use in all countries, including primary care.

(c) DSM-5-TR and comparison with ICD-11 (5 marks) DSM-5-TR

  • Published by the American Psychiatric Association; DSM-5 appeared in 2013 and the text revision (DSM-5-TR) in 2022.
  • Section I – basics and use of the manual; Section II – diagnostic criteria and codes in about 20 diagnostic classes (e.g. schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders, bipolar and related, depressive, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive and related, trauma- and stressor-related, dissociative, somatic symptom and related, sleep–wake, substance-related and addictive, neurocognitive and personality disorders); Section III – emerging measures and models (cultural formulation interview, alternative model for personality disorders, conditions for further study).
  • The multiaxial system has been removed; diagnoses are recorded with specifiers and severity ratings.
  • DSM-5-TR added prolonged grief disorder and codes for suicidal behaviour and non-suicidal self-injury.

Comparison of ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR

  • Publisher – ICD-11: World Health Organization; DSM-5-TR: American Psychiatric Association.
  • Scope – ICD-11 classifies all diseases (mental disorders in Chapter 06); DSM covers only mental disorders.
  • Use – ICD is the official system for health statistics in India and worldwide, free to use; DSM is used mainly in the USA and in research.
  • Approach – ICD-11 gives flexible clinical descriptions and diagnostic requirements; DSM-5-TR gives operational criteria with exact symptom counts and durations.
  • Some differences – schizophrenia: symptom duration of 1 month in ICD-11 versus 6 months of disturbance in DSM-5-TR; ICD-11 has complex PTSD and a dimensional personality model, while DSM-5-TR keeps categorical personality disorders in Section II.
  • Similarities – both are descriptive, avoid assumptions about cause, use similar groupings and have been harmonised in many areas.

Nursing implications

  • Knowing the diagnosis helps the nurse anticipate symptoms, risks and treatment; but the nurse plans care by nursing diagnoses (e.g. disturbed thought processes, risk for suicide) based on the patient's individual responses, avoiding labelling and stigma.

Classification in ICD-10 (still seen in older records and textbooks) In ICD-10 (WHO, 1992), mental disorders formed Chapter V (F00–F99):

  • F00–F09 – organic, including symptomatic, mental disorders (dementia, delirium).
  • F10–F19 – mental and behavioural disorders due to psychoactive substance use.
  • F20–F29 – schizophrenia, schizotypal and delusional disorders.
  • F30–F39 – mood (affective) disorders.
  • F40–F48 – neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders.
  • F50–F59 – behavioural syndromes associated with physiological disturbances (eating, sleep, sexual dysfunction).
  • F60–F69 – disorders of adult personality and behaviour.
  • F70–F79 – mental retardation (now "disorders of intellectual development").
  • F80–F89 – disorders of psychological development.
  • F90–F98 – behavioural and emotional disorders with onset in childhood and adolescence.
  • F99 – unspecified mental disorder.

Limitations of classification

  • Labelling and stigma – a diagnosis can be misused to label the person rather than describe the condition.
  • Overlap and comorbidity – many patients meet criteria for more than one disorder; boundaries between categories are not sharp.
  • Categories versus dimensions – symptoms exist on a continuum, which fixed categories may not reflect.
  • Cultural bias – criteria developed in one culture may not fit another; cultural formulation is needed.
  • Classification describes disorders but does not explain their causes or the person's unique experience.

Conclusion Classification provides a common language for diagnosis, treatment, statistics, research and legal purposes. ICD-11 (WHO, in effect since 2022) places mental disorders in Chapter 06 with about twenty groups and introduces changes such as removal of schizophrenia subtypes, complex PTSD and dimensional personality disorders. DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022) uses operational criteria in about twenty diagnostic classes without the multiaxial system; the two systems are broadly similar, ICD being the official system in India.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: (a) Explain the biological factors in the aetiology of mental disorders. (6 marks) (b) Explain the psychological factors. (5 marks) (c) Explain the socio-cultural factors, with reference to the biopsychosocial and stress–vulnerability models. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Biopsychosocial model of mental illness
labels: social support) – mental disorder at the centre where they overlap

answer_html:
Introduction Mental disorders do not have a single cause. They result from an interaction of biological, psychological and social factors acting on a vulnerable person – the biopsychosocial model (George Engel, 1977).

(a) Biological factors (6 marks)

  1. Genetic factors
    • Family, twin and adoption studies show that many disorders run in families.
    • Heritability is high in schizophrenia (about 80%) and bipolar disorder (about 60–85%), and moderate in depression (about 35–40%); the risk of schizophrenia is about 10% in a child with one affected parent and about 40–50% in an identical twin.
    • Inheritance is polygenic (many genes of small effect), interacting with the environment; some disorders have specific genetic causes (Down syndrome, fragile X syndrome).
  2. Neuroanatomical factors
    • Changes in the limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus, hypothalamus), prefrontal cortex and basal ganglia.
    • Schizophrenia – enlarged ventricles, reduced grey matter; depression and PTSD – smaller hippocampus; anxiety – overactive amygdala; OCD – overactivity of the orbitofrontal cortex–basal ganglia circuit.
  3. Neurochemical factors (neurotransmitters)
    • Dopamine – excess in the mesolimbic pathway in schizophrenia (positive symptoms) and mania.
    • Serotonin and noradrenaline – reduced in depression; serotonin also in anxiety and OCD.
    • GABA – reduced inhibitory activity in anxiety disorders.
    • Glutamate – NMDA receptor hypofunction in schizophrenia.
    • Acetylcholine – reduced in Alzheimer's dementia.
  4. Neuroendocrine factors – overactivity of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis (raised cortisol) in depression; thyroid disorders causing anxiety or depression; hormonal changes after childbirth (postpartum disorders) and in the premenstrual phase.
  5. Neurodevelopmental factors – maternal infections (influenza, rubella), malnutrition and stress in pregnancy, obstetric complications (hypoxia at birth), low birth weight – increase the risk of schizophrenia and neurodevelopmental disorders.
  6. Physical illnesses and brain insults – head injury, epilepsy, brain tumours, infections (encephalitis, HIV, neurosyphilis), stroke, metabolic and endocrine disorders, Vitamin B12 deficiency.
  7. Substances and medicines – alcohol, cannabis (psychosis), stimulants, opioids; steroids and some other medicines causing mood changes.
  8. Other – disturbed circadian rhythms (seasonal and bipolar mood changes), inflammatory and immune changes, ageing (dementia).

(b) Psychological factors (5 marks)

  1. Psychoanalytic (psychodynamic) factors – Freud: unresolved unconscious conflicts, fixation at early psychosexual stages and excessive use of defence mechanisms produce symptoms (e.g. anxiety in neurosis).
  2. Learning (behavioural) factors – maladaptive behaviour is learned through classical conditioning (a phobia after a frightening experience), operant conditioning (behaviour maintained by reward or relief) and modelling (learning from parents).
  3. Cognitive factors – negative automatic thoughts and distorted thinking; Beck's cognitive triad (negative views of self, world and future) in depression; catastrophic thinking in panic disorder; learned helplessness (Seligman).
  4. Early childhood experiences – maternal deprivation, insecure attachment, loss of a parent, child abuse and neglect, harsh or inconsistent parenting.
  5. Personality factors – anxious, perfectionist, dependent or emotionally unstable traits (high neuroticism) increase vulnerability.
  6. Stress and life events – death of a close person, failure in examinations, unemployment, divorce, migration; the cumulative effect of stressful events (Holmes and Rahe).
  7. Poor coping skills and low self-esteem, and interpersonal problems (Sullivan's interpersonal theory).

(c) Socio-cultural factors and models (4 marks) Socio-cultural factors

  • Poverty, unemployment, debt and low education – both cause and result of mental illness (farmers' distress and suicides).
  • Family factors – broken families, marital conflict, domestic violence, alcoholism in a parent, high "expressed emotion" (criticism, hostility, over-involvement) which increases relapse in schizophrenia.
  • Urbanisation and migration – loss of the joint-family support system, loneliness, overcrowding.
  • Gender – women face domestic violence, dowry harassment and dual burden of work; men have higher rates of substance use and suicide.
  • Social isolation, discrimination and stigma; war, disasters, terrorism and pandemics.
  • Culture – shapes symptoms and help-seeking; culture-bound syndromes such as dhat syndrome (anxiety about loss of semen) in South Asia, possession states and koro outbreaks.
  • Availability of alcohol and drugs; excessive use of social media and gaming in adolescents.

Models that integrate these factors

  • Biopsychosocial model – illness results from the interaction of biological, psychological and social factors, so treatment must address all three.
  • Stress–vulnerability (diathesis–stress) model (Zubin and Spring) – each person has a certain vulnerability (genes, brain development, early experiences); illness appears when stress exceeds the person's threshold; protective factors (coping skills, social support, treatment) raise the threshold.
  • The "4 Ps" formulation – predisposing (genes, childhood adversity), precipitating (life events, substance use), perpetuating (ongoing stress, poor adherence, family conflict) and protective factors (support, skills, faith).

Nursing implications

  • Holistic assessment of all three areas; reducing stressors and expressed emotion through family psychoeducation; teaching coping skills; promoting adherence; early intervention in high-risk groups; and preventive work in the community (maternal care, child protection, substance prevention).

Application of aetiology to common disorders (examples)

  • Schizophrenia – strong genetic loading, neurodevelopmental insults (obstetric complications), dopamine and glutamate dysfunction, enlarged ventricles; precipitated by stress or cannabis; relapse increased by high expressed emotion and stopping medicines.
  • Depression – moderate genetic risk, serotonin and noradrenaline deficiency, raised cortisol, smaller hippocampus; negative thinking and learned helplessness; precipitated by loss, chronic illness, poverty, domestic violence; protected by social support.
  • Bipolar disorder – high heritability, disturbed circadian rhythms, dopamine and noradrenaline changes; episodes triggered by sleep loss, stress, antidepressants or substances.
  • Anxiety disorders and phobias – inherited anxious temperament, overactive amygdala, low GABA; conditioning after frightening events; overprotective parenting; avoidance maintains the fear.
  • Obsessive-compulsive disorder – genetic factors, serotonin dysfunction, overactive orbitofrontal–basal ganglia circuit; compulsions maintained by relief of anxiety (negative reinforcement).
  • Alcohol and drug dependence – genetic vulnerability, dopamine reward pathway, peer pressure, easy availability, family history and stress.

Protective factors

  • Secure attachment and supportive family, good physical health and nutrition, education and employment, coping and problem-solving skills, self-esteem, faith and spirituality, social networks, and timely access to health care.

Common precipitating and perpetuating factors seen in practice

  • Precipitating (triggering) factors – sudden loss or bereavement, examination failure, financial loss, marital conflict, childbirth, physical illness or surgery, lack of sleep, alcohol or cannabis use, migration or a sudden change of environment, and stopping medicines in a person already ill.
  • Perpetuating (maintaining) factors – continuing stress at home or work, poor adherence to treatment, high expressed emotion in the family, substance use, social isolation, stigma that delays help-seeking, and lack of follow-up and rehabilitation services.
  • Recognising these factors allows the nurse to target interventions – sleep hygiene, adherence counselling, family psychoeducation and relapse prevention plans.

Spiritual and existential factors

  • Loss of meaning and purpose, guilt, hopelessness and spiritual distress can contribute to depression and suicidal thoughts, while faith, prayer, meditation and belonging to a supportive religious community often act as protective factors.
  • In India many families first approach temples, dargahs or faith healers; the nurse respects these beliefs while explaining the need for medical treatment, and can involve spiritual leaders as partners in early referral.

Conclusion Mental disorders result from the interaction of biological factors (genes, brain structure, neurotransmitters, hormones, neurodevelopmental insults, illnesses and substances), psychological factors (unconscious conflicts, learning, cognitive distortions, early experiences, personality, stress and coping) and socio-cultural factors (poverty, family, migration, gender, culture). The biopsychosocial and stress–vulnerability models explain how these combine, and guide holistic nursing care and prevention.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the conceptual models used in psychiatric nursing – psychoanalytic, interpersonal, behavioural and existential – with the role of the nurse in each. Add a note on the other models.

diagram.caption: Conceptual models in psychiatric nursing – view of behaviour and therapy
labels: interpretation; interpersonal: anxiety from relationships – therapeutic relationship; behavioural: learned behaviour – behaviour modification; existential: alienation from self – self-awareness
finding meaning; social: environment – crisis intervention

answer_html:
Introduction A conceptual model is a set of ideas that explains why people behave as they do, what causes mental illness and how it should be treated. Each model defines the roles of the patient and the therapist, and guides nursing care. In practice, nurses use an eclectic approach – combining useful parts of several models.

1. Psychoanalytic model

  • Theorists – Sigmund Freud; later Erik Erikson, Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, Melanie Klein.
  • View of behaviour – behaviour is determined by unconscious forces and early childhood experiences; the personality has three parts – id, ego and superego; anxiety arises from conflicts between them; the ego uses defence mechanisms; symptoms result from unresolved conflicts and fixation at psychosexual stages.
  • Therapeutic process – long-term psychoanalysis: free association, dream analysis, analysis of transference and resistance, and interpretation to bring unconscious conflicts into awareness (insight).
  • Roles – patient verbalises all thoughts and dreams; therapist listens, remains neutral and interprets.
  • Role of the nurse
    • Understand that behaviour has meaning; recognise defence mechanisms, transference and countertransference.
    • Help the patient express feelings and gain insight; avoid judging.
    • Apply developmental concepts (e.g. Erikson's stages) in assessment and planning.
  • Limitations – long and costly, needs specialists, difficult to test scientifically, less useful in severe psychosis.

2. Interpersonal model

  • Theorists – Harry Stack Sullivan (psychiatrist) and Hildegard Peplau (nurse).
  • View of behaviour – personality develops through interpersonal relationships; behaviour is shaped by the need for satisfaction and security; anxiety arises from fear of rejection and disapproval in relationships; mental illness results from disturbed relationships.
  • Therapeutic process – a corrective interpersonal experience in a trusting relationship, in which the patient learns healthier ways of relating.
  • Roles – patient shares concerns and takes part in the relationship; therapist is a participant observer.
  • Role of the nurse (Peplau)
    • Build a therapeutic nurse–patient relationship through the phases of orientation, identification, exploitation and resolution.
    • Take roles of stranger, resource person, teacher, leader, surrogate and counsellor.
    • Assess and reduce levels of anxiety; help the patient develop trust, communicate and relate to others.
  • This model forms the foundation of psychiatric nursing.

3. Behavioural model

  • Theorists – Ivan Pavlov (classical conditioning), J. B. Watson, B. F. Skinner (operant conditioning), Joseph Wolpe (systematic desensitisation), Hans Eysenck, Albert Bandura (social learning).
  • View of behaviour – all behaviour, normal or abnormal, is learned; maladaptive behaviour results from faulty learning and is maintained by its consequences; the symptom itself is the problem.
  • Therapeutic process – behaviour therapy / behaviour modification – unlearning maladaptive behaviour and learning adaptive behaviour: positive reinforcement, token economy, systematic desensitisation, flooding, aversion therapy, modelling, assertiveness and social skills training.
  • Roles – patient practises new behaviours; therapist designs and teaches the programme.
  • Role of the nurse
    • Observe and record target behaviours (baseline); reinforce desired behaviour consistently; ignore or set limits on undesired behaviour.
    • Carry out token economy and skills training programmes in the ward; teach relaxation; involve the family so that changes continue at home.
  • Strengths – short-term, measurable and effective for phobias, OCD, habit disorders and in rehabilitation.

4. Existential model

  • Theorists – Carl Rogers (client-centred therapy), Viktor Frankl (logotherapy), Fritz Perls (gestalt therapy), William Glasser (reality therapy), Albert Ellis (rational emotive therapy).
  • View of behaviour – the person is free and responsible for his choices; illness arises when he is alienated from himself and others, lacks self-awareness and meaning in life, and lives according to others' expectations.
  • Therapeutic process – helping the person become aware of himself, accept responsibility, make choices and find meaning: client-centred therapy (unconditional positive regard, empathy, genuineness), logotherapy, gestalt therapy (awareness of the "here and now"), reality therapy and rational emotive therapy.
  • Roles – patient takes responsibility; therapist is a genuine, accepting guide in an equal relationship.
  • Role of the nurse
    • Show genuineness, unconditional acceptance and empathy; encourage self-exploration and honest expression.
    • Help the patient identify values and goals, make choices and accept responsibility; use the "here and now".
    • Support spiritual and existential concerns (meaning, hope).

5. Other models (in brief)

  • Social model (Gerald Caplan, Thomas Szasz) – social conditions, poverty and labelling cause and maintain illness; therapy: crisis intervention, environmental change, social support, community psychiatry; nurse works in the community, mobilises resources and advocates.
  • Communication model (Eric Berne – transactional analysis; Paul Watzlawick) – disturbed communication leads to problems; therapy improves communication patterns (parent–adult–child ego states); nurse models clear communication and gives feedback.
  • Medical (biological) model – mental illness is a disease of the brain with genetic and biochemical causes; diagnosis by ICD/DSM; treatment with drugs, ECT and other physical therapies; nurse observes, administers treatment, monitors side effects and educates.
  • Cognitive model (Aaron Beck, Albert Ellis) – distorted thoughts lead to emotional disturbance; cognitive behaviour therapy corrects them; nurse helps identify and challenge negative thoughts.
  • Nursing models – Peplau's interpersonal theory, Orem's self-care model, Roy's adaptation model and Neuman's systems model guide holistic care through the nursing process.

Application of the models – example of a patient with depression

  • Psychoanalytic – depression is seen as anger turned inward after a loss; the nurse encourages the patient to express grief and anger.
  • Interpersonal – depression follows disturbed relationships or role changes; the nurse builds a trusting relationship and helps the patient improve relationships (as in interpersonal therapy).
  • Behavioural – depression is maintained by lack of rewarding activities; the nurse plans pleasant activities (behavioural activation) and reinforces efforts.
  • Cognitive – negative thoughts about self, world and future cause depression; the nurse helps identify and challenge them.
  • Existential – the patient has lost meaning and purpose; the nurse helps him explore values and find meaning.
  • Social – poverty, isolation or loss of job contribute; the nurse links him with social support and community resources.
  • Medical – depression is due to reduced serotonin and noradrenaline; the nurse gives antidepressants or assists with ECT and monitors response. Using these views together (eclectic approach) gives the most complete care.

Evaluation of the models

  • Psychoanalytic – deep understanding of inner conflicts, but long, costly and difficult to test.
  • Interpersonal – practical and central to nursing, but needs time and skill to build relationships.
  • Behavioural – short, measurable and effective, but may ignore underlying feelings.
  • Existential – respects freedom and dignity, but less suitable for severely disturbed patients.
  • Medical – effective treatments and clear diagnosis, but may neglect psychosocial needs and can increase labelling.

Nursing importance

  • No single model explains all mental illness. Knowing the models allows the nurse to understand behaviour from several angles and to choose suitable interventions – relationship (interpersonal), insight (psychoanalytic), skills and reinforcement (behavioural), meaning and responsibility (existential), medication and physical care (medical) and community support (social).

Conclusion The psychoanalytic model explains behaviour through unconscious conflict and treats by insight; the interpersonal model sees illness in disturbed relationships and treats through the therapeutic relationship; the behavioural model treats learned maladaptive behaviour by behaviour modification; and the existential model helps the alienated person find self-awareness, responsibility and meaning. With the social, communication, medical, cognitive and nursing models, these give the psychiatric nurse an eclectic framework for holistic care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the principles of mental health nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction The principles of mental health nursing are basic guidelines that help the nurse provide safe, effective and humane care to persons with mental illness.

Principles

  1. Accept the patient as he is – accept the person (not necessarily the behaviour) without judging, criticising or rejecting; behaviour has meaning and is the patient's way of coping.
  2. Respect the dignity and rights of the patient – address by name, ensure privacy and confidentiality, informed consent, the least restrictive care, and the rights given by the Mental Healthcare Act 2017.
  3. Use self therapeutically – self-awareness of one's own feelings, attitudes and prejudices; genuineness, empathy and warmth.
  4. Establish a therapeutic nurse–patient relationship – trust, clear limits and goals, termination planned in advance.
  5. Be consistent – consistent approach, rules and routines by all staff give security and reduce manipulation.
  6. Reassure honestly – reassurance based on facts and actions rather than false promises.
  7. Avoid unnecessary physical force and verbal punishment – use de-escalation; restraint only as a last resort, as per law and policy.
  8. Maintain safety – of the patient, other patients and staff (suicide and violence precautions, safe environment, observation).
  9. Help the patient to test and maintain contact with reality – do not argue with or agree to delusions; present reality gently.
  10. Encourage the patient's participation and independence – involve him in planning care and decisions; gradually increase responsibility.
  11. Individualised and holistic care – consider physical, psychological, social, cultural and spiritual needs; physical health care is not neglected.
  12. Observe and record accurately – behaviour, mood, speech, sleep, food intake and response to treatment, in objective language.
  13. Use simple, clear communication – explain procedures; listen actively.
  14. Involve the family – education, support and partnership in care and rehabilitation.
  15. Work as a team member and follow legal and ethical standards.

Nursing importance

  • These principles guide every interaction – from admission to discharge – and help create a therapeutic environment in which patients feel safe, respected and understood.

Conclusion The main principles of mental health nursing are acceptance, respect for dignity and rights, therapeutic use of self, a therapeutic relationship, consistency, honest reassurance, avoidance of force, safety, reality orientation, patient participation, individualised holistic care, accurate observation, clear communication, family involvement and teamwork.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the primary prevention of mental illness and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Primary prevention aims to prevent the occurrence of mental illness – to reduce the incidence (new cases) – by promoting mental health and protecting people against specific risk factors, before any illness appears. It is directed at the whole population and especially at high-risk groups. (Secondary prevention is early diagnosis and treatment; tertiary prevention is rehabilitation.)

A. Mental health promotion

  • Good nutrition, adequate sleep, physical activity and yoga.
  • Healthy family life – warm, consistent parenting, good communication, family harmony.
  • Education and employment, adequate housing, reduction of poverty.
  • Life skills and coping skills for stress; healthy recreation; social support and community participation; spiritual well-being.
  • Awareness of mental health and reduction of stigma through mass media and community programmes.

B. Specific protection – across the life span

  1. Before and during pregnancy
    • Genetic counselling for families with hereditary disorders; avoid consanguineous marriage where risk is high.
    • Good antenatal care – maternal nutrition, iodised salt (preventing cretinism), folic acid, avoiding alcohol, tobacco, drugs and teratogenic medicines, preventing infections (rubella vaccination), managing maternal stress and depression.
    • Safe delivery to prevent birth asphyxia and head injury; care of low birth weight babies.
  2. Infancy and childhood
    • Early childhood development – breastfeeding, nurturing care, play and stimulation, secure attachment.
    • Immunisation (measles, Japanese encephalitis) and prevention of brain infections and lead poisoning.
    • Prevention of child abuse and neglect; parenting education; early identification of developmental delay.
  3. School age and adolescence
    • Life skills education (WHO's core life skills – self-awareness, empathy, problem solving, decision making, effective communication, coping with stress and emotions).
    • School mental health and counselling services, anti-bullying programmes, prevention of examination stress, safe use of the internet.
    • Adolescent health programmes (RKSK) and school health and wellness programmes that include emotional well-being and substance-use prevention.
  4. Adults
    • Stress management, workplace mental health, prevention of burnout, premarital and marital counselling, prevention of domestic violence, responsible alcohol policies.
  5. Elderly – social engagement, physical activity, support for those living alone, prevention of isolation.

C. Protection of vulnerable groups

  • People facing crises – bereavement, divorce, job loss, migration, farmers in distress: crisis intervention and social support.
  • Disaster and conflict survivors – psychological first aid.
  • Persons with chronic physical illnesses, people living with HIV, refugees, homeless people, women facing violence, children of parents with mental illness.

D. Suicide prevention and substance-use prevention

  • Restricting access to means (pesticides, poisons, firearms), responsible media reporting, crisis helplines (Tele-MANAS – 14416), gatekeeper training.
  • Prevention of tobacco, alcohol and drug use through education, legislation and community action.

Role of the nurse

  • Identify high-risk individuals and families during home visits, antenatal and child health clinics.
  • Provide health education on mental health, parenting, stress management and substance use.
  • Conduct life skills and stress management sessions in schools, colleges and workplaces.
  • Offer counselling and crisis intervention, psychological first aid in disasters.
  • Work with ASHAs, Anganwadi workers, teachers and community leaders; advocate for supportive policies.
  • Model and promote mental well-being in her own life and among colleagues.

Conclusion Primary prevention reduces new cases of mental illness through mental health promotion and specific protection across the life span – from genetic counselling, antenatal care and nurturing childhood to life skills, workplace mental health, crisis support, suicide and substance-use prevention – with the nurse as educator, counsellor and community organiser.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain psychiatric (psychosocial) rehabilitation and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Psychiatric (psychosocial) rehabilitation is the process of helping persons with mental illness, especially severe and chronic illness, to regain the highest possible level of functioning and independence and to live, learn, work and socialise in the community with the least professional support. It is tertiary prevention – reducing disability and preventing relapse.

Recovery approach – recovery means living a satisfying, hopeful life even with some symptoms; its key elements are Connectedness, Hope, Identity, Meaning and Empowerment (CHIME).

Goals

  • Reduce disability and relapse; improve self-care, social and work skills.
  • Enable independent community living and social inclusion.
  • Improve quality of life and support families.

Principles

  • Begin early, even during hospital stay; individualised plans based on the person's strengths, needs and choices.
  • Holistic and team-based; involvement of the person and family as partners.
  • Community-based, using local resources; continuity of care; hope and respect for rights.

Components and services

  1. Assessment of disability – using tools such as the Indian Disability Evaluation and Assessment Scale (IDEAS); mental illness is a recognised disability under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, which allows a disability certificate (UDID card) and access to welfare benefits.
  2. Training in activities of daily living – personal hygiene, grooming, cooking, managing money, using transport.
  3. Social skills training – conversation, assertiveness, problem solving, through role play and feedback.
  4. Vocational rehabilitation – pre-vocational training, sheltered workshops, supported employment and job placement.
  5. Cognitive remediation – exercises to improve attention, memory and planning.
  6. Psychoeducation and family intervention – understanding the illness, medicines, early warning signs of relapse, reducing expressed emotion and caregiver burden.
  7. Residential services – day-care centres, half-way homes, long-stay homes, group homes and supported housing.
  8. Self-help and peer-support groups; recreational and leisure activities.
  9. Case management and follow-up – regular review, depot injection clinics, home visits, relapse prevention plan.
  10. Welfare and legal support – pensions, travel concessions, guardianship and legal aid where needed.

Role of the nurse

  • Assess the patient's functioning, strengths and needs; plan rehabilitation goals with the patient and family.
  • Teach daily living and social skills; organise occupational and recreational activities in the ward.
  • Provide psychoeducation to patients and families; teach early signs of relapse and medication adherence.
  • Link patients with day-care centres, vocational units, NGOs, DMHP services and disability benefits.
  • Conduct home visits and follow-up; support caregivers; run self-help groups.
  • Fight stigma in the community and advocate for the rights and inclusion of persons with mental illness.

Conclusion Psychiatric rehabilitation is tertiary prevention that helps persons with mental illness regain function and live meaningfully in the community, guided by the recovery model. Disability assessment, daily living, social and vocational skills training, cognitive remediation, family psychoeducation, residential and day-care services, self-help groups and case management form its core, with the nurse acting as assessor, teacher, coordinator, counsellor and advocate.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the ethical principles and responsibilities of the mental health nurse.
tags: rights of persons with mental illness
answer_html:
Introduction Persons with mental illness are vulnerable to stigma, coercion and abuse, and may sometimes lack the capacity to make decisions. The mental health nurse must therefore practise with high ethical standards and in accordance with the law, especially the Mental Healthcare Act (MHCA) 2017.

Ethical principles

  1. Autonomy – respect the patient's right to make decisions; assume capacity unless proved otherwise; respect advance directives and involve the nominated representative where the patient lacks capacity (MHCA 2017).
  2. Beneficence – act for the patient's good – effective treatment, comfort, support.
  3. Non-maleficence – do no harm – avoid unnecessary restraint, over-sedation, neglect, abuse and humiliation.
  4. Justice – fair and equal care for all, without discrimination by diagnosis, caste, religion, gender or income; MHCA gives every person the right to access mental health care.
  5. Veracity – truthfulness; honest information about illness and treatment in a way the patient can understand.
  6. Fidelity – keeping promises, being faithful to commitments and loyal to the patient's interests.
  7. Confidentiality – information about the patient is protected (a right under MHCA 2017). It may be shared only with the treatment team, the nominated representative, or when required to protect the patient or others from serious harm or by law (court orders, mandatory reporting).
  8. Respect for dignity – privacy during care, address by name, protection from cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.

Common ethical issues

  • Involuntary admission and treatment – balancing autonomy with safety; following legal procedures.
  • Restraint and seclusion – under MHCA 2017, seclusion and solitary confinement are not allowed; physical restraint only as a last resort to prevent imminent harm, authorised by the psychiatrist, for the shortest time, with monitoring and documentation; chaining is prohibited.
  • Consent for ECT and research; ECT is permitted only with anaesthesia and muscle relaxants.
  • Boundary violations – personal or financial relationships with patients.
  • Pressures from family versus the patient's wishes; stigma in staff attitudes.

Responsibilities of the mental health nurse

  • Protect patients' rights – information, consent, confidentiality, personal contacts, complaints.
  • Provide care in the least restrictive environment; use de-escalation before restraint.
  • Accurate, objective documentation of observations, incidents, restraint and consent.
  • Maintain professional boundaries; avoid exploitation; manage countertransference with supervision.
  • Report abuse, neglect or unsafe practice; follow legal procedures for admission and discharge.
  • Maintain competence through continuing education; follow INC and institutional standards.
  • Advocate for patients and families; reduce stigma; practise culturally sensitive care.
  • Care for her own mental health and seek support to prevent burnout.

Conclusion The mental health nurse is guided by autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, veracity, fidelity, confidentiality and respect for dignity, applied within the MHCA 2017 framework. Her responsibilities include protecting rights, least restrictive care, careful documentation, professional boundaries, reporting abuse, maintaining competence and advocacy.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: Explain the role of the limbic system and neurotransmitters in mental disorders.
answer_html:
Introduction Mental disorders are associated with changes in brain structures that control emotion, memory and behaviour (especially the limbic system and prefrontal cortex) and in the neurotransmitters that carry messages between neurons. Most psychiatric drugs act by changing neurotransmitter activity.

A. Limbic system – the "emotional brain"

  • Structures – hippocampus, amygdala, hypothalamus, anterior thalamic nuclei, cingulate gyrus, septal nuclei, fornix and mammillary bodies, closely linked with the prefrontal cortex.
  • Functions and disorders
    • Amygdala – fear, anger and emotional memory; overactive in anxiety disorders and PTSD.
    • Hippocampus – formation of new memories; reduced in size in depression, PTSD and Alzheimer's disease.
    • Hypothalamus – appetite, sleep, sex drive, body temperature and the stress (HPA) axis; disturbed in depression (sleep and appetite changes).
    • Cingulate gyrus and prefrontal cortex – attention, judgement, planning and control of emotions; dysfunction in schizophrenia, depression and OCD.

B. Neurotransmitters

  1. Dopamine – reward, motivation, movement and thinking. Four pathways:
    • Mesolimbic – excess activity causes positive symptoms of schizophrenia (hallucinations, delusions); also involved in addiction and mania.
    • Mesocortical – reduced activity linked to negative and cognitive symptoms.
    • Nigrostriatal – movement; blocking it with antipsychotics causes extrapyramidal side effects; loss causes Parkinson's disease.
    • Tuberoinfundibular – controls prolactin; blocking it raises prolactin (galactorrhoea, menstrual problems).
  2. Serotonin (5-HT) – mood, sleep, appetite, impulse control; reduced in depression, anxiety and OCD (SSRIs increase it).
  3. Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) – arousal, attention, stress response; reduced in depression, increased in mania, anxiety and panic.
  4. GABA – the main inhibitory neurotransmitter; reduced activity in anxiety; benzodiazepines and alcohol enhance GABA (hence tolerance and withdrawal).
  5. Glutamate – the main excitatory neurotransmitter; NMDA receptor hypofunction in schizophrenia; excess causes neuronal damage (excitotoxicity) in dementia and alcohol withdrawal.
  6. Acetylcholine – memory and learning; reduced in Alzheimer's dementia (treated with cholinesterase inhibitors); anticholinergic drugs cause confusion in the elderly.
  7. Histamine – wakefulness and appetite; blocking it causes sedation and weight gain (some antipsychotics and antidepressants).
  8. Endorphins and other neuropeptides – pain relief and reward; involved in opioid dependence.

Nursing implications

  • Understanding neurotransmitters explains why drugs work and why side effects occur (EPS, raised prolactin, sedation, weight gain, anticholinergic effects), helping the nurse monitor patients, explain treatment and promote adherence.
  • It also helps to explain mental illness to families as a brain-based illness, reducing blame and stigma.

Conclusion The limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus, hypothalamus and cingulate gyrus) and the prefrontal cortex regulate emotion, memory and behaviour, and changes in them are seen in anxiety, depression, PTSD, schizophrenia and dementia. Disturbances of dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline, GABA, glutamate and acetylcholine underlie many mental disorders and are the targets of psychiatric drugs.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: Differentiate between psychosis and neurosis.
answer_html:
Psychosis vs Neurosis

  • Contact with reality – psychosis: lost (impaired reality testing); neurosis: maintained.
  • Insight – psychosis: usually absent (patient does not accept he is ill); neurosis: present (patient knows he has a problem and seeks help).
  • Hallucinations and delusions – psychosis: present; neurosis: absent.
  • Personality – psychosis: disorganised, behaviour often bizarre; neurosis: intact.
  • Social and occupational functioning – psychosis: markedly impaired; neurosis: mildly to moderately affected.
  • Cause – psychosis: strong biological factors; neurosis: mainly psychological stress and conflict.
  • Treatment – psychosis: often hospitalisation, antipsychotics, ECT; neurosis: outpatient care, psychotherapy, antidepressants or anxiolytics.
  • Examples – psychosis: schizophrenia, mania, delusional disorder; neurosis: anxiety disorders, phobias, OCD. (ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR no longer use the term "neurosis", but the distinction is clinically useful.)

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: What is the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia?
answer_html:
The dopamine hypothesis states that schizophrenia is related to abnormal dopamine activity in the brain:

  • Overactivity of dopamine (D2) transmission in the mesolimbic pathway causes positive symptoms – hallucinations, delusions, excitement.

  • Underactivity in the mesocortical pathway (prefrontal cortex) is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms. Evidence

  • Antipsychotic drugs block D2 receptors, and their potency is related to D2 blockade.

  • Drugs that increase dopamine (amphetamine, cocaine, levodopa) can produce psychotic symptoms. Limitations – it does not explain everything; glutamate, serotonin and other systems are also involved (e.g. the effectiveness of clozapine).

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: What are culture-bound syndromes? Give examples.
answer_html:
