Culture-bound syndromes (cultural concepts of distress) are patterns of distress or abnormal behaviour that are recognised as illnesses within a particular culture and are shaped by its beliefs. Examples

  1. Dhat syndrome (India and South Asia) – anxiety, weakness and fatigue attributed to loss of semen in urine or night emissions.
  2. Koro – acute fear that the penis (or breasts) will retract into the body and cause death; epidemics in China and parts of North-East India and West Bengal.
  3. Possession syndrome – trance-like states attributed to spirits or deities (India).
  4. Amok (Malaysia) – sudden outburst of violent behaviour after brooding.
  5. Latah (South-East Asia) – exaggerated startle with imitation of words or actions.
  6. Susto (Latin America) – illness attributed to a frightening event causing "soul loss". Nurses must assess such complaints with cultural sensitivity, without ridicule.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Principles and Concepts of Mental Health Nursing
question: What is the duty to warn? State the limits of confidentiality in mental health care.
answer_html:
Duty to warn (duty to protect) – when a patient makes a serious threat of violence against an identifiable person, the mental health professional has a duty to take reasonable steps to protect the intended victim (e.g. warning the person, informing the police, hospitalising the patient). It arose from the Tarasoff case (California, 1976). Limits of confidentiality – information may be disclosed:

  1. When there is serious risk of harm to the patient (suicide) or to others.
  2. To the treating team and to the patient's nominated representative where needed for care (MHCA 2017).
  3. When ordered by a court or required by law (medico-legal cases, child abuse under POCSO).
  4. With the patient's informed consent.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Mental Health Assessment
question: (a) Explain the components of psychiatric history taking. (6 marks) (b) Describe the mental status examination (MSE). (9 marks)

diagram.caption: Components of the mental status examination
labels: general appearance and behaviour – speech – mood and affect – thought (stream/form

answer_html:
Introduction Psychiatric assessment is the systematic collection of information about the patient's problems, life and mental state. It consists of history taking (from the patient and reliable informants), the mental status examination (MSE), physical and neurological examination and investigations. Together they form the basis of diagnosis and of the nursing care plan.

Interview technique (general points)

  • Quiet, private place; introduce yourself, explain the purpose and assure confidentiality.
  • Build rapport; begin with open-ended questions, then specific ones; listen attentively; observe non-verbal behaviour.
  • Interview family members or other informants separately when needed and note their reliability.
  • Be non-judgemental and culturally sensitive; record important statements in the patient's own words.

(a) Components of psychiatric history (6 marks)

  1. Identification data – name, age, sex, marital status, education, occupation, religion, socio-economic status, address, date of admission, type of admission (independent or supported under MHCA 2017), informant (relationship, duration of contact) and reliability and adequacy of the information.
  2. Chief complaints – the main problems in the patient's or informant's own words, with their duration, in chronological order (e.g. "not sleeping for 1 month", "talking to himself for 15 days").
  3. History of present illness
    • Onset (sudden, acute or insidious), duration, course (continuous, episodic, progressive) and precipitating factors (stress, substance use, stopping medicines).
    • Detailed description of each symptom and its effect on work, family and self-care.
    • Biological functions – sleep, appetite, weight, bowel and bladder, sexual function, menstruation.
    • Any suicidal or homicidal ideas or attempts, violence, wandering.
    • Negative history – absence of fever, head injury, seizures or substance use (to rule out organic causes).
    • Treatment taken so far (including faith healing), response, side effects and adherence.
  4. Past history
    • Psychiatric – previous episodes, their treatment and recovery, hospitalisations, relapses.
    • Medical and surgical – head injury, epilepsy, diabetes, hypertension, thyroid disease, HIV, operations, allergies, current medicines.
  5. Family history
    • Family type and genogram (family tree of three generations).
    • Mental illness, suicide, epilepsy or substance use in relatives.
    • Family relationships, expressed emotion, communication, support, attitude towards the illness, socio-economic condition and recent stressful events.
  6. Personal history
    • Birth and early development – antenatal and birth complications, developmental milestones, childhood illnesses.
    • Childhood – home atmosphere, separation from parents, neurotic traits (night terrors, bedwetting, temper tantrums, nail biting), abuse.
    • Education – age at schooling, performance, failures, relations with teachers and peers, reasons for stopping.
    • Occupation – jobs, changes and reasons, job satisfaction, income.
    • Menstrual and obstetric history in women; sexual and marital history (age at marriage, marital adjustment, children).
    • Substance use – tobacco, alcohol, cannabis, opioids, sedatives: age at first use, pattern, quantity, dependence features, last use.
    • Forensic history – arrests, court cases, violence.
  7. Premorbid personality (before the illness) – social relations (friends, sociable or withdrawn), intellectual interests, predominant mood, character traits (anxious, perfectionist, suspicious, dependent), attitudes to self and others, moral and religious standards, habits, hobbies and leisure activities, coping with stress.

(b) Mental status examination (9 marks) The MSE is a systematic, cross-sectional assessment of the patient's mental functioning at the time of examination, based on observation and questioning.

  1. General appearance and behaviour
    • Appearance – looks his age or not, build, nutrition, grooming, hygiene and dress (unkempt in schizophrenia and depression, gaudy in mania), facial expression, posture.
    • Attitude towards the examiner – cooperative, guarded, suspicious, hostile, evasive, seductive; eye contact; whether rapport could be established.
    • Psychomotor activity – normal, increased (restless, agitated, overactive in mania), decreased (retardation in depression, stupor); abnormal movements – tremors, tics, mannerisms, stereotypies, posturing, waxy flexibility, echopraxia (catatonia), dyskinesias from drugs.
  2. Speech
    • Rate (fast, pressured in mania; slow in depression), volume and tone, quantity (talkative or poverty of speech), reaction time, spontaneity, relevance and coherence; mutism, stuttering, neologisms (new words) and echolalia.
  3. Mood and affect
    • Mood – the subjective, sustained emotional state as described by the patient ("How do you feel?") – e.g. sad, happy, anxious, irritable; recorded in his own words.
    • Affect – the objective expression of emotion observed by the nurse – described by quality (euthymic, depressed, elated, anxious), range (full, restricted, blunted, flat), stability (stable or labile), appropriateness to thought content (inappropriate – laughing while describing a death) and congruence with mood.
  4. Thought
    • Form and stream (thought process) – how ideas are connected and their speed: normal, flight of ideas (mania), loosening of associations, circumstantiality, tangentiality, thought block, perseveration, clang associations, word salad, poverty of thought (schizophrenia, depression).
    • Content – what the patient thinks about: delusions (persecution, reference, grandeur, guilt, nihilism, jealousy, infidelity, love), obsessions, phobias, preoccupations, ideas of worthlessness, hopelessness, suicidal and homicidal ideas (always ask directly).
    • Possession of thought – thought insertion, thought withdrawal, thought broadcasting (passivity phenomena), and obsessions (recognised as one's own but intrusive).
  5. Perception
    • Hallucinations – perception without a stimulus: auditory (most common in schizophrenia; second-person or third-person voices, commenting or command hallucinations), visual (common in delirium and substance withdrawal), olfactory, gustatory, tactile (e.g. insects crawling in cocaine use).
    • Illusions – misinterpretation of real stimuli (in delirium).
    • Depersonalisation and derealisation; pseudohallucinations.
    • Ask: "Do you hear voices when no one is around?"; observe for hallucinatory behaviour (talking or laughing to self, looking around, gesturing).
  6. Cognitive functions
    • Consciousness – alert, drowsy, clouded, stuporous or comatose (Glasgow Coma Scale if impaired).
    • Orientation – to time (date, day, month, year, time of day), place (where is he now) and person (who are the people around) – lost first for time in organic disorders.
    • Attention and concentration – digit span (forward and backward), serial subtraction of 7 from 100, naming the days of the week or months backwards.
    • Memory
      • Immediate – repeat three unrelated words or a series of digits immediately.
      • Recent – recall the three words after 5 minutes; events of the past 24 hours (what he ate for breakfast).
      • Remote – personal past events (date of marriage, school), historical events.
    • General information and intelligence – current events, names of the Prime Minister or Chief Minister, simple arithmetic, vocabulary – compared with his education and background.
    • Abstract thinking – similarities ("How are an orange and an apple alike?") and proverb interpretation ("What does 'a stitch in time saves nine' mean?"); concrete answers suggest schizophrenia, dementia or low intelligence.
  7. Judgement
    • Personal judgement – realistic plans for the future; social judgement – behaviour in social situations; test judgement – response to a hypothetical situation ("What would you do if you saw a fire in a cinema hall?").
  8. Insight – awareness and understanding of one's illness, graded from grade 1 – complete denial of illness to grade 6 – true emotional insight (awareness leading to change in behaviour).

Screening tools – the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) (30 points; below about 24 suggests cognitive impairment) and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) give a quick, scored assessment of cognitive functions.

Recording the MSE

  • Use objective, descriptive language and quote the patient's own words; avoid labels such as "patient is mad".
  • Record the date and time, since the MSE describes the mental state at that moment and changes from day to day.

Role of the nurse

  • Collects history from the patient and family at admission and continues the assessment through 24-hour observation (sleep, eating, hallucinatory behaviour, interaction, suicidal risk).
  • Performs a nursing MSE and risk assessment (suicide, violence, absconding, self-neglect).
  • Uses the findings to formulate nursing diagnoses and goals; communicates changes to the team.

Nursing importance

  • A careful history and MSE identify the patient's problems, risks and strengths, allow early recognition of changes in the mental state and provide a baseline for evaluating treatment.

Conclusion Psychiatric history covers identification data, chief complaints, history of present illness, past, family and personal history and premorbid personality. The mental status examination assesses appearance and behaviour, speech, mood and affect, thought (form, content, possession), perception, cognitive functions (consciousness, orientation, attention, memory, intelligence, abstraction), judgement and insight. Together with physical examination and investigations, they guide diagnosis and individualised nursing care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Mental Health Assessment
question: Explain the investigations used in psychiatry and the nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction There is no laboratory test that confirms most mental disorders. Investigations are done to rule out physical (organic) causes of psychiatric symptoms, to obtain baseline values before treatment, to monitor drug levels and side effects and to detect substance use.

A. Blood and urine tests

  • Complete blood count – anaemia, infection; neutrophil counts with clozapine (risk of agranulocytosis) and carbamazepine.
  • Blood glucose, HbA1c and lipid profile – baseline and regular metabolic monitoring with atypical antipsychotics (weight gain, diabetes, high lipids).
  • Renal and liver function tests – before lithium and valproate; in alcohol dependence.
  • Electrolytes – low sodium (with SSRIs, carbamazepine, excessive water drinking), calcium, magnesium.
  • Thyroid function tests – hypothyroidism can mimic depression; hyperthyroidism mimics anxiety or mania; lithium can cause hypothyroidism.
  • Vitamin B12, folate – deficiency can cause depression and dementia.
  • VDRL, HIV and hepatitis tests – neurosyphilis and HIV can present with psychiatric symptoms.
  • Serum drug levels – lithium (12 hours after the last dose), valproate, carbamazepine; clozapine levels where available.
  • Urine drug screen – cannabis, opioids, amphetamines, benzodiazepines.
  • Pregnancy test – before drugs harmful in pregnancy (valproate) and before ECT.
  • Prolactin – raised by some antipsychotics.

B. Electrophysiological tests

  • ECG – baseline and monitoring for QTc prolongation with antipsychotics, tricyclic antidepressants, lithium; before ECT in older patients.
  • EEG – epilepsy, delirium, encephalitis, non-epileptic seizures; also used to monitor seizures during ECT.
  • Polysomnography – sleep disorders (sleep apnoea, narcolepsy).

C. Neuroimaging

  • CT scan and MRI – tumours, stroke, subdural haematoma, atrophy in dementia; indicated in first-episode psychosis with neurological signs, late-onset symptoms, cognitive decline or head injury.
  • PET and SPECT – functional imaging, mainly in dementia and research.

D. Others – cerebrospinal fluid examination (encephalitis), genetic tests (fragile X), psychological tests and rating scales.

Nursing responsibilities

  1. Explain the test simply to the patient and family and obtain consent; reduce fear (especially in suspicious patients).
  2. Prepare the patient – fasting for glucose and lipids; hair washed and free of oil for EEG; removal of metal objects and screening for implants before MRI; sedation only as ordered.
  3. Collect samples correctly and on time – e.g. lithium level 12 hours after the last dose; label and send promptly.
  4. Ensure safety – escort restless or confused patients; observe during and after procedures.
  5. Record and report results; inform the team of abnormal values (high lithium, low neutrophils, low sodium).
  6. Educate the patient about regular monitoring for long-term medicines.

Conclusion Investigations in psychiatry – blood tests, drug levels, urine drug screens, ECG, EEG and neuroimaging – help exclude organic causes, establish baselines and monitor treatment. The nurse explains and prepares, collects samples correctly, ensures safety and reports abnormal results.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Mental Health Assessment
question: Explain the psychological tests used in psychiatry.
answer_html:
Introduction Psychological tests are standardised tools for objective measurement of intelligence, personality, cognitive functions, symptoms and behaviour. They are usually administered by a clinical psychologist and help in diagnosis, planning treatment, measuring progress, research and certification (e.g. intellectual disability).

1. Tests of intelligence

  • Binet–Kamat test (Indian adaptation of the Stanford–Binet), Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) and Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC); Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC).
  • Performance tests – Bhatia's battery, Seguin form board, Raven's Progressive Matrices (non-verbal).
  • Vineland Social Maturity Scale – social competence (used with IQ tests in intellectual disability).
  • Result expressed as IQ (average 90–109; below 70 suggests intellectual disability).

2. Tests of personality

  • Objective (questionnaire) tests – Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI), Cattell's 16 Personality Factor (16PF) questionnaire, Eysenck Personality Questionnaire.
  • Projective tests – the person projects inner feelings onto ambiguous stimuli: Rorschach inkblot test, Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), sentence completion test, draw-a-person test.

3. Neuropsychological tests – assess brain damage and cognitive deficits

  • Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test, PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction, NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (frontal lobe function).

4. Rating scales (symptom severity and screening)

  • Psychosis – Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS), Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS).
  • Depression – Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D), Beck Depression Inventory, PHQ-9.
  • Anxiety – Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, GAD-7.
  • Mania – Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS).
  • OCD – Yale–Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS).
  • Cognition – MMSE, MoCA.
  • Substance use – AUDIT, CAGE; alcohol withdrawal – CIWA-Ar.
  • Children – Conners' scales (ADHD), Childhood Autism Rating Scale and the Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism (ISAA), Child Behaviour Checklist.
  • Drug side effects – Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS) for tardive dyskinesia.

5. Other tests – aptitude, interest and achievement tests; tests for specific learning disability.

Role of the nurse

  • Explain the purpose of the test and reduce anxiety; ensure the patient is rested, fed and not over-sedated.
  • Provide a quiet room; do not coach or help with answers.
  • Observe and report behaviour during testing (cooperation, attention, fatigue).
  • Administer simple screening tools where trained (PHQ-9, GAD-7, MMSE, AUDIT, CIWA-Ar) and use rating scales to monitor progress.
  • Keep results confidential.

Conclusion Psychological tests measure intelligence (Binet–Kamat, WAIS, WISC, Raven's), personality (MMPI, 16PF, Rorschach, TAT), neuropsychological functions (Bender Gestalt, PGI and NIMHANS batteries) and symptom severity (BPRS, HAM-D, PHQ-9, YMRS, Y-BOCS, MMSE, AUDIT). The nurse prepares and supports the patient, observes behaviour and uses simple screening scales.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Mental Health Assessment
question: Explain the physical and neurological examination of a psychiatric patient and its importance.
answer_html:
Importance

  • Many physical and neurological illnesses present with psychiatric symptoms (hypothyroidism, brain tumour, encephalitis, epilepsy, head injury, HIV, delirium); examination helps rule them out.
  • People with mental illness have high rates of physical illness (diabetes, hypertension, infections) which are often neglected.
  • It provides a baseline before treatment and helps detect drug side effects (EPS, tardive dyskinesia, lithium tremor).
  • It may reveal signs of self-harm, injuries, substance use or abuse.

A. General physical examination

  • Height, weight, BMI and waist circumference (metabolic risk), vital signs.
  • Nutrition and hydration, pallor, jaundice, signs of self-neglect, lice and scabies.
  • Injection marks, scars of self-harm, burns, bruises (abuse), tobacco staining, signs of alcohol misuse (spider naevi, enlarged liver).
  • Examination of thyroid, heart, lungs and abdomen.

B. Neurological examination

  1. Higher mental functions – consciousness, orientation, speech (aphasia, dysarthria).
  2. Cranial nerves – smell, vision and fundus (papilloedema in raised intracranial pressure), pupils, eye movements, facial sensation and movement, hearing, swallowing, tongue.
  3. Motor system
    • Muscle bulk, tone (lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity in drug-induced parkinsonism), power.
    • Involuntary movements – tremor (anxiety, lithium, alcohol withdrawal), akathisia (restlessness), dystonia, chorea, tardive dyskinesia (lip smacking, tongue movements).
  4. Reflexes – deep tendon reflexes, plantar response; primitive (frontal release) reflexes – grasp, palmomental and glabellar tap – suggest diffuse brain damage (dementia).
  5. Sensory system – touch, pain, vibration, position sense (peripheral neuropathy in alcohol dependence).
  6. Coordination and cerebellar functions – finger–nose test, heel–shin test, rapid alternating movements, gait and Romberg's test (alcohol-related damage).
  7. Meningeal signs – neck stiffness, Kernig's sign (meningitis, encephalitis).
  8. Soft neurological signs – minor difficulties in coordination, sensory integration and sequencing, more common in schizophrenia.

C. Rating of drug-induced movement disorders

  • Simpson–Angus Scale (parkinsonism), Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale, Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS) for tardive dyskinesia.

Role of the nurse

  • Prepare the patient and explain the examination; ensure privacy and a chaperone; approach suspicious or agitated patients calmly.
  • Assist the doctor; record vital signs, weight, BMI and findings.
  • Observe daily for new physical or neurological signs – fever, rigidity, confusion (neuroleptic malignant syndrome), tremors, falls, seizures – and report promptly.
  • Promote physical health – diet, exercise, smoking cessation, screening for diabetes and hypertension.

Conclusion Physical and neurological examination of psychiatric patients is essential to exclude organic causes, detect physical illness and self-harm, and provide a baseline and monitoring for drug side effects. It covers general examination, cranial nerves, motor and sensory systems, reflexes, coordination, meningeal and soft signs, with rating scales for movement disorders, and the nurse assists, observes and reports.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Mental Health Assessment
question: What is insight? Write its grades.
answer_html:
Insight is the patient's awareness and understanding of his own illness – that he is ill, that the symptoms are due to illness and that he needs treatment. Grades of insight

  1. Complete denial of illness.
  2. Slight awareness of being sick and needing help, but denying it at the same time.
  3. Awareness of being sick but blaming it on others, external factors or physical causes.
  4. Awareness that the illness is due to something unknown in himself.
  5. Intellectual insight – admits illness and knows its cause, but does not apply this knowledge to change behaviour.
  6. True emotional insight – understanding that leads to change in behaviour and cooperation with treatment. Insight is usually poor in psychosis and better in neurotic disorders; it affects adherence to treatment.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Mental Health Assessment
question: What is judgement? Name its types.
answer_html:
Judgement is the ability to assess a situation correctly and act appropriately – to understand the consequences of one's actions and choose a reasonable course. Types

  1. Personal judgement – ability to make realistic plans for one's own future (e.g. job, treatment, family).
  2. Social judgement – appropriateness of behaviour in social situations, as observed and reported by the family.
  3. Test judgement – response to a hypothetical situation, e.g. "What would you do if you found a stamped, addressed envelope on the road?" or "...if you saw smoke in a cinema hall?" Judgement is impaired in psychosis, mania, dementia and intoxication.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Mental Health Assessment
question: How is orientation assessed in the mental status examination?
answer_html:
Orientation is the awareness of time, place and person in relation to oneself. It is assessed by asking:

  1. Time – the time of day, date, day of the week, month and year (allowing a small error).
  2. Place – where he is now (name of the hospital, ward, city).
  3. Person – who the people around him are (nurse, doctor, relatives), and his own name. Significance – disorientation indicates organic brain dysfunction (delirium, dementia, intoxication, head injury). Orientation is usually lost first for time, then place, and last for person; it is usually preserved in schizophrenia and mood disorders.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Mental Health Assessment
question: Differentiate between mood and affect.
answer_html:
• Mood – the sustained, pervasive emotional state experienced by the person over a period of time; it is subjective and reported by the patient in his own words ("I feel sad"); like the climate. Examples: euthymic, depressed, elated, anxious, irritable.
  • Affect – the immediate, observable expression of emotion, seen in facial expression, voice and gestures; it is objective and observed by the examiner; like the weather. It is described by quality, range (full, restricted, blunted, flat), stability (labile) and appropriateness to the content of thought.
  • Examples – blunted or flat affect and inappropriate affect in schizophrenia; labile affect in mania and organic disorders.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Mental Health Assessment
question: How is abstract thinking assessed? What is its significance?
answer_html:
Abstract thinking is the ability to understand general concepts, meanings and relationships beyond the literal. Assessment

  1. Similarities – "How are an apple and a banana alike?" (abstract answer: both are fruits; concrete answer: both can be eaten).
  2. Differences – "What is the difference between a child and a dwarf?"
  3. Proverb interpretation – "What is the meaning of 'a stitch in time saves nine'?" – the patient should explain the general meaning, not the literal one (consider education and culture). Significance – concrete thinking (literal interpretation) is seen in schizophrenia, dementia, intellectual disability and organic brain damage.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Therapeutic Communication and Nurse-Patient Relationship
question: (a) Define the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship and explain its characteristics and goals. (4 marks) (b) Explain the elements of the nurse–patient contract. (3 marks) (c) Describe the phases of the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship with the tasks of the nurse in each phase. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Phases of the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship

answer_html:
(a) Definition, characteristics and goals (4 marks) Definition The therapeutic nurse–patient relationship is a planned, purposeful, time-limited professional relationship between the nurse and the patient, in which the nurse uses her knowledge, communication skills and therapeutic use of self to help the patient grow, cope with problems and achieve better mental health. Hildegard Peplau described it as the core of psychiatric nursing.

Characteristics

  • Purposeful and goal-directed – focused on the patient's needs, not on the nurse's needs.
  • Professional, not social – clear boundaries; no personal, financial or romantic involvement.
  • Time-limited – it has a beginning, a working period and a planned end.
  • Based on trust, respect, empathy, genuineness and acceptance (unconditional positive regard).
  • Confidential, within the limits of safety and law.
  • Mutual but patient-centred – the patient participates actively; the nurse facilitates.
  • Consistent and honest – the nurse keeps appointments and promises.
  • Requires self-awareness – the nurse understands her own feelings, values and reactions.

Goals

  1. Self-realisation, self-acceptance and improved self-respect of the patient.
  2. A clear sense of personal identity and improved personal integration.
  3. Ability to form intimate, interdependent and satisfying relationships.
  4. Improved functioning and ability to satisfy needs and achieve realistic goals.
  5. Insight into problems and the development of effective coping.

(b) Elements of the nurse–patient contract (3 marks) The contract is a mutual agreement, verbal or written, made in the orientation phase. It includes:

  1. Names and roles of the nurse and the patient.
  2. Purpose and goals of the meetings, agreed by both.
  3. Responsibilities of the patient (attending, sharing concerns) and of the nurse (being available, listening, helping).
  4. Time, place, frequency and duration of the meetings (e.g. 30 minutes daily in the interview room).
  5. Total duration and conditions for termination – the expected end of the relationship (e.g. at discharge or end of clinical posting).
  6. Confidentiality and its limits – information will be shared with the treatment team and disclosed if there is risk to self or others.
  7. Expectations and rules – e.g. no physical harm, respect for each other.

(c) Phases of the relationship and tasks of the nurse (8 marks) 1. Pre-interaction phase (before meeting the patient)

  • Self-exploration – examining her own feelings, fears, misconceptions and stigma about mental illness (e.g. fear of violence, anxiety about not knowing what to say), and her strengths and limitations.
  • Gathering data about the patient from the case file, records and staff.
  • Planning the first meeting – time, place and objectives.
  • Seeking guidance from the supervisor.

2. Orientation (introductory) phase

  • Introduce herself and explain her role; call the patient by his preferred name.
  • Establish trust, rapport and open communication – be consistent, punctual and honest.
  • Formulate the contract (as above), including the plan for termination.
  • Assess the patient's thoughts, feelings, actions, strengths and problems; identify the reason for seeking help.
  • Explore the patient's feelings about the relationship; deal with testing behaviour (e.g. lateness, silence, demands) calmly.
  • Set mutual goals and formulate nursing diagnoses.
  • Peplau's corresponding phase: orientation – the patient seeks help and the nurse helps him recognise and understand his problem.

3. Working phase – the main therapeutic work

  • Explore relevant stressors and help the patient express feelings, thoughts and experiences.
  • Promote insight and help him link feelings with behaviour.
  • Help the patient use problem-solving and develop adaptive coping; practise new behaviours (role play, social skills).
  • Overcome resistance and other therapeutic impasses (transference, countertransference, boundary violations).
  • Encourage independence, responsibility and self-care; give positive feedback.
  • Continuously evaluate progress towards goals and revise the plan.
  • Provide health education about illness and medicines.
  • Peplau's corresponding phases: identification (the patient identifies with the nurse who can help) and exploitation (the patient makes full use of the services offered).

4. Termination (resolution) phase

  • Termination is planned from the beginning and is discussed in advance.
  • Review progress and the goals achieved; reinforce the patient's strengths.
  • Help the patient express feelings about ending – sadness, anger, anxiety, rejection; patients may react with regression (return of symptoms), withdrawal, denial or anger.
  • Help him plan to use the learning in the future; plan follow-up, referral and community support.
  • Share the nurse's own feelings appropriately; end the relationship on time and professionally (no exchange of personal addresses or continuing social contact).
  • Peplau's corresponding phase: resolution – old needs are resolved and the patient becomes independent.

Peplau's roles of the nurse during the relationship

  • Stranger – receives the patient with courtesy and respect.
  • Resource person – gives specific information.
  • Teacher – helps the patient learn.
  • Leader – helps the patient take responsibility in a democratic way.
  • Surrogate – may be seen by the patient as a parent or sibling; helps him differentiate.
  • Counsellor – helps the patient understand and integrate his experiences.

Skills and attitudes the nurse needs

  • Self-awareness (e.g. Johari window), empathy, genuineness, respect, warmth, concreteness and active listening.
  • Therapeutic communication techniques – open-ended questions, reflection, clarification, restating, focusing, silence, summarising and giving information.
  • Ability to set limits and maintain boundaries; use of supervision and process recordings to improve skills.

Factors that help or hinder the relationship

  • Help – privacy, consistency, punctuality, honesty, a non-judgemental attitude, cultural sensitivity, adequate time.
  • Hinder – the nurse's anxiety or stigma, false reassurance, giving advice, arguing, frequent change of staff, lack of privacy, unresolved impasses.

Core conditions of a therapeutic relationship

  • Responsive dimensions (build trust in the orientation phase)
    • Genuineness – the nurse is open, honest and real, not hiding behind a professional "mask".
    • Respect – unconditional positive regard for the patient as a worthwhile person.
    • Empathic understanding – seeing the situation from the patient's point of view and communicating this understanding.
    • Concreteness – using specific, clear terms rather than vague generalities.
  • Action dimensions (promote insight and change in the working phase)
    • Confrontation – pointing out, with care, discrepancies between the patient's words and actions.
    • Immediacy – discussing what is happening in the relationship "here and now".
    • Nurse self-disclosure – brief, purposeful sharing for the patient's benefit.
    • Emotional catharsis – helping the patient release feelings safely.
    • Role playing – rehearsing new ways of behaving and responding.

Nursing importance

  • The therapeutic relationship is itself a treatment – through it the patient experiences trust, acceptance and new ways of relating, which supports recovery and adherence to other treatments.

Conclusion The therapeutic nurse–patient relationship is a purposeful, professional, time-limited relationship based on trust, empathy, genuineness and respect, aiming at the patient's self-acceptance, coping and better relationships. It is guided by a mutually agreed contract and passes through the pre-interaction, orientation, working and termination phases (Peplau's orientation, identification, exploitation and resolution), in each of which the nurse has specific tasks – from self-exploration and building trust to promoting insight and change and finally ending the relationship in a planned, healthy way.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Therapeutic Communication and Nurse-Patient Relationship
question: Explain the Johari window and its use in psychiatric nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction The Johari window is a model of self-awareness developed by Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham (1955; the name combines their first names). It shows how much a person knows about himself and how much others know about him, and is used to improve self-awareness and interpersonal relationships.

The four quadrants

  1. Open (public) area – known to self and known to others – behaviour, feelings and information shared openly (e.g. name, profession, obvious traits).
  2. Blind area – unknown to self but known to others – things others notice that the person is not aware of (e.g. habit of interrupting, appearing irritated).
  3. Hidden (private) area – known to self but not known to others – feelings, fears, past experiences the person keeps to himself.
  4. Unknown area – unknown to self and to others – unconscious feelings, potential and abilities not yet discovered.

How the window changes

  • The open area grows – and the blind and hidden areas shrink – through:
    • Feedback from others (reduces the blind area).
    • Self-disclosure (reduces the hidden area).
    • Self-discovery and shared discovery (reduces the unknown area).
  • A large open area is associated with better self-awareness, trust and communication.

Use in psychiatric nursing

  • Developing the nurse's self-awareness – the nurse becomes aware of her own feelings, prejudices and reactions (e.g. fear of aggressive patients, irritation with manipulative behaviour) so that they do not interfere with care.
  • Therapeutic use of self – a self-aware nurse responds to the patient's needs rather than her own.
  • Clinical supervision and process recording – feedback from teachers and colleagues reduces the nurse's blind area.
  • With patients – helps them understand themselves through feedback and appropriate self-disclosure (e.g. in group therapy and social skills training).
  • Team functioning – open communication among staff reduces conflict.

Example – during supervision a student nurse learns that she avoids eye contact with an aggressive patient (her blind area becomes known), and she shares her fear of being hurt (her hidden area is disclosed). With guidance she practises calm, open communication, her open area enlarges, and her interactions become more therapeutic.

Conclusion The Johari window describes four areas of the self – open, blind, hidden and unknown. Feedback and self-disclosure enlarge the open area. Psychiatric nurses use it to increase self-awareness, improve the therapeutic use of self and communication, and help patients and teams relate better.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Therapeutic Communication and Nurse-Patient Relationship
question: What are therapeutic impasses? Explain resistance, transference, countertransference and boundary violations and their management.
answer_html:
Definition Therapeutic impasses are blocks in the progress of the nurse–patient relationship that arise from various causes and produce intense feelings in both the nurse and the patient. They must be identified and resolved, or the relationship stops being therapeutic.

Types and management 1. Resistance

  • The patient's attempt to avoid becoming aware of anxiety-producing aspects of himself or to avoid change.
  • Signs – lateness, missing sessions, silence, changing the subject, superficial talk, intellectualisation, acting out, "flight into health" (suddenly claiming to be well).
  • Management – listen and accept; help the patient recognise and talk about the resistance; review the contract and goals; proceed at the patient's pace; maintain consistency.

2. Transference

  • An unconscious response in which the patient experiences feelings and attitudes towards the nurse that were originally associated with significant persons in his past (parent, sibling, spouse).
  • Types – positive (affection, dependency, idealisation) and negative (hostility, distrust).
  • Management – listen and clarify; help the patient recognise that his feelings belong to past relationships; reality-test the current relationship; maintain boundaries; do not take hostile transference personally; discuss with the supervisor.

3. Countertransference

  • The nurse's emotional response to the patient, arising from her own past experiences, that is inappropriate to the present situation.
  • Signs – strong liking or disliking a patient, feeling bored, angry or anxious with him, over-identification, giving special favours, wanting to "rescue" him, avoiding him, arguing, feeling hurt by his remarks.
  • Management – self-awareness, recognising one's feelings, clinical supervision or peer discussion, process recording, and if necessary transfer of care.

4. Boundary violations

  • When the nurse goes beyond the professional relationship into a personal, social, financial or romantic one.
  • Examples – sharing personal problems, meeting socially, lending or borrowing money, accepting expensive gifts, giving a personal phone number, physical intimacy, special treatment.
  • Management – keep the relationship professional and patient-centred; explain limits kindly; follow institutional policy on gifts (small token gifts may be accepted in some situations after discussion); seek supervision.

5. Gift giving

  • The meaning of a gift must be explored – gratitude, attempt to manipulate, need for closeness – and handled according to policy.

General principles for managing impasses

  • Recognise the impasse early; explore it openly and non-judgementally with the patient.
  • Return to the contract and goals of the relationship.
  • Use clinical supervision and team discussion.
  • Maintain consistency, honesty and professional boundaries.

Conclusion Therapeutic impasses – resistance, transference, countertransference and boundary violations – block the progress of the nurse–patient relationship. The nurse manages them through early recognition, open discussion, reality testing, self-awareness, supervision and firm professional boundaries.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Therapeutic Communication and Nurse-Patient Relationship
question: Explain the blocks (barriers) to therapeutic communication with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Blocks to therapeutic communication are responses or conditions that discourage the patient from expressing feelings, shift the focus to the nurse or close the conversation. Recognising them helps the nurse replace them with therapeutic techniques.

Non-therapeutic responses (with examples)

  1. False reassurance – "Don't worry, everything will be all right." It dismisses the patient's concern. Better: "You seem worried about the test. Tell me more."
  2. Giving advice – "You should leave that job." It takes away the patient's responsibility. Better: "What options do you see?"
  3. Giving approval or disapproval – "That's good" / "That's wrong." It sets the nurse up as a judge.
  4. Agreeing or disagreeing – "You're right" / "That's not true." It prevents the patient from changing his opinion later.
  5. Belittling feelings – "Everybody feels sad sometimes." It minimises the patient's experience.
  6. Defending – "The doctor is very good; he wouldn't do that." It prevents the patient from expressing his feelings.
  7. Asking "why" questions – "Why did you do that?" It sounds accusing and asks for reasons the patient may not know.
  8. Probing – persistent questioning about topics the patient does not wish to discuss.
  9. Changing the subject – introducing unrelated topics when the nurse feels uncomfortable.
  10. Stereotyped or clichéd comments – "Keep your chin up," "It's for your own good."
  11. Challenging or arguing – "If you are dead, why is your heart beating?" (arguing with delusions increases resistance).
  12. Literal responses to figurative statements; interpreting too early; excessive self-disclosure; testing the patient.
  13. Rejecting – "Let's not talk about that."

Other barriers

  • Nurse-related – anxiety, fear of the patient, stigma, prejudice, fatigue, hurry, lack of knowledge, language differences.
  • Patient-related – symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, mania, depression, confusion), sedation, hearing or speech problems, mistrust.
  • Environmental – noise, lack of privacy, interruptions, uncomfortable seating, distance.

How the nurse overcomes these barriers

  • Develop self-awareness; listen actively; use open-ended questions, reflection, clarification, focusing, silence and summarising.
  • Accept the patient's feelings without judgement; give information instead of advice.
  • Provide a quiet, private setting; adapt communication to the patient's mental state and language.

Conclusion False reassurance, giving advice, approving or disapproving, agreeing or disagreeing, belittling, defending, "why" questions, probing, changing the subject, clichés, arguing and rejecting are common blocks to therapeutic communication, along with nurse, patient and environmental barriers. Replacing them with therapeutic techniques helps the patient express feelings and solve problems.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Therapeutic Communication and Nurse-Patient Relationship
question: Explain process recording – its purposes, format and analysis.
answer_html:
Definition Process recording is a written, verbatim (word-for-word) account of an interaction between the nurse and the patient, including verbal and non-verbal behaviour of both, the nurse's thoughts and feelings, and an analysis of the interaction. It is an important learning tool in psychiatric nursing education.

Purposes

  1. To improve communication and interviewing skills.
  2. To develop self-awareness of the nurse's feelings, attitudes and responses.
  3. To identify therapeutic and non-therapeutic responses and better alternatives.
  4. To understand the patient's thoughts, feelings, behaviour and needs, and to follow his progress.
  5. To provide a basis for clinical supervision and evaluation by teachers.
  6. To plan further interactions and nursing care.

Format

  • Introductory data – patient's name (or initials), age, diagnosis, date, time, duration and place of the interaction, number of the interaction, and its objectives.
  • Description of the setting and the patient's condition at the start.
  • Columns of the recording
    1. Nurse's verbal and non-verbal communication (what she said and did).
    2. Patient's verbal and non-verbal communication.
    3. Nurse's inferences / thoughts and feelings at that moment.
    4. Analysis – the communication technique used, whether it was therapeutic or non-therapeutic, and a better alternative response where needed.
  • Evaluation and summary – whether the objectives were achieved, the patient's main concerns, the nurse's learning, and the plan for the next interaction.

Guidelines

  • Write the record as soon as possible after the interaction (taking notes during the interaction may disturb the patient).
  • Record exactly what was said, including silences and gestures; be honest about the nurse's own mistakes and feelings.
  • Maintain confidentiality – use initials, and keep records secure.
  • Discuss the recording with the supervisor and apply the feedback.

Limitations – depends on the nurse's memory; time-consuming; may make the student self-conscious initially.

Sample entry (one exchange)

  • Nurse (verbal/non-verbal): "Good morning, Mr R. How did you sleep last night?" (sits beside him, smiling)
  • Patient: "Not good." (looks down, speaks softly)
  • Nurse's inference: he appears sad and unwilling to talk; I felt slightly anxious.
  • Analysis: a broad opening question – therapeutic; a better follow-up would be reflection: "You didn't sleep well… you seem low today," inviting him to share his feelings.

Conclusion Process recording is a verbatim written record of nurse–patient interaction with the nurse's inferences and an analysis of each response. It improves communication skills and self-awareness, reveals the patient's needs and progress, and forms the basis of clinical supervision.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Therapeutic Communication and Nurse-Patient Relationship
question: Explain the communication approach with patients who are withdrawn, hallucinating, suspicious, aggressive, manic and depressed.
answer_html:
Introduction Symptoms of mental illness affect how patients send and receive messages. The nurse adapts her communication to the patient's mental state, while keeping the basic principles of acceptance, honesty and respect.

1. Withdrawn patient

  • Make brief, frequent contacts; sit with him even in silence; use his name.
  • Ask simple, concrete questions; accept silence and do not force conversation.
  • Use non-verbal communication (a smile, offering tea); gradually involve him in one-to-one and then small group activities.

2. Hallucinating patient

  • Observe for cues (talking to self, listening, laughing); ask directly: "Are you hearing voices?"
  • Ask about the content, especially command hallucinations (risk of harm).
  • Do not argue or agree: "I don't hear the voices, but I understand they are real and frightening for you."
  • Focus on reality and present activities; teach coping (humming, talking to someone, listening to music).

3. Suspicious (paranoid / delusional) patient

  • Be honest, consistent and predictable; keep promises; explain everything before doing it.
  • Avoid whispering or laughing near him, touching unexpectedly or hiding medicines in food.
  • Do not argue with delusions or reinforce them; respond to the feelings ("It must be frightening to feel unsafe") and present reality simply.
  • Allow him some control and personal space.

4. Aggressive patient

  • Speak calmly, slowly and in a low voice; maintain a safe distance and an open posture; do not corner him or turn your back.
  • Acknowledge his feelings, set clear limits ("I can't let you hit anyone"), offer choices.
  • Reduce stimulation; call for help early; use de-escalation before medication or restraint.

5. Manic patient

  • Use brief, clear and firm statements; be consistent in limits; avoid arguments and power struggles.
  • Reduce stimuli; redirect energy into simple physical activities; do not respond to provocative or flirtatious remarks.
  • Do not laugh at his jokes or encourage grandiose ideas.

6. Depressed (and suicidal) patient

  • Approach with warmth and patience; speak slowly and simply; allow time to answer.
  • Ask directly about suicidal thoughts – asking does not increase risk.
  • Avoid false cheerfulness and clichés; acknowledge feelings; focus on strengths and small achievements.

7. Anxious patient – stay with him; calm voice, short sentences, simple instructions; reduce stimuli; teach slow breathing.

8. Confused patient (delirium, dementia) – face him, speak slowly and clearly, one instruction at a time; reorient frequently with clocks, calendars and familiar objects; use gestures.

Conclusion Withdrawn patients need brief frequent contacts and acceptance of silence; hallucinating and suspicious patients need honesty, consistency and gentle reality orientation without arguing; aggressive patients need calm de-escalation and limits; manic patients need brief, firm, consistent communication with low stimulation; and depressed patients need warmth, patience and direct enquiry about suicide.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Therapeutic Communication and Nurse-Patient Relationship
question: What is the therapeutic use of self?
answer_html:
Therapeutic use of self is the nurse's conscious and purposeful use of her own personality, knowledge, feelings and communication skills to bring about a positive change in the patient. It is called the art of psychiatric nursing. Requirements

  1. Self-awareness – knowing one's own values, feelings, prejudices and reactions.
  2. Genuineness, empathy, warmth and respect.
  3. Effective communication and listening skills.
  4. Focus on the patient's needs, not one's own.
  5. Professional boundaries and use of supervision. Through it the nurse becomes a model of healthy behaviour and a source of support, trust and corrective experience for the patient.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Therapeutic Communication and Nurse-Patient Relationship
question: Differentiate between transference and countertransference.
answer_html:
• Transference – an unconscious process in which the patient experiences feelings and attitudes towards the nurse that originally belonged to an important person in his past (parent, spouse). It may be positive (affection, dependency) or negative (hostility). Example: a patient angrily accuses a nurse of controlling him, as his mother did.
  • Countertransference – the nurse's emotional reaction to the patient, arising from her own past experiences, which is inappropriate to the present situation. Example: a nurse feels unusually protective of a patient who reminds her of her brother, or angry with one who resembles a difficult relative.
  • Management – transference is explored and reality-tested with the patient; countertransference is handled by the nurse's self-awareness and clinical supervision.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Therapeutic Communication and Nurse-Patient Relationship
question: What is active listening?
answer_html:
Active listening is attending fully to the patient's verbal and non-verbal messages in order to understand his thoughts and feelings, and showing that one has understood. Components

  1. Attending behaviour – the SOLER posture: Sit squarely facing the patient, Open posture, Lean slightly forward, Eye contact, Relaxed manner.
  2. Listening to content, feelings and themes; noticing non-verbal cues.
  3. Avoiding interruptions, premature advice and planning one's reply while the patient talks.
  4. Using minimal encouragers ("Go on", nodding), reflection, paraphrasing, clarification and summarising. Active listening conveys respect and acceptance, builds trust and encourages the patient to talk.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Therapeutic Communication and Nurse-Patient Relationship
question: Write the guidelines for self-disclosure by the nurse.
answer_html:
Self-disclosure is the nurse sharing personal information, experiences or feelings with the patient. It can build trust when used carefully, but may shift the focus to the nurse. Guidelines

  1. Use it only for the patient's benefit – to model behaviour, show understanding or encourage the patient to talk.
  2. Keep it brief, relevant and appropriate; avoid intimate details.
  3. Return the focus to the patient immediately ("...How was it for you?").
  4. Be honest; do not burden the patient with the nurse's problems.
  5. Avoid giving personal contact details or information that blurs professional boundaries.
  6. Consider the patient's condition – avoid with manipulative or suspicious patients.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: (a) Define electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) and list its indications and contraindications. (4 marks) (b) Describe the pre-ECT preparation and the procedure of modified ECT. (6 marks) (c) Explain the post-ECT nursing care and the complications of ECT. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: Electrode placement in ECT
labels: bitemporal (bilateral) – one electrode on each temple

about 2.5 cm above the midpoint of the line from the outer canthus to the tragus; bifrontal – both electrodes on the forehead above the outer eyebrows; right unilateral – one electrode on the right temple and one on the right side of the vertex; bite block in the mouth
pulse oximeter and BP cuff in place

answer_html:
(a) Definition, indications and contraindications (4 marks) Definition Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a treatment in which a controlled, brief electrical current is passed through the brain to induce a generalised seizure, under general anaesthesia and muscle relaxation, for the treatment of certain severe mental disorders. It was introduced by Ugo Cerletti and Lucio Bini in Italy in 1938. Modern modified ECT is safe and effective.

Mechanism (not fully known) – changes in neurotransmitters (increased monoamine activity), neuroendocrine changes, increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (neuroplasticity) and an anticonvulsant effect.

Indications

  1. Severe depression – especially with high suicidal risk, psychotic features, stupor, or refusal to eat and drink.
  2. Catatonia (of any cause) – often dramatically responsive.
  3. Treatment-resistant depression, mania or schizophrenia (including clozapine-resistant schizophrenia).
  4. Severe mania with exhaustion or not responding to drugs.
  5. Schizophrenia – catatonic, acute excitement, schizoaffective disorder.
  6. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (after stopping antipsychotics).
  7. Postpartum psychosis and severe depression; pregnancy, when drugs are risky.
  8. Elderly patients who cannot tolerate medicines.

Contraindications – there is no absolute contraindication, but the risk is high in:

  • Raised intracranial pressure (brain tumour, space-occupying lesion) – the most important.
  • Recent myocardial infarction, unstable angina, severe heart failure, uncontrolled hypertension, aortic or cerebral aneurysm.
  • Recent stroke or intracranial bleeding; retinal detachment; phaeochromocytoma.
  • Severe respiratory disease and high anaesthetic risk; loose teeth (precautions).
  • Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (section 95), ECT without anaesthesia and muscle relaxants (unmodified ECT) is prohibited, and ECT for minors is allowed only in special circumstances with the guardian's consent and the Mental Health Review Board's permission.

Types

  • By electrode placement – bilateral (bitemporal) (most effective, more memory effects), bifrontal, and right unilateral (fewer cognitive side effects).
  • By stimulus – brief-pulse or ultra-brief pulse square-wave stimulus.
  • Frequency – usually 2–3 times a week, a course of about 6–12 treatments; maintenance ECT in selected patients.

(b) Pre-ECT preparation and procedure (6 marks) Pre-ECT preparation

  1. Informed consent – explain the procedure, benefits and side effects to the patient (and nominated representative where applicable) and obtain written informed consent; reduce fear and myths.
  2. Pre-anaesthetic evaluation and investigations – history, physical examination, CBC, blood sugar, urea, creatinine, electrolytes, ECG, chest X-ray if indicated, pregnancy test in women; fundoscopy if raised intracranial pressure is suspected.
  3. Nil by mouth for about 6 hours before ECT (clear fluids as per the anaesthetist).
  4. Medication review – withhold drugs that raise the seizure threshold (benzodiazepines, anticonvulsants) and lithium (risk of delirium) as ordered; give important medicines (e.g. antihypertensives) with a sip of water if prescribed.
  5. Physical preparation – bath and hair washed and dried, without oil (for good electrode contact); remove dentures, jewellery, hairpins, contact lenses, nail polish and make-up; loose clothing; empty bladder and bowel.
  6. Record vital signs, weight and the time of last food; check the identification band.
  7. Premedication as ordered – atropine or glycopyrrolate (reduces secretions and prevents bradycardia).
  8. Prepare the ECT room and equipment – ECT machine, electrodes and conductive gel, bite block (mouth gag), suction, oxygen, Ambu bag, airway, laryngoscope and endotracheal tubes, emergency drugs, ECG, EEG, pulse oximeter and BP monitor, IV set.
  9. Emotional support – stay with the patient, answer questions, reassure.

Procedure of modified ECT

  1. The patient lies supine on the ECT table; an IV line is secured; monitors (ECG, SpO2, BP, EEG electrodes) are attached.
  2. Pre-oxygenation with 100% oxygen.
  3. The anaesthetist gives a short-acting anaesthetic (propofol, thiopentone or methohexital).
  4. A BP cuff is inflated on one arm or leg above systolic pressure (cuff method), so that the motor seizure can be seen in that limb.
  5. Muscle relaxant – succinylcholine – is given to prevent violent muscle contractions and fractures.
  6. A bite block is placed between the teeth to protect the teeth and tongue; the chin is supported.
  7. The electrodes are placed (bitemporal, bifrontal or right unilateral) with conductive gel and the electrical stimulus is delivered.
  8. The seizure is observed in the cuffed limb (motor seizure) and monitored on the EEG – an adequate seizure usually lasts about 25 seconds or more on EEG; a seizure lasting more than 2–3 minutes is terminated with IV diazepam or propofol as ordered.
  9. The patient is ventilated with 100% oxygen by bag and mask until spontaneous breathing returns.
  10. The nurse records the time, drugs, stimulus dose, seizure duration and vital signs.

(c) Post-ECT nursing care and complications (5 marks) Post-ECT care

  1. Airway – place the patient in the lateral (recovery) position; suction secretions; give oxygen; keep the bite block until he can protect his airway.
  2. Vital signs and SpO2 every 15 minutes until stable; watch for prolonged apnoea (pseudocholinesterase deficiency), arrhythmias and hypertension.
  3. Safety – side rails up; stay with the patient; post-ictal confusion and restlessness are common for some minutes – reorient gently (name, place, time).
  4. When fully awake, with a gag reflex present, give fluids and then breakfast; then resume medicines as ordered.
  5. Relieve headache and muscle pain with analgesics as prescribed.
  6. Reassure about memory problems – usually temporary; help the patient reorient; do not test memory repeatedly.
  7. Observe for switch to mania in depressed patients.
  8. Record the procedure and response; evaluate improvement after each session.
  9. Advice – no driving or important decisions during the course; patient to be accompanied home if treated as an outpatient.

Complications

  • Cognitive – post-ictal confusion and delirium; memory impairment – anterograde (for new information) and retrograde (for events before and during the course), mostly temporary and less with unilateral and brief-pulse ECT.
  • Headache, muscle aches (succinylcholine), nausea, jaw pain.
  • Cardiovascular – bradycardia or asystole (vagal stimulation), tachycardia and hypertension, arrhythmias.
  • Prolonged seizures or status epilepticus; prolonged apnoea.
  • Aspiration, injury to teeth, tongue and lips.
  • Fractures and dislocations – mainly with unmodified ECT.
  • Switch to mania; anaesthetic complications; death is extremely rare.

Nursing importance

  • Careful preparation, safe airway management, close monitoring and reassurance make ECT a safe, often life-saving treatment, especially for severely depressed, suicidal and catatonic patients, and help reduce the fear and stigma attached to it.

Conclusion ECT is the induction of a controlled seizure under anaesthesia and muscle relaxation, highly effective in severe and suicidal depression, catatonia, resistant mania and schizophrenia, and NMS; raised intracranial pressure and recent cardiac or cerebrovascular events carry the highest risk. Nursing care includes informed consent, investigations, fasting, medication review, physical preparation and equipment readiness; assisting during anaesthesia, muscle relaxation, electrode placement and seizure monitoring; and post-ECT airway care, monitoring, reorientation, safety and management of headache and memory complaints. Unmodified ECT is prohibited by the Mental Healthcare Act 2017.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: (a) Explain the nurse's role in the administration of psychotropic drugs. (5 marks) (b) Describe the nursing management of the common side effects of psychotropic drugs, including neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome. (7 marks) (c) Explain the measures to improve medication adherence. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Extrapyramidal side effects of antipsychotics and their timing
labels: tardive dyskinesia (months to years – lip smacking

answer_html:
Introduction Psychopharmacology is the use of drugs that act on the brain to treat mental disorders – antipsychotics (e.g. haloperidol, chlorpromazine, risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole, clozapine), antidepressants (SSRIs such as fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram; SNRIs; tricyclics; MAO inhibitors), mood stabilisers (lithium, sodium valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine), anxiolytics and hypnotics (benzodiazepines, buspirone, zolpidem), anticholinergic drugs for EPS (trihexyphenidyl), and drugs for dementia, ADHD and substance dependence. The nurse has the main responsibility for their safe use, monitoring and patient education.

(a) Nurse's role in the administration of psychotropic drugs (5 marks) Before starting treatment

  • Baseline assessment – vital signs, weight, BMI and waist circumference, mental state, physical illnesses, allergies, pregnancy and breastfeeding status, current medicines and substance use.
  • Baseline investigations as ordered – blood counts, glucose, lipids, renal, liver and thyroid function, ECG, serum sodium.
  • Ensure informed consent (or decision of the nominated representative where the patient lacks capacity, as per MHCA 2017) and explain the purpose, expected effects and common side effects.

During administration

  • Follow the rights of medication administration (right patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation).
  • Ensure that oral medicines are actually swallowed – stay with the patient, offer water, and if required check the mouth (patients may "cheek" or hoard tablets – especially suicidal patients who may save them for an overdose, or suspicious patients who fear poisoning).
  • Use liquid or orally dissolving forms where needed; never hide medicines in food without proper authority (covert medication raises ethical and legal issues and destroys trust).
  • Give IM injections (including depot injections) correctly using the Z-track technique; rotate sites.
  • Handle refusals calmly: explore reasons, explain again, inform the doctor.

After administration – monitoring

  • Therapeutic effects – improvement in sleep, agitation, hallucinations, mood; note that antidepressants take 2–4 weeks for full effect.
  • Side effects, toxicity and drug interactions – observe and ask regularly; use rating scales (AIMS for tardive dyskinesia).
  • Drug levels – serum lithium; blood counts with clozapine.
  • Suicide risk – may rise in the first weeks of antidepressant treatment as energy returns before mood improves (especially in young people); dispense limited quantities.
  • Accurate documentation and reporting.

Patient and family education

  • Name, dose, purpose and timing of each drug; continuing medicines even when well; not stopping suddenly; avoiding alcohol; common side effects and what to do; when to report urgently; regular follow-up and blood tests.

(b) Nursing management of common side effects (7 marks)

  1. Sedation and drowsiness – give the larger dose at bedtime; avoid driving or operating machinery; caution about falls.
  2. Anticholinergic effects (tricyclics, chlorpromazine, clozapine, trihexyphenidyl)
    • Dry mouth – frequent sips of water, sugar-free gum, mouth care.
    • Constipation – high-fibre diet, fluids, exercise, laxatives as ordered (severe constipation with clozapine can be dangerous).
    • Urinary retention – monitor output; report.
    • Blurred vision – reassure that it usually improves; caution with activities.
    • Confusion in the elderly – report.
  3. Orthostatic hypotension (chlorpromazine, clozapine, tricyclics) – check lying and standing BP; teach to rise slowly; sit on the bed edge before standing; prevent falls.
  4. Extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) of antipsychotics (especially high-potency typical drugs such as haloperidol)
    • Acute dystonia – sudden painful spasms of the neck (torticollis), eyes rolling upwards (oculogyric crisis), jaw or tongue; frightening and occasionally affects the larynx – an emergency: stay with the patient and give an anticholinergic (e.g. promethazine or another prescribed drug) by injection as ordered; reassure.
    • Akathisia – inner restlessness, inability to sit still, pacing; may be mistaken for agitation and may increase suicidal risk; report; dose reduction or propranolol as ordered.
    • Drug-induced parkinsonism – tremor, rigidity, mask-like face, shuffling gait, drooling – trihexyphenidyl as ordered; assist with mobility and eating.
    • Tardive dyskinesia – late, involuntary movements of the lips, tongue and face (lip smacking, chewing) and limbs; may be irreversible; monitor regularly (AIMS) and report early so the drug can be changed.
  5. Weight gain and metabolic syndrome (olanzapine, clozapine and other atypicals) – healthy diet, exercise, regular monitoring of weight, waist, glucose, lipids and BP.
  6. Hyperprolactinaemia (risperidone, typical antipsychotics) – breast enlargement, galactorrhoea, menstrual irregularities, sexual dysfunction; encourage reporting.
  7. Photosensitivity and skin pigmentation (chlorpromazine) – sunscreen, protective clothing.
  8. Lowered seizure threshold (clozapine, bupropion, tricyclics) – seizure precautions.
  9. Agranulocytosis with clozapine – regular blood counts; report sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers at once.
  10. Sexual dysfunction and gastrointestinal upset (SSRIs) – discuss openly; give drugs with food; report.
  11. Hyponatraemia (SSRIs, carbamazepine), especially in the elderly – confusion, headache; check sodium.
  12. Lithium toxicity – early signs: coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness, slurred speech, unsteadiness, confusion; stop the dose and check serum level; maintain adequate fluid and salt intake; avoid diuretics and NSAIDs; monitor thyroid and kidney function.
  13. Benzodiazepine dependence and over-sedation – short-term use, gradual tapering, avoid alcohol; watch for falls and breathing depression in the elderly.

Serious reactions

  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) – a rare, life-threatening reaction to antipsychotics: high fever, severe "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability (fluctuating BP, tachycardia, sweating), raised CPK and white cell count.
    • Nursing action – stop the antipsychotic (inform the doctor immediately), cool the patient, IV fluids, monitor vital signs, urine output (risk of renal failure from muscle breakdown) and consciousness, prepare for ICU care; drugs such as dantrolene and bromocriptine as ordered.
  • Serotonin syndrome – due to excess serotonin (e.g. SSRI combined with an MAO inhibitor, tramadol or linezolid): agitation, confusion, fever, sweating, diarrhoea, tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus and clonus (especially in the legs), dilated pupils.
    • Nursing action – stop the serotonergic drugs, supportive care, cooling, IV fluids, benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine as ordered.
  • Hypertensive crisis with MAO inhibitors – after eating tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, fermented foods, red wine) – severe headache, very high BP; teach dietary restrictions.
  • Tricyclic overdose – dangerous cardiac arrhythmias; dispense small quantities to suicidal patients.

(c) Measures to improve medication adherence (3 marks) Reasons for non-adherence – poor insight, side effects, feeling better and stopping, stigma, fear of addiction, cost and distance, complex regimens, forgetfulness, family beliefs, substance use. Measures

  • Psychoeducation of patient and family about the illness, the need for long-term treatment and the risk of relapse.
  • Simplify the regimen – once-daily dosing, combined timing, pill organisers, reminders.
  • Manage side effects promptly, so that the patient does not stop medicines on his own.
  • Long-acting injectable (depot) antipsychotics – fluphenazine decanoate, haloperidol decanoate, flupentixol decanoate, paliperidone palmitate – for patients with repeated relapses due to non-adherence.
  • Supervision by a family member; regular follow-up, home visits and depot clinics; free medicines under the DMHP and government hospitals.
  • Motivational interviewing and shared decision-making; building a trusting therapeutic relationship.

Conclusion The nurse plays the central role in psychopharmacology – baseline assessment, informed consent, safe administration with checks against cheeking and hoarding, monitoring of effects, side effects, drug levels and suicide risk, and education. She manages common side effects – sedation, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, EPS, metabolic effects, raised prolactin, agranulocytosis, lithium toxicity – and recognises emergencies such as NMS, serotonin syndrome and MAOI hypertensive crisis. Psychoeducation, simple regimens, side-effect management, depot injections, supervision and follow-up improve adherence and prevent relapse.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: (a) Define group therapy and explain its types. (4 marks) (b) Explain the therapeutic (curative) factors and the stages of group development. (6 marks) (c) Describe the role of the nurse as group leader. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: Seating arrangement in group therapy
labels: 6–10 members and the leader (with a co-leader opposite) seated in a circle so that everyone can see each other; no table in the middle; quiet
private room; fixed time of 60–90 minutes

answer_html:
(a) Definition and types (4 marks) Definition Group therapy is a form of psychotherapy in which a small number of patients (usually 6–10) meet regularly with a trained leader and use the interaction among group members to understand themselves, express feelings, learn from one another and change maladaptive behaviour.

Types of groups

  1. Psychotherapy groups – psychodynamic, interpersonal or cognitive behavioural groups that aim at insight and change.
  2. Psychoeducational (teaching) groups – about illness, medicines, relapse prevention, stress management; for patients and families.
  3. Supportive groups – share feelings and support one another (e.g. caregivers of persons with dementia or schizophrenia).
  4. Self-help groups – led by members themselves, without a professional leader – Alcoholics Anonymous (AA), Narcotics Anonymous, groups of persons recovering from mental illness.
  5. Activity and recreational groups – games, art, music, crafts, exercise.
  6. Social skills training groups – role play of conversation, assertiveness and problem-solving.
  7. Reminiscence and reality orientation groups – for elderly persons and those with dementia.
  8. Task groups – working together to complete a task (e.g. ward newsletter).
  9. Family and multi-family groups. - Closed groups keep the same members until the end; open groups accept new members as others leave (common in wards). - Homogeneous groups have members with similar problems; heterogeneous groups have varied members.

(b) Therapeutic factors and stages of group development (6 marks) Therapeutic (curative) factors – Irvin Yalom

  1. Instillation of hope – seeing others improve gives hope.
  2. Universality – realising that one is not alone; others have similar problems.
  3. Imparting of information – learning about illness and coping from the leader and members.
  4. Altruism – the experience of helping others raises self-esteem.
  5. Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group – re-experiencing family relationships in the group and correcting them.
  6. Development of socialising techniques – learning social skills.
  7. Imitative behaviour – learning by observing and copying others.
  8. Interpersonal learning – gaining insight into how one relates to others through feedback.
  9. Group cohesiveness – a sense of belonging and acceptance.
  10. Catharsis – expressing strong emotions in a safe setting.
  11. Existential factors – accepting responsibility for one's life and facing realities such as death and loneliness.

Stages of group development

  1. Initial (orientation / forming) stage – members are anxious, polite and dependent on the leader; they test the group and learn its rules; the leader explains purpose and norms (confidentiality, attendance, respect).
  2. Conflict (storming) stage – members challenge the leader and one another; struggles for control; anger and resistance appear; the leader accepts and handles conflict openly.
  3. Cohesiveness (norming) stage – trust and group identity develop; members support and give feedback.
  4. Working (performing) stage – members work on problems, give and receive feedback, try new behaviours; the leader acts as facilitator.
  5. Termination (adjourning) stage – members review progress, express feelings about separation and plan to continue gains; the leader prepares members in advance.

Roles of members

  • Task roles – initiator, information seeker and giver, coordinator, evaluator.
  • Maintenance roles – encourager, harmoniser, compromiser, gatekeeper (helps others to speak).
  • Individual (self-centred) roles – monopoliser (talks all the time), aggressor, blocker, recognition seeker, help-rejecting complainer, silent member.

(c) Role of the nurse as group leader (5 marks) Before the group

  • Decide the purpose, type, size, composition and duration; select suitable members (those in acute psychosis, severe paranoia, extreme agitation or high suicidal risk are not suitable for most groups); prepare members individually; arrange a quiet room with chairs in a circle; plan with the co-leader.

During the group

  • Set norms – confidentiality, punctuality, one person speaks at a time, respect, no violence.
  • Facilitate communication – encourage participation, link members' experiences, reflect feelings, clarify, summarise; keep the group focused on its goals.
  • Promote the therapeutic factors – hope, universality, cohesiveness, feedback and support.
  • Manage difficult behaviours – gently limit the monopoliser, invite the silent member, handle hostility and conflict openly, prevent scapegoating; protect vulnerable members.
  • Model healthy communication, honesty and acceptance.
  • Choose an appropriate leadership style – democratic for most groups, more autocratic (directive) for acutely ill or task groups, laissez-faire only with mature, self-directed groups.

After each session

  • Discuss the process with the co-leader; record attendance, themes, interactions and individual progress; seek supervision; plan the next session.
  • Termination – prepare members in advance and help them express feelings about ending.

Advantages of group therapy

  • Economical – one therapist treats many patients; members learn from each other; reduces isolation and stigma; provides a "real-life" social setting for practising skills.

Limitations

  • Less individual attention; confidentiality may be breached; not suitable for some acutely ill patients; dominant members may disturb the group; needs a skilled leader.

Common problems in groups and their management

  • Prolonged silence of the whole group – the leader comments on the silence, explores its meaning ("The group seems quiet today; what might be happening?") and invites members to share.
  • Monopolising member – acknowledge his contribution, set gentle limits ("Let us hear from others too"), and discuss the pattern individually if it continues.
  • Silent or withdrawn member – invite participation with simple, non-threatening questions; respect his pace; use activities.
  • Conflict and hostility – keep the discussion safe and respectful; focus on feelings and behaviour, not on attacking persons; help members resolve the issue.
  • Scapegoating – one member blamed by the others; the leader protects him and helps the group examine its own feelings.
  • Subgrouping and absenteeism – reinforce the norms of open communication and attendance; discuss reasons.
  • Anxiety at termination – prepare members early; review gains and future plans.

Indications and contraindications

  • Useful for – anxiety and depressive disorders, adjustment problems, substance use (with AA-type groups), chronic schizophrenia in the recovery phase (skills and psychoeducation groups), personality and relationship difficulties, caregivers and families.
  • Not suitable (or deferred) – acutely disturbed, severely paranoid, manic or highly suicidal patients, patients with severe cognitive impairment (except reality orientation groups), and those who are very hostile or disruptive.

Evaluation of the group
