  • Attendance and participation, achievement of group goals, changes in members' behaviour and functioning, members' feedback and the leader's self-evaluation through supervision.

Documentation of a group session – date, time and duration, type and purpose of the group, members present and absent, main themes discussed, important interactions, each member's participation and mood, problems arising, and the plan for the next session.

Nursing importance

  • Nurses lead many ward groups – psychoeducation, social skills, activity and medication groups – that help patients gain insight, practise relationships and support each other, preparing them for life in the community.

Conclusion Group therapy uses the interaction of a small group of patients with a trained leader to bring about change. Groups may be psychotherapeutic, educational, supportive, self-help, activity or skills-based, open or closed. Yalom's eleven therapeutic factors – such as hope, universality, altruism, interpersonal learning, cohesiveness and catharsis – operate through stages from orientation and conflict to cohesion, work and termination. The nurse as leader plans and composes the group, sets norms, facilitates communication, manages difficult members, models healthy behaviour, documents and evaluates.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: Explain behaviour therapy – its principles, techniques and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Behaviour therapy is a form of psychotherapy based on learning theory (classical conditioning – Pavlov; operant conditioning – Skinner; social learning – Bandura), which aims to change maladaptive behaviour and teach adaptive behaviour by applying principles of learning. It treats the symptom (behaviour) itself rather than searching for unconscious causes.

Principles

  • Behaviour, normal or abnormal, is learned and can be unlearned.
  • Focus on present, observable and measurable behaviour.
  • Behavioural analysis – identifying the Antecedents (what triggers the behaviour), the Behaviour and its Consequences (what maintains it), and recording a baseline.
  • Specific, measurable goals; active participation of the patient; homework; regular evaluation.

Techniques A. To increase desirable behaviour

  • Positive reinforcement – rewarding desired behaviour (praise, privileges).
  • Token economy – tokens earned for desired behaviour and exchanged for rewards.
  • Shaping – reinforcing successive approximations of the target behaviour; chaining – teaching a complex task step by step.
  • Modelling – learning by watching others perform the behaviour.
  • Social skills and assertiveness training – role play, feedback and practice.
  • Contingency contracting – a written agreement of behaviour and rewards.

B. To decrease undesirable behaviour

  • Extinction – withdrawing the reinforcement (e.g. ignoring attention-seeking behaviour).
  • Time-out – brief removal from a reinforcing situation (used with children).
  • Response cost – loss of tokens or privileges for undesired behaviour.
  • Aversion therapy – pairing the unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus (e.g. disulfiram with alcohol); used rarely and with ethical safeguards.

C. To reduce anxiety and fear

  • Relaxation training – Jacobson's progressive muscle relaxation, deep breathing.
  • Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) – the patient learns relaxation, builds a hierarchy of feared situations from least to most anxiety-provoking, and is gradually exposed (in imagination or real life) while relaxed.
  • Flooding (implosion) – prolonged exposure to the most feared situation until anxiety falls.
  • Exposure and response prevention (ERP) – for OCD: exposure to the feared stimulus while preventing the compulsion.
  • Biofeedback – learning to control bodily responses (muscle tension, heart rate) with the help of feedback from instruments.

Indications

  • Phobias, panic, OCD, PTSD; habit disorders (tics, nail biting), enuresis (bell-and-pad alarm), childhood behaviour problems, autism and intellectual disability, substance use, chronic schizophrenia (token economy, skills training), sexual dysfunction, insomnia.

Role of the nurse

  • Observe and record baseline and target behaviours; carry out behaviour programmes consistently throughout the day.
  • Give immediate reinforcement of desired behaviour; ignore or set limits on undesired behaviour as planned.
  • Teach and practise relaxation; assist in graded exposure; supervise homework.
  • Run token economy and social skills groups; involve the family so that changes continue at home.
  • Evaluate progress and revise the plan with the team.

Conclusion Behaviour therapy applies learning principles to replace maladaptive behaviour with adaptive behaviour. Its techniques include reinforcement, token economy, shaping, modelling and skills training; extinction, time-out and response cost; and relaxation, systematic desensitisation, flooding, ERP and biofeedback. The nurse observes, implements programmes consistently, reinforces progress and teaches the family.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: Explain cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT).
answer_html:
Definition Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) is a structured, short-term, problem-focused psychotherapy based on the idea that our thoughts influence our feelings and behaviour. Distorted, negative thinking leads to emotional distress and maladaptive behaviour; changing thoughts and behaviour improves mood and functioning. It was developed mainly by Aaron Beck (cognitive therapy) and Albert Ellis (rational emotive behaviour therapy).

Basic concepts

  • Automatic thoughts – quick, negative thoughts that come up in situations ("I'll fail", "Nobody likes me").
  • Core beliefs and schemas – deep beliefs about self, others and the world formed in early life ("I am worthless").
  • Beck's cognitive triad in depression – negative view of self, world and future.
  • Ellis's ABC model – Activating event → Belief about it → emotional and behavioural Consequence; therapy Disputes irrational beliefs to produce a new Effect.

Common cognitive distortions

  • All-or-nothing thinking ("If I am not perfect, I am a failure").
  • Overgeneralisation ("I failed once, I always fail").
  • Mental filter / disqualifying the positive – seeing only the negative.
  • Jumping to conclusions – mind reading, fortune telling.
  • Catastrophising – expecting the worst.
  • Emotional reasoning ("I feel useless, so I am useless").
  • "Should" statements, labelling and personalisation (blaming oneself for events not under one's control).

Process and techniques

  • Collaborative relationship; usually 12–20 sessions, each with an agenda, review of homework and feedback.
  • Psychoeducation about the CBT model.
  • Identifying automatic thoughts using thought records (situation – thought – emotion – evidence – alternative thought).
  • Socratic questioning and cognitive restructuring – examining evidence for and against the thought and forming a balanced alternative.
  • Behavioural techniques – activity scheduling and behavioural activation (depression), graded task assignment, behavioural experiments, exposure (anxiety), problem-solving, relaxation.
  • Homework between sessions; relapse prevention at the end.

Indications

  • Depression, anxiety disorders, panic, phobias, OCD, PTSD, eating disorders, insomnia (CBT-I), substance use, anger problems, chronic pain; adjunct in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (CBT for psychosis).

Advantages – evidence-based, short-term, teaches lifelong skills, reduces relapse; can be given individually, in groups, online or by trained non-specialists.

Role of the nurse

  • Help patients identify negative thoughts and link thoughts, feelings and behaviour.
  • Encourage completion of thought records and homework; plan activity schedules.
  • Reinforce coping statements and problem-solving in daily ward life; trained nurses can conduct CBT sessions.

Conclusion CBT, developed by Beck and Ellis, teaches patients to identify and correct automatic thoughts and cognitive distortions and to change behaviour, using thought records, Socratic questioning, cognitive restructuring, behavioural activation, exposure and homework. It is effective in depression, anxiety, OCD and many other conditions, and nurses support and deliver it.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: Explain family therapy and family psychoeducation in mental illness.
answer_html:
Definition Family therapy is a form of psychotherapy that treats the family as a unit (system), aiming to improve communication, relationships and problem-solving within the family, rather than focusing only on the individual patient (the "identified patient").

Basic assumption – the family is a system; a change in one member affects all; the patient's symptoms may be maintained by family patterns (poor communication, unclear boundaries, conflict, over-involvement).

Indications

  • Child and adolescent problems (conduct problems, school refusal), eating disorders.
  • Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder – to reduce expressed emotion and relapse.
  • Substance use disorders, marital conflict, family crises, chronic illness and disability, grief.

Approaches

  • Structural family therapy (Salvador Minuchin) – restructuring family boundaries, hierarchy and alliances.
  • Strategic family therapy (Jay Haley) – directives and tasks to change problem-maintaining patterns.
  • Bowen family systems therapy – differentiation of self, intergenerational patterns.
  • Systemic family therapy – circular questioning and reframing.
  • Behavioural family therapy and psychoeducational family intervention – education, communication and problem-solving skills training.

Process

  1. Assessment – family structure (genogram), communication patterns, roles, rules, boundaries, strengths, stressors and caregiver burden.
  2. Contract – goals, number and frequency of sessions, who will attend.
  3. Intervention – improving communication (speaking for oneself, listening), problem-solving, setting clear boundaries, reframing problems positively, assigning tasks and homework.
  4. Termination and follow-up.

Family psychoeducation (in severe mental illness)

  • Information about the illness, its causes (reducing blame), treatment and medicines.
  • Early warning signs of relapse and a relapse plan.
  • Reducing expressed emotion – criticism, hostility and emotional over-involvement increase relapse.
  • Communication and problem-solving skills; stress management for caregivers.
  • Support groups, welfare schemes and community resources.

Role of the nurse

  • Assess family functioning and burden; involve the family from admission.
  • Conduct psychoeducation sessions and support groups; teach practical caregiving skills.
  • Model good communication; help the family solve everyday problems; co-facilitate family therapy if trained.
  • Provide home visits and follow-up; link with social workers and NGOs.

Conclusion Family therapy treats the family as a system to improve communication, boundaries and problem-solving, using structural, strategic, Bowen, systemic, behavioural and psychoeducational approaches. Family psychoeducation in severe mental illness reduces expressed emotion and relapse, and the nurse assesses, educates, supports and involves families throughout care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: Explain the therapeutic community and milieu therapy, with the role of the nurse.
tags: role of nurse as milieu manager
answer_html:
Definitions

  • Milieu therapy – the purposeful use of the whole environment of the ward – people, physical setting, routines and activities – as a therapeutic tool to help patients develop more adaptive behaviour. "Milieu" means surroundings.
  • Therapeutic community – a form of milieu therapy developed by Maxwell Jones (UK, 1950s), in which patients and staff share responsibility for running the ward and the community itself is the main agent of treatment.

Principles of a therapeutic community (Rapoport)

  1. Democratisation – all members (patients and staff) take part in decisions about the ward.
  2. Permissiveness – members tolerate and accept each other's behaviour within limits, so feelings can be expressed.
  3. Communalism – shared activities, open communication and close relationships; everyone contributes.
  4. Reality confrontation – patients receive honest feedback about how their behaviour affects others.

Features

  • Daily community meetings of patients and staff; patient government or ward committee.
  • Open communication; shared responsibilities (keeping the ward clean, planning activities).
  • A structured daily programme – group therapies, occupational and recreational activities.
  • Clear rules and limits, decided and reviewed together.

Functions of a therapeutic milieu (Gunderson)

  1. Containment – safety, physical care, protection from harm.
  2. Support – acceptance, comfort and encouragement that raise self-esteem.
  3. Structure – predictable routines, schedules and clear limits.
  4. Involvement – active participation in the ward community and its activities.
  5. Validation – recognition of the patient's individuality and feelings.

Characteristics of a therapeutic ward environment

  • Clean, homely, well-lit and ventilated, with privacy, personal belongings, a dining area, recreation room, garden and safe furniture.
  • Safety measures without a prison-like atmosphere (no chains or cages; least restrictive).
  • Respectful, consistent, hopeful staff attitudes.

Role of the nurse (milieu manager)

  • Creates and maintains a safe, structured and supportive environment; assesses risks.
  • Organises community meetings and daily activities; encourages participation and responsibility.
  • Sets and maintains consistent limits; gives honest feedback.
  • Uses every interaction (meals, bathing, recreation) as a therapeutic opportunity; models healthy behaviour.
  • Coordinates with the team and families; evaluates the milieu.

Conclusion Milieu therapy uses the whole ward environment therapeutically, and the therapeutic community (Maxwell Jones) makes patients and staff partners in running the ward, guided by democratisation, permissiveness, communalism and reality confrontation. A therapeutic milieu provides containment, support, structure, involvement and validation, with the nurse as its manager.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: Explain occupational therapy, recreational therapy and expressive (art, music and dance) therapies in psychiatry.
answer_html:
Introduction Activity-based therapies use purposeful and enjoyable activities to improve functioning, express feelings, develop skills and use time constructively. They are especially useful in long-stay patients and in rehabilitation.

1. Occupational therapy (OT)

  • Definition – the use of purposeful activity or work to help patients develop, regain or maintain the skills needed for daily living, work and leisure.
  • Activities – activities of daily living, cooking, gardening, tailoring, weaving, carpentry, candle and paper-bag making, computer skills, clerical work.
  • Purposes – divert attention from symptoms, improve concentration, coordination and work habits, build confidence and self-esteem, provide vocational skills and sometimes income, encourage socialisation.
  • Principles – individualised and graded according to the patient's ability and interest; short, simple tasks first; meaningful and success-oriented; regular evaluation.

2. Recreational therapy

  • Activities – indoor and outdoor games, sports, yoga, walks, picnics, outings, cultural programmes, festival celebrations, television, reading, puzzles.
  • Purposes – pleasure and relaxation, release of tension and aggression in acceptable ways, social interaction and cooperation, physical fitness, constructive use of leisure time, improvement of mood.

3. Expressive therapies

  • Art therapy – drawing, painting and clay modelling for non-verbal expression of feelings; useful in children and in patients who cannot talk about their feelings.
  • Music therapy – listening, singing and playing instruments to relax, improve mood, stimulate memory (dementia) and promote socialisation.
  • Dance and movement therapy – expression of emotions through movement, improving body awareness and coordination.
  • Drama therapy and psychodrama (J. L. Moreno) – acting out conflicts and situations to gain insight and practise new behaviour.
  • Play therapy – for children to express feelings through toys and play.
  • Bibliotherapy – guided reading of selected books.

Role of the nurse

  • Assess the patient's interests, abilities and limitations; plan suitable, graded activities with the occupational therapist.
  • Motivate and accompany patients; praise effort and achievement.
  • Supervise safety (sharp tools, matches); observe and record participation, concentration, mood and social interaction.
  • Organise ward recreational programmes and celebrations; link vocational skills to rehabilitation.

Conclusion Occupational therapy uses purposeful work to build daily living and vocational skills; recreational therapy provides enjoyment, socialisation and release of tension; and art, music, dance, drama, play and bibliotherapy allow expression of feelings. The nurse plans, motivates, supervises and records these activities as part of holistic care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: Explain the alternative and complementary therapies – yoga, meditation and relaxation techniques – in mental health.
answer_html:
Introduction Complementary therapies are used along with standard treatment to promote relaxation, reduce stress and improve well-being. Many have their roots in Indian traditions and are increasingly supported by research for anxiety, depression, insomnia and stress-related disorders. They are not substitutes for medical treatment of severe mental illness.

1. Yoga

  • An ancient Indian discipline uniting body, mind and breath: asanas (postures), pranayama (breathing exercises) and dhyana (meditation).
  • Benefits – reduces stress hormones and anxiety, improves mood, sleep, concentration and physical fitness; used as an add-on in depression, anxiety and schizophrenia (e.g. at NIMHANS); reduces weight gain from medicines.

2. Meditation

  • Focusing attention on breath, a word (mantra) or the present moment to calm the mind.
  • Types – mindfulness meditation, transcendental meditation, Vipassana.
  • Benefits – reduces anxiety and rumination, prevents relapse of depression (mindfulness-based cognitive therapy), improves emotional regulation.

3. Relaxation techniques

  • Deep (diaphragmatic) breathing – slow breaths through the nose, expanding the abdomen.
  • Progressive muscle relaxation (Jacobson) – tensing and then relaxing groups of muscles one by one, from feet to face.
  • Guided imagery – imagining a calm, pleasant scene.
  • Autogenic training – self-suggestions of warmth and heaviness in the limbs.
  • Biofeedback – using instruments to learn control of muscle tension, heart rate or skin temperature.

4. Other therapies – massage, aromatherapy, music, spiritual practices and prayer; AYUSH systems (Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy) used by many families.

Indications – anxiety, stress-related disorders, mild depression, insomnia, tension headache, substance use recovery, and as an adjunct in many disorders; stress management for healthy people and caregivers.

Precautions

  • Should not replace prescribed treatment; check for herb–drug interactions.
  • Deep meditation may not suit acutely psychotic or severely dissociative patients; yoga postures may need modification for physical illness.
  • Use trained instructors.

Role of the nurse

  • Teach and practise simple breathing, PMR and guided imagery with patients (individually or in groups).
  • Organise daily yoga sessions in the ward; encourage continuation at home.
  • Use relaxation to reduce anxiety before procedures and at bedtime.
  • Respect patients' cultural and spiritual practices and integrate them where safe.

Conclusion Yoga, meditation and relaxation techniques such as deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery and biofeedback reduce stress and anxiety and improve mood and sleep. Used alongside standard treatment, with suitable precautions, they are valuable tools that nurses can teach and practise with patients.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: Explain individual psychotherapy – its types and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Psychotherapy is the treatment of emotional and behavioural problems by psychological means, through a professional relationship between a trained therapist and the patient, using verbal and non-verbal communication, with the aim of relieving symptoms, changing maladaptive patterns and promoting growth. In individual psychotherapy, the therapist works with one patient at a time.

Types (by depth) 1. Supportive psychotherapy – strengthens existing defences and coping, without aiming at deep change; for patients in crisis, with severe illness or limited capacity for insight.

  • Techniques – ventilation (allowing expression of feelings), reassurance (realistic), guidance and advice, persuasion and suggestion, environmental manipulation (reducing stressors at home or work), encouragement, education.

2. Re-educative psychotherapy – helps the patient change attitudes and behaviour through learning and conscious effort.

  • Cognitive behaviour therapy, behaviour therapy, counselling, problem-solving therapy, motivational interviewing (substance use).
  • Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) – a short-term therapy for depression focusing on four problem areas: grief, role disputes, role transitions and interpersonal deficits.

3. Reconstructive psychotherapy – aims at deep personality change by bringing unconscious conflicts into awareness.

  • Psychoanalysis (free association, dream analysis, interpretation of transference), psychodynamic psychotherapy.

Other forms – brief (time-limited) psychotherapies, crisis intervention, client-centred therapy (Rogers), dialectical behaviour therapy (for emotional dysregulation and self-harm).

Essential elements of psychotherapy

  • A trusting therapeutic relationship; a contract (goals, time, frequency, confidentiality); active listening and empathy; the patient's motivation and participation; regular evaluation; planned termination.

Indications – anxiety and stress-related disorders, depression, adjustment problems, personality and relationship difficulties, substance use; as an adjunct to medication in severe illness.

Role of the nurse

  • Provides supportive psychotherapy and counselling in day-to-day care – listening, encouraging ventilation, realistic reassurance, problem-solving and health education.
  • Reinforces the work of the therapist (e.g. CBT homework); observes and reports the patient's responses.
  • With advanced training, nurses practise individual psychotherapies (CBT, IPT, motivational interviewing) as nurse therapists.
  • Maintains confidentiality and boundaries; refers patients for specialised therapy.

Conclusion Individual psychotherapy treats mental and emotional problems through a professional relationship. It may be supportive (ventilation, reassurance, guidance, environmental manipulation), re-educative (CBT, behaviour therapy, IPT, counselling, motivational interviewing) or reconstructive (psychoanalysis, psychodynamic therapy). Nurses provide supportive therapy and counselling, reinforce other therapies and, with training, practise specific psychotherapies.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: Explain the special considerations in psychopharmacology for children, the elderly, pregnant and breastfeeding women.
answer_html:
Introduction Children, the elderly, pregnant and breastfeeding women and people with physical illness respond differently to psychotropic drugs, so dosing and monitoring need special care.

1. Children and adolescents

  • Doses are based on weight and age; start low and increase slowly.
  • Stimulants (methylphenidate) for ADHD – monitor appetite, sleep, growth and heart rate.
  • Antidepressants – may increase suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents and young adults in the first weeks – close monitoring and family education; fluoxetine is commonly preferred.
  • Antipsychotics cause weight gain, metabolic changes and raised prolactin more in young people – monitor growth and metabolism.
  • Psychological treatments are often first-line; involve parents and school.

2. Elderly

  • "Start low, go slow" – reduced liver and kidney function, more body fat and less water increase drug levels and duration; more sensitivity to side effects; multiple medicines (polypharmacy) and interactions.
  • Avoid drugs with strong anticholinergic effects (tricyclics, chlorpromazine) – cause confusion, delirium, urinary retention, constipation.
  • Orthostatic hypotension and sedation cause falls and fractures.
  • Benzodiazepines – avoid if possible (confusion, falls, dependence).
  • SSRIs – risk of hyponatraemia and bleeding; check sodium.
  • Antipsychotics in dementia increase the risk of stroke and death – use only when essential, at the lowest dose, for the shortest time.
  • Lithium – lower doses and levels; risk of toxicity with dehydration and diuretics.

3. Pregnancy

  • Decisions balance the risk of untreated illness (relapse, suicide, poor self-care) against risks to the fetus; plan pregnancy with the psychiatrist.
  • Sodium valproate – high risk of neural tube defects and developmental problems – avoided in women who may become pregnant unless there is no alternative and effective contraception is used.
  • Carbamazepine – neural tube defects; give folic acid.
  • Lithium – small risk of cardiac anomaly (Ebstein's anomaly); needs fetal echocardiography and close level monitoring, especially around delivery.
  • SSRIs (e.g. sertraline) are commonly used; possible neonatal adaptation symptoms after birth; paroxetine is generally avoided.
  • ECT is a relatively safe option for severe depression or psychosis in pregnancy.
  • Monitor the newborn for withdrawal or toxicity.

4. Breastfeeding

  • Most drugs pass into milk in small amounts; sertraline and some others have low levels and are often preferred; lithium and clozapine are generally avoided; observe the baby for sedation, poor feeding and jaundice.

5. Physically ill patients

  • Kidney disease – reduce lithium and some other drugs; liver disease – care with valproate and benzodiazepines; heart disease – avoid drugs that prolong QTc; epilepsy – avoid drugs that lower the seizure threshold.

Nursing considerations

  • Accurate weight and baseline investigations; careful dose calculation; observation for side effects, falls and confusion.
  • Teaching of patients and families in simple language; contraception counselling for women on valproate and other teratogenic drugs.
  • Coordination with obstetricians, paediatricians and physicians.

Conclusion Psychotropic drugs require special care in children (weight-based doses, suicidality and metabolic monitoring), the elderly (start low, go slow, avoid anticholinergic drugs and benzodiazepines, caution with antipsychotics in dementia), pregnancy (avoid valproate, careful use of lithium, SSRIs often used, ECT as a safe option), breastfeeding (prefer drugs with low milk levels) and physical illness (adjust for kidney, liver and heart disease), with the nurse ensuring safe dosing, monitoring and education.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: List the techniques of behaviour therapy.
answer_html:
Techniques of behaviour therapy

  1. Systematic desensitisation – graded exposure to a fear hierarchy while relaxed (Wolpe).
  2. Flooding / implosion – prolonged exposure to the most feared situation.
  3. Exposure and response prevention (ERP) – for OCD.
  4. Relaxation training – progressive muscle relaxation, deep breathing; biofeedback.
  5. Aversion therapy – pairing an unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus.
  6. Positive reinforcement and token economy.
  7. Shaping and chaining – step-by-step learning of complex behaviour.
  8. Modelling – learning by observation.
  9. Social skills and assertiveness training.
  10. Extinction, time-out and response cost – to reduce undesired behaviour.
  11. Contingency contracting; bell-and-pad alarm for enuresis.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: What is a token economy?
answer_html: A token economy is a behaviour modification programme based on operant conditioning, in which patients earn tokens (coins, stars, points – secondary reinforcers) for specified desired behaviours and exchange them for rewards (privileges, snacks, outings, television time). Requirements – clearly defined target behaviours (e.g. bathing, making the bed, attending activities); immediate and consistent award of tokens by all staff; a "price list" of rewards; gradual fading of tokens as natural rewards (praise, satisfaction) take over. Uses – chronic schizophrenia and long-stay patients, intellectual disability, children with behaviour problems, rehabilitation and de-addiction settings.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: Write the features and management of neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS).
answer_html: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare, life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic drugs (usually high-potency drugs, rapid dose increase, depot injections, dehydration). Features – high fever, severe "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity, altered consciousness (confusion, stupor), autonomic instability (labile BP, tachycardia, sweating, incontinence), raised CPK, leucocytosis; may lead to renal failure, respiratory failure and death. Management – stop the antipsychotic immediately; cooling, IV fluids, monitoring of vital signs, urine output and CPK; ICU care; dantrolene (muscle relaxant) and bromocriptine (dopamine agonist) as ordered; ECT in severe cases. Antipsychotics are restarted cautiously after recovery.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: What is serotonin syndrome?
answer_html:
Serotonin syndrome is a potentially dangerous condition caused by excess serotonin activity, usually from combinations of serotonergic drugs – SSRIs or SNRIs with MAO inhibitors, tramadol, linezolid, triptans or St John's wort – or overdose. Features (triad)

  1. Mental changes – agitation, restlessness, confusion.
  2. Autonomic hyperactivity – fever, sweating, tachycardia, diarrhoea, dilated pupils.
  3. Neuromuscular abnormalities – tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus and clonus (especially in the legs). Management – stop the serotonergic drugs, supportive care, cooling and IV fluids, benzodiazepines for agitation, cyproheptadine (serotonin antagonist) as ordered; ICU for severe cases.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: What are depot antipsychotics? State the nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Depot (long-acting injectable) antipsychotics are oily or long-acting preparations given by deep intramuscular injection every 2–4 weeks (or longer), releasing the drug slowly. Examples – fluphenazine decanoate, haloperidol decanoate, flupentixol decanoate, paliperidone palmitate, long-acting aripiprazole. Uses – patients with schizophrenia who relapse because of non-adherence or prefer occasional injections. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Give a test dose first for first-generation depots, as ordered.
  2. Give by deep IM (Z-track) injection in the gluteal or deltoid muscle; rotate sites; do not massage.
  3. Maintain a depot register with due dates; follow up defaulters.
  4. Observe for EPS and injection-site pain or swelling.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: What is repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS)?
answer_html:
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a non-invasive brain stimulation treatment in which a magnetic coil placed on the scalp produces brief magnetic pulses that induce small electric currents in the underlying cortex (usually the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex), changing brain activity.

  • No anaesthesia is needed and the patient remains awake; sessions are given daily, 5 days a week for about 4–6 weeks.
  • Uses – treatment-resistant depression; also OCD and persistent auditory hallucinations (under evaluation).
  • Side effects – headache, scalp discomfort; seizures (rare).
  • Contraindications – metal implants in or near the head, cochlear implants, history of seizures (relative).

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Treatment Modalities and Therapies Used in Mental Disorders
question: Write the monitoring required in a patient on clozapine.
answer_html:
Clozapine is the most effective drug for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, but needs close monitoring:

  1. Agranulocytosis – blood counts (WBC and neutrophils) before starting, weekly for the first 18 weeks and then regularly (monthly) as per protocol; stop if counts fall; report fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers.
  2. Myocarditis – in the first weeks: fever, chest pain, tachycardia, breathlessness.
  3. Seizures – dose-related.
  4. Severe constipation – may lead to intestinal obstruction; fibre, fluids, laxatives.
  5. Hypersalivation (especially at night), sedation, orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, fever.
  6. Weight gain and metabolic syndrome – weight, glucose and lipids.
  7. Stopping smoking raises clozapine levels – watch for toxicity.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: (a) Define schizophrenia and explain its aetiology. (3 marks) (b) Describe its clinical features, types and diagnostic criteria. (5 marks) (c) Explain the management and nursing care of a patient with schizophrenia. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Symptom groups of schizophrenia
labels: psychomotor (catatonia) – leading to social and occupational decline

answer_html:
(a) Definition and aetiology (3 marks) Definition Schizophrenia is a severe, usually chronic psychotic disorder characterised by disturbances of thinking, perception, emotion, behaviour and volition – such as delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech and behaviour and negative symptoms – with impaired reality testing and decline in social and occupational functioning, in clear consciousness. The term was coined by Eugen Bleuler (1911); Kraepelin called it "dementia praecox".

  • Lifetime prevalence – about 1%; onset usually in late adolescence or early adulthood (men about 15–25 years, women about 25–35 years); equal in both sexes.

Aetiology

  • Genetic – risk about 10% if one parent is affected, about 40–50% in an identical twin; polygenic.
  • Neurochemical – dopamine hypothesis (excess mesolimbic dopamine – positive symptoms; reduced mesocortical dopamine – negative symptoms); glutamate (NMDA) hypofunction; serotonin.
  • Neurodevelopmental and structural – obstetric complications, maternal infection and malnutrition, winter/spring birth; enlarged ventricles, reduced grey matter.
  • Psychosocial – stressful life events, urban living, migration, high expressed emotion in the family (relapse), childhood adversity.
  • Substance use – cannabis increases risk, especially in adolescence.
  • Stress–vulnerability model – illness appears when stress acts on a biologically vulnerable person.

(b) Clinical features, types and diagnostic criteria (5 marks) Clinical features

  1. Positive symptoms (excess or distortion of normal functions)
    • Delusions – persecution, reference, control, grandeur, jealousy, bizarre delusions.
    • Hallucinations – mostly auditory: voices talking about the patient in the third person, commenting on his actions or giving commands.
    • Disorganised speech – loosening of associations, tangentiality, neologisms, word salad, thought block.
    • Disorganised or bizarre behaviour; inappropriate affect (laughing without reason).
  2. Negative symptoms (loss of normal functions) – the "5 As": alogia (poverty of speech), affective flattening (blunted affect), avolition (lack of motivation), anhedonia, asociality (social withdrawal); poor self-care.
  3. Cognitive symptoms – poor attention, memory and executive function (planning, abstract thinking).
  4. Passivity phenomena – thought insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting; made feelings, impulses and actions.
  5. Catatonic symptoms – stupor, mutism, negativism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia, echopraxia, excitement.
  6. Affective symptoms – depression, anxiety; suicide risk (about 5% die by suicide).
  7. Poor insight and judgement; social and occupational decline.

Bleuler's fundamental symptoms – the "4 As" – Association disturbance (loosening), Affective disturbance (blunted or inappropriate affect), Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal into a private world).

Schneider's first-rank symptoms – audible thoughts, voices arguing or discussing, voices commenting on one's actions, somatic passivity, thought withdrawal, thought insertion, thought broadcasting, made feelings, made impulses, made volitional acts and delusional perception.

Types (classical subtypes of ICD-10; removed in ICD-11)

  1. Paranoid schizophrenia – commonest; prominent persecutory or grandiose delusions and auditory hallucinations; relatively preserved personality; later onset; better prognosis.
  2. Hebephrenic (disorganised) schizophrenia – early onset (15–25 years); disorganised speech and behaviour, silly, inappropriate affect, mannerisms; poor prognosis.
  3. Catatonic schizophrenia – psychomotor disturbances – stupor or excitement, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, mutism.
  4. Undifferentiated schizophrenia – features of more than one type.
  5. Residual schizophrenia – chronic stage with negative symptoms after earlier positive symptoms.
  6. Simple schizophrenia – insidious negative symptoms without prominent positive symptoms.
  7. Post-schizophrenic depression. - ICD-11 replaces subtypes with symptom specifiers (positive, negative, depressive, manic, psychomotor and cognitive symptoms) and course specifiers.

Diagnostic criteria

  • ICD-11 – at least two characteristic symptoms (at least one being persistent delusions, persistent hallucinations, disorganised thinking or experiences of influence/passivity) present for at least 1 month, not due to another condition or substance.
  • DSM-5-TR – two or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour and negative symptoms (at least one of the first three) for a significant part of 1 month, with continuous signs of disturbance for at least 6 months and decline in functioning.

(c) Management and nursing care (7 marks) Medical management

  • Antipsychotic drugs – first-generation (haloperidol, chlorpromazine, fluphenazine) and second-generation (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole); clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; depot injections for non-adherence; maintenance treatment usually for at least 1–2 years after a first episode and longer after relapses.
  • ECT – catatonia, acute excitement, suicidal risk, treatment resistance.
  • Psychosocial interventions – psychoeducation, family intervention to reduce expressed emotion, social skills training, CBT for psychosis, cognitive remediation, vocational rehabilitation, case management, day care and community follow-up.

Nursing assessment

  • History and MSE; observation of hallucinatory behaviour, delusions, suspiciousness, withdrawal, self-care, sleep and food intake.
  • Risk assessment – violence, suicide (including command hallucinations), absconding, self-neglect; physical health and side effects; family's knowledge, attitude and burden.

Nursing diagnoses and interventions

  1. Disturbed sensory perception (auditory hallucinations)
    • Observe for hallucinatory cues; ask directly about voices and their content, especially commands.
    • Do not argue or agree; present reality ("I don't hear voices, but I can see you are frightened").
    • Engage in reality-based activities; teach coping (talking to someone, humming, music, activity); give antipsychotics as ordered.
  2. Disturbed thought processes (delusions)
    • Build trust through consistency and honesty; do not argue with or reinforce delusions; respond to underlying feelings; focus on real events; avoid whispering or laughing near a suspicious patient; show sealed medicines and food if he fears poisoning.
  3. Risk for violence (self- or other-directed)
    • Observe closely; remove harmful objects; reduce stimulation; recognise early signs of agitation; de-escalate; set limits; PRN medication; restraint only as a last resort, as per law; suicide precautions when needed.
  4. Social isolation and impaired social interaction
    • Brief, frequent one-to-one contacts; gradually involve in small groups and activities; social skills training; praise every effort.
  5. Self-care deficit (bathing, grooming, feeding, toileting)
    • Encourage and assist; set a simple daily routine; give step-by-step prompts; praise independence; monitor nutrition, weight, bowel habits and sleep.
  6. Disturbed sleep pattern – sleep hygiene, daytime activity, reduce night-time stimulation, medicines as ordered.
  7. Ineffective health maintenance / non-adherence
    • Explain the illness and medicines; manage side effects; supervise intake (check for cheeking); involve the family; consider depot injections.
  8. Interrupted family processes and caregiver strain
    • Family psychoeducation; teach early warning signs of relapse; reduce criticism and over-involvement; link with support groups and welfare schemes (disability certificate).

Discharge planning and rehabilitation

  • A written relapse prevention plan; regular follow-up at the hospital or DMHP clinic; day care, vocational training and supported employment; avoidance of alcohol and cannabis; regular routine and sleep.

Prognosis

  • Better with acute onset, later onset, a clear precipitating stress, good premorbid adjustment, prominent positive or mood symptoms, being married, good family support and early treatment.
  • Worse with insidious early onset, poor premorbid functioning, prominent negative symptoms, family history of schizophrenia, long duration of untreated psychosis, substance use and poor adherence.

Nursing importance

  • Because schizophrenia is long-lasting and relapsing, the nurse's trusting relationship, close observation, safety measures, skills training, adherence support and family education determine how well the patient recovers and stays in the community.

Conclusion Schizophrenia is a severe psychotic disorder affecting about 1% of people, arising from genetic, neurochemical (dopamine, glutamate), neurodevelopmental and psychosocial factors. It presents with positive, negative, cognitive, passivity and catatonic symptoms (Bleuler's 4 As and Schneider's first-rank symptoms), classically divided into paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic, undifferentiated, residual and simple types (replaced by specifiers in ICD-11). Management combines antipsychotics (clozapine for resistance, depots for non-adherence), ECT when indicated and psychosocial interventions, while nursing care addresses hallucinations, delusions, risk of violence and suicide, isolation, self-care, sleep, adherence and the family, with rehabilitation and relapse prevention.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: Prepare a nursing care plan for a patient with catatonic schizophrenia.
answer_html:
Introduction Catatonic schizophrenia is marked by psychomotor disturbances – catatonic stupor (immobility, mutism, negativism, posturing, waxy flexibility, rigidity, refusal of food) or catatonic excitement (purposeless, uncontrolled overactivity). Patients may switch suddenly from stupor to excitement. Treatment is with lorazepam and ECT, along with antipsychotics; nursing care prevents life-threatening complications.

Nursing care plan 1. Imbalanced nutrition and risk for deficient fluid volume related to refusal of food and fluids (stupor, negativism)

  • Goal – adequate intake; no dehydration or weight loss.
  • Interventions – offer small, frequent soft feeds and fluids patiently, spoon-feeding when needed; nasogastric feeding or IV fluids as ordered if intake is inadequate; keep an intake–output chart and daily weight; watch for dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.
  • Evaluation – intake adequate, weight stable, urine output normal.

2. Self-care deficit (bathing, grooming, toileting, oral hygiene)

  • Provide complete care while encouraging any participation; oral and eye care (eyes may remain open); regular toileting; watch for urinary retention and constipation (catheterisation or laxatives as ordered).

3. Impaired physical mobility and risk for pressure ulcers, contractures and deep vein thrombosis

  • Change position 2-hourly; pressure-area care and a ripple mattress; passive range-of-motion exercises; DVT prophylaxis as ordered; observe calves for swelling.

4. Risk for aspiration

  • Feed in an upright position; check swallowing; suction available; lateral position if drowsy.

5. Risk for violence (during catatonic excitement)

  • Close observation; safe environment with minimal stimulation; remove harmful objects; adequate staff; calm, firm approach; medication as ordered; restraint only as a last resort, as per law.

6. Impaired verbal communication related to mutism

  • Talk to the patient in a calm, simple way and explain every procedure – patients in stupor are often aware of everything and may remember it later; do not discuss the patient in front of him; use touch and non-verbal communication carefully; give time to respond.

7. Risk for complications – malignant catatonia and NMS

  • Monitor temperature, pulse, BP and level of consciousness at least 4-hourly; watch for fever, increasing rigidity and autonomic instability and report immediately (antipsychotics may need to be stopped).

8. Care related to treatment

  • Give lorazepam as ordered and observe for improvement and over-sedation; prepare the patient for ECT and give pre- and post-ECT care.

9. Interrupted family processes

  • Explain the condition and its good response to treatment; involve the family in care and feeding; prepare them for follow-up.

Conclusion Nursing care of catatonic schizophrenia focuses on maintaining nutrition and fluids, complete self-care including bladder and bowel care, prevention of immobility complications and aspiration, safety during excitement, continuous gentle communication, monitoring for malignant catatonia and NMS, and care during lorazepam and ECT treatment, with family support.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: Explain the nursing management of a patient with hallucinations.
answer_html:
Definition A hallucination is a perception in the absence of an external stimulus, experienced as real, in any sensory modality – auditory (most common in schizophrenia), visual (common in delirium and substance withdrawal), olfactory, gustatory or tactile.

Assessment

  • Behavioural cues – talking or laughing to oneself, pausing as if listening, looking around, covering ears, gesturing, sudden anger or fear, poor concentration, not responding to others.
  • Ask directly and calmly: "Do you hear voices when no one is around? What do they say?"
  • Type, content, frequency, duration and triggers; whether the voices are commanding (to harm self or others); the patient's response and degree of control; insight; effect on sleep, eating and activities.

Nursing diagnosis – Disturbed sensory perception (auditory) related to altered brain chemistry/psychosis, as evidenced by talking and laughing to self and statements about hearing voices.

Nursing interventions

  1. Build trust – brief, frequent, consistent contacts; calm, simple language; call the patient by name before approaching.
  2. Observe closely for hallucinatory behaviour and risk; record the content and the patient's response.
  3. Do not argue or agree with the hallucination – acknowledge the experience without confirming it: "I know the voices are real to you, but I do not hear them."
  4. Respond to the feelings (fear, anger) and present reality; keep the patient engaged in reality-based activities and conversation.
  5. Safety – with command hallucinations to harm self or others, increase observation, remove dangerous objects, inform the team and take suicide or violence precautions.
  6. Reduce stimulation – a quiet environment; avoid noisy, crowded places when the patient is disturbed.
  7. Teach coping strategies – talking to a trusted person, humming or singing, listening to music with earphones, reading aloud, physical activity, telling the voices to stop, keeping busy; note which strategies help.
  8. Medication – give antipsychotics as ordered; monitor response and side effects; encourage adherence.
  9. Meet basic needs – food, fluids, sleep and hygiene, which may be neglected.
  10. Family education – recognising hallucinatory behaviour, responding calmly, ensuring medication and follow-up.

Evaluation – the patient recognises hallucinations as symptoms, uses coping strategies, engages in activities, remains safe and takes medicines.

Conclusion Hallucinations are perceptions without a stimulus, mostly auditory in schizophrenia. The nurse assesses their nature and risk (especially command hallucinations), builds trust, neither argues nor agrees, presents reality, reduces stimulation, keeps the patient safe, teaches coping strategies, gives medication and educates the family.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: Explain the nursing management of a patient with delusions (suspicious patient).
answer_html:
Definition A delusion is a false, firm, fixed belief, not in keeping with the person's social, cultural and educational background, which is held with conviction despite clear evidence to the contrary and cannot be corrected by reasoning. Common types – persecution, reference, control, grandeur, jealousy (infidelity), love (erotomania), guilt, nihilism, somatic and religious delusions.

Assessment

  • Type, content, conviction, fixity and how much the patient acts on the delusion; emotional intensity.
  • Risk – persecutory delusions may lead to violence or absconding; delusions of infidelity to harm of the spouse; nihilistic delusions to refusal of food; guilt to suicide; poisoning delusions to refusal of food and medicines.
  • Effect on sleep, eating, self-care and relationships; insight.

Nursing diagnosis – Disturbed thought processes related to psychosis, as evidenced by fixed false beliefs of persecution and suspiciousness.

Nursing interventions

  1. Build trust – be honest, consistent and reliable; keep promises; introduce yourself; explain every procedure beforehand; same staff where possible.
  2. Do not argue with, challenge or ridicule the delusion, and do not agree with or reinforce it ("I understand you believe that, but I don't see it that way").
  3. Respond to the feelings and needs behind the delusion (fear, insecurity, low self-esteem) rather than its content.
  4. Focus on reality – talk about real events and people; engage the patient in simple, reality-based activities; limit discussion of the delusion once it has been assessed.
  5. For the suspicious patient
    • Avoid whispering, laughing or talking in low tones near him; avoid sudden movements or unexpected touch; maintain personal space.
    • Medicines – show them in the sealed strip, let him see them being taken out; never hide them in food.
    • Food – if he fears poisoning, offer sealed or packed food, or let him serve himself or eat with others.
    • Allow some control over decisions; involve him in planning care.
  6. Safety – observe for aggression or self-harm; remove dangerous objects; inform the team about threats to specific persons.
  7. Medication – antipsychotics as ordered; monitor response and side effects.
  8. Gently provide feedback and reinforce reality-based thinking; praise when the patient talks about reality.
  9. Family education – not to argue with the patient, ensure medication, recognise early relapse signs and danger to others.

Evaluation – the patient trusts staff, talks less about the delusion, carries out daily activities, eats and takes medicines, and does not harm self or others.

Conclusion Delusions are fixed false beliefs that cannot be corrected by reasoning. Nursing management includes assessment of type and risk, building trust through honesty and consistency, neither arguing with nor reinforcing the delusion, responding to underlying feelings, focusing on reality, special measures for suspicious patients (sealed medicines and food, no whispering, respect for space), safety, medication and family education.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: Explain delusional disorder and the other psychotic disorders.
answer_html:
Introduction Besides schizophrenia, ICD-11 includes delusional disorder, acute and transient psychotic disorder, schizoaffective disorder and schizotypal disorder among the primary psychotic disorders. Psychosis may also be due to substances or medical conditions.

1. Delusional disorder (persistent delusional disorder)

  • Persistent, well-systematised delusions lasting at least 3 months, without prominent hallucinations, disorganisation or negative symptoms; behaviour and functioning are relatively normal apart from the delusion; onset usually in middle age.
  • Types – persecutory (commonest), jealous (morbid jealousy, "Othello syndrome" – dangerous to the spouse), erotomanic (belief that a person of higher status loves the patient), grandiose, somatic (infestation, body odour, deformity) and mixed.
  • Management – antipsychotics, supportive psychotherapy and CBT, treatment of anxiety and depression; risk assessment (separation of spouses may be needed in morbid jealousy).
  • Nursing – build trust, avoid confrontation, focus on feelings and functioning, safety of others.

2. Acute and transient psychotic disorder (ATPD)

  • Acute onset (within about 2 weeks) of psychotic symptoms that change rapidly in nature and intensity (polymorphic) – delusions, hallucinations, confusion, emotional turmoil – often after acute stress.
  • Lasts days to weeks and resolves within about 3 months; good prognosis; more common in women and in developing countries (DSM-5-TR equivalents: brief psychotic disorder and schizophreniform disorder).
  • Management – short-term antipsychotics and benzodiazepines, reduction of stress, observation for recurrence.

3. Schizoaffective disorder

  • Symptoms of schizophrenia and a mood episode (manic, depressive or mixed) present at the same time, during the same episode.
  • Management – antipsychotics with mood stabilisers or antidepressants; psychosocial care; prognosis intermediate between schizophrenia and mood disorders.

4. Schizotypal disorder

  • A lasting pattern of eccentric behaviour, odd beliefs, magical thinking, unusual perceptual experiences, suspiciousness and social discomfort, without definite psychosis; may precede schizophrenia.

5. Secondary psychoses

  • Substance-induced psychotic disorder – alcohol (alcoholic hallucinosis), cannabis, amphetamines, steroids.
  • Psychosis due to medical conditions – epilepsy, encephalitis, HIV, thyroid disorders, brain tumours, SLE.
  • Postpartum psychosis – within weeks of delivery; an emergency because of risk to mother and baby.

Nursing management (common to all)

  • Safety and risk assessment; trust-building; reality orientation; meeting basic needs; medication and monitoring; reducing stress; family education; follow-up and early detection of recurrence.

Conclusion Delusional disorder (persistent systematised delusions of at least 3 months with preserved functioning), acute and transient psychotic disorder (sudden, changing symptoms resolving within 3 months, good prognosis), schizoaffective disorder (concurrent schizophrenic and mood symptoms), schizotypal disorder (eccentricity without frank psychosis) and secondary psychoses are the other psychotic disorders, managed with antipsychotics, psychosocial support and careful nursing.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: Explain relapse prevention, follow-up and home care of a patient with schizophrenia.
answer_html:
Introduction Schizophrenia is a relapsing illness. Each relapse brings suffering, risk, rehospitalisation and further decline, so relapse prevention, regular follow-up and home care are central to recovery.

Causes of relapse

  • Stopping or irregular intake of medicines – the commonest cause.
  • Alcohol, cannabis and other drugs.
  • Stressful life events; high expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, over-involvement) in the family.
  • Lack of follow-up, poor insight, side effects, stigma and poverty.

Early warning signs (prodromal signs of relapse)

  • Sleep disturbance, irritability, restlessness, anxiety.
  • Social withdrawal, neglect of self-care, poor concentration, loss of interest in work.
  • Suspiciousness, talking or laughing to oneself, unusual ideas, increased religious preoccupation.
  • Refusal of medicines, aggressive outbursts.
  • Each patient has his own pattern ("relapse signature"), which the family should learn.

Measures for relapse prevention

  1. Medication adherence – psychoeducation, simple regimens, side-effect management, family supervision, depot injections where needed.
  2. Psychoeducation and family intervention – understanding the illness, reducing expressed emotion, improving communication and problem-solving.
  3. Written relapse prevention plan – the patient's warning signs, what to do (contact the nurse or doctor, increase support), emergency numbers.
  4. Stress management and a regular routine – sleep, meals, activity.
  5. Avoid alcohol and drugs.
  6. Regular follow-up – OPD, DMHP clinics, depot clinics, Tele-MANAS (14416) for support.

Home care and follow-up by the nurse

  • Home visits – assess mental state, early warning signs, adherence, side effects, physical health, daily routine, occupation and family burden.
  • Supervise medicines; give depot injections; check stock and refill.
  • Teach the family how to respond to symptoms (calmly, without argument), to encourage self-care and activity, and to seek help early.
  • Rehabilitation – encourage household tasks and work, link with day-care, vocational training and supported employment.
  • Welfare – disability certificate (UDID), pension, concessions, legal guidance; support groups for caregivers.
  • Physical health – weight, diabetes and BP screening, smoking cessation.
  • Crisis plan – what to do if the patient becomes violent or suicidal; ambulance and emergency services.

Conclusion Relapse in schizophrenia is mainly due to non-adherence, substance use, stress and high expressed emotion. It is prevented by adherence support (including depots), family psychoeducation, a written relapse prevention plan based on early warning signs, healthy routine, abstinence from drugs and regular follow-up, with the nurse providing home visits, monitoring, teaching, rehabilitation and crisis support.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: List Schneider's first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia.
answer_html:
Kurt Schneider described the following first-rank symptoms, which strongly suggest schizophrenia in the absence of organic disease:

  1. Audible thoughts (thought echo).
  2. Voices arguing or discussing about the patient (third person).
  3. Voices commenting on the patient's actions (running commentary).
  4. Somatic passivity – bodily sensations imposed by an outside agency.
  5. Thought withdrawal.
  6. Thought insertion.
  7. Thought broadcasting (diffusion).
  8. Made feelings.
  9. Made impulses.
  10. Made volitional acts (actions controlled by an outside force).
  11. Delusional perception – a normal perception given a sudden delusional meaning.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: What are Bleuler's four As of schizophrenia?
answer_html:
Eugen Bleuler, who coined the term schizophrenia (1911), described its fundamental symptoms – the "4 As":

  1. Association disturbance – loosening of associations; illogical, disconnected thinking.
  2. Affective disturbance – blunted, flat or inappropriate affect.
  3. Ambivalence – simultaneous opposing feelings, wishes or ideas towards the same person or thing, leading to indecision.
  4. Autism – withdrawal from reality into a private inner world of fantasy. He considered hallucinations and delusions to be accessory (secondary) symptoms. The 4 As highlight the "splitting" of thought, emotion and behaviour (not a split personality), and help the nurse recognise withdrawal, emotional blunting and indecision in daily care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: Differentiate between positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
answer_html:
• Positive symptoms – an excess or distortion of normal functions: hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech (loosening of associations), bizarre or disorganised behaviour, catatonic excitement. They are linked to excess mesolimbic dopamine, respond well to antipsychotics and are common in acute episodes.
  • Negative symptoms – a loss or reduction of normal functions: alogia (poverty of speech), affective flattening, avolition (lack of motivation), anhedonia and asociality (social withdrawal), poor self-care. They are linked to reduced prefrontal (mesocortical) activity, respond poorly to most antipsychotics, are common in chronic illness and indicate a poorer prognosis.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: List the types of delusions with examples.
answer_html:
Types of delusions

  1. Persecutory – "People are plotting to kill me."
  2. Reference – "The newsreader is talking about me."
  3. Grandiose – "I am a great leader with special powers."
  4. Jealousy (infidelity) – unfounded belief that the spouse is unfaithful.
  5. Erotomanic (love) – belief that a famous person is in love with the patient.
  6. Guilt (sin) – "I have committed a terrible sin and deserve punishment" (depression).
  7. Nihilistic – "My intestines have rotted; I am dead" (severe depression).
  8. Somatic / hypochondriacal – false belief of disease or infestation.
  9. Control (passivity) – "My actions are controlled by a machine."
  10. Poverty – false belief of being ruined financially.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: What is expressed emotion?
answer_html:
Expressed emotion (EE) refers to the attitudes and emotions shown by family members towards a relative with mental illness, measured by the Camberwell Family Interview. Components of high EE

  1. Critical comments – frequent criticism of the patient's behaviour.
  2. Hostility – rejection and negative attitudes towards the patient as a person.
  3. Emotional over-involvement – excessive anxiety, over-protection, self-sacrifice. Significance – patients with schizophrenia (and mood disorders) living with high-EE families relapse two to three times more often. Family psychoeducation and communication training reduce EE and relapse.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Schizophrenia and Other Psychotic Disorders
question: Define the following catatonic signs: waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia and echopraxia.
answer_html:
1. Waxy flexibility (catalepsy) – the patient's limbs can be moved into any position by the examiner, offering slight resistance like soft wax, and are maintained in that position for a long time.
  2. Negativism – motiveless resistance to all instructions or attempts to move the patient; he may do the opposite of what is asked (active negativism) or not respond at all (passive).
  3. Echolalia – repetition of words or phrases spoken by others.
  4. Echopraxia – imitation of the movements or actions of others. Other catatonic signs include stupor, mutism, posturing, stereotypy, mannerisms, grimacing, automatic obedience and catatonic excitement.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Mood Disorders
question: (a) Define major depressive disorder. (2 marks) (b) Explain its aetiology and clinical manifestations. (5 marks) (c) Describe the nursing management of a patient with suicidal ideas. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Suicide precautions in the psychiatric ward
labels: bed near the nursing station; one-to-one observation for high risk; removal of sharp objects

medicines; secured windows and collapse-proof fittings without ligature points; bathroom checks; mouth check after medicines; search of belongings and visitors' articles; unpredictable observation times

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a mood disorder characterised by one or more depressive episodes – a period of at least 2 weeks of persistent low (depressed) mood or loss of interest and pleasure (anhedonia), accompanied by other symptoms such as changes in sleep and appetite, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration and thoughts of death or suicide, causing significant distress or impairment of functioning. It is called recurrent depressive disorder when episodes repeat. It is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide, about twice as common in women, and the National Mental Health Survey found a lifetime prevalence of about 5% in Indian adults.

(b) Aetiology and clinical manifestations (5 marks) Aetiology

  • Genetic – a family history increases the risk two to three times.
  • Biochemical – monoamine hypothesis: deficiency of serotonin and noradrenaline (and dopamine); reduced neuroplasticity (BDNF).
  • Neuroendocrine – HPA axis overactivity (raised cortisol), hypothyroidism.
  • Physical illness and drugs – diabetes, heart disease, stroke, cancer, chronic pain, Parkinson's disease, steroids, beta-blockers, alcohol.
  • Psychological – loss and anger turned inward (Freud), Beck's cognitive triad (negative views of self, world and future), learned helplessness (Seligman), low self-esteem, poor coping.
  • Social – stressful life events (bereavement, divorce, unemployment, debt, failure), poverty, domestic violence, isolation, lack of support; postpartum period.

Clinical manifestations

  1. Mood – persistent sadness, emptiness, irritability; may be "masked" by physical complaints.
  2. Anhedonia – loss of interest and pleasure in previously enjoyed activities.
  3. Thinking – slowed thinking, poor concentration and memory, indecision; worthlessness, guilt, hopelessness, helplessness; suicidal thoughts; in severe depression, delusions of guilt, poverty or nihilism and hallucinations (psychotic depression).
  4. Biological (somatic) symptoms – sleep disturbance (typically early morning awakening; sometimes excessive sleep), loss of appetite and weight (or increase), fatigue and loss of energy, loss of libido, constipation, menstrual changes.
  5. Psychomotor changes – retardation (slow movements and speech, long pauses; in extreme form, depressive stupor) or agitation (restlessness, hand-wringing).
  6. Diurnal variation – mood worse in the morning (melancholic depression).
  7. Behaviour – social withdrawal, neglect of self-care, crying spells, reduced work output, alcohol use.
  8. Physical complaints – headache, body aches, weakness, "burning" sensations – a common presentation in India.

Diagnosis (ICD-11) – at least five of ten characteristic symptoms (including depressed mood or anhedonia) most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks; graded as mild, moderate or severe, with or without psychotic symptoms. Screening with PHQ-9.

Treatment (in brief) – antidepressants (SSRIs first-line), psychotherapy (CBT, interpersonal therapy, behavioural activation), ECT for severe, psychotic or highly suicidal depression and depressive stupor, rTMS for resistant depression; treatment continued for at least 6–9 months after recovery.

(c) Nursing management of a patient with suicidal ideas (8 marks) 1. Assessment of suicide risk

  • Ask directly and calmly – "Have you had thoughts of ending your life?" Asking about suicide does not increase the risk; it often brings relief.
  • Assess ideation, intent, plan (method, time, place), access to means (pesticides, medicines, rope), preparations (writing a note or will, giving away belongings), past attempts and their seriousness, hopelessness, and protective factors (family, children, faith, reasons for living).
  • Risk factors – previous attempt (strongest predictor), depression and other mental illness, alcohol and drug use, hopelessness, male sex and old age (for completed suicide), adolescents and young adults, being single, widowed or divorced, unemployment, debt, chronic physical illness and pain, family history of suicide, recent loss, social isolation, easy access to pesticides, recent discharge from a psychiatric ward.
  • Warning signs – talking about wanting to die or being a burden, searching for means, withdrawal, sudden calmness after a period of depression, increased alcohol use, saying goodbye.
  • Tools such as the SAD PERSONS scale help, but clinical judgement is essential; document the assessment.

2. Nursing diagnosis – Risk for suicide related to depressed mood, hopelessness and suicidal ideas with a plan.

3. Providing a safe environment

  • Admit to a room near the nursing station; remove potentially harmful objects – blades, scissors, glass, belts, dupattas, ropes, cords, shoelaces, plastic bags, medicines, pesticides; check belongings and items brought by visitors.
  • Ensure windows are secured and fittings are free of ligature points (fans, hooks, door hinges, curtain rails); supervise bathroom use.
  • Levels of observation according to risk:
    • Constant one-to-one observation (within arm's reach, including in the toilet) for high risk.
    • Close observation – sighting at least every 15 minutes, at unpredictable times.
    • Routine observation as risk decreases.
  • Medication safety – administer medicines personally, check the mouth to prevent hoarding; dispense limited quantities at discharge.
  • High-risk times – nights, early mornings, weekends, shift changes, and the early recovery phase (when energy returns before mood improves); after bad news or family conflict.

4. Therapeutic relationship and communication

  • Spend time with the patient; listen without judging; acknowledge pain ("You feel that nothing will change"); avoid false reassurance, arguing about the right to die, or moral lectures.
  • Instil hope – depression is treatable; explore reasons for living and strengths.
  • Encourage expression of feelings, including anger, in safe ways.
  • No-suicide contracts are not reliable and do not replace observation; instead develop a safety plan with the patient – warning signs, coping strategies, people and places for distraction, family members to contact, professional help (Tele-MANAS 14416), and making the environment safe.

5. Meeting basic needs and promoting activity

  • Nutrition and fluids (monitor intake and weight), sleep (sleep hygiene, medicines as ordered), personal hygiene, elimination.
  • Simple, achievable activities and behavioural activation; praise small achievements; gradually involve in group activities.

6. Assisting in treatment

  • Give antidepressants and monitor effects (2–4 weeks for response), side effects and increased risk in the early weeks; care during ECT; reinforce CBT and problem-solving.

7. Family involvement

  • Educate about warning signs, means restriction at home (lock pesticides and medicines), supervision, and how to respond supportively; involve them in the safety plan.

8. Care after an attempt

  • Medical stabilisation first; then psychiatric assessment, close observation and support; avoid blaming. Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (section 115), a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and is not punished; the government must provide care, treatment and rehabilitation.

9. Discharge and follow-up

  • The period after discharge is high-risk – plan a follow-up visit within the first week; ensure medicines, a crisis plan and helpline numbers; home visits; link with DMHP services and support groups.

10. Support for staff and families after a suicide (postvention) – debriefing, counselling, review of care.

Evaluation – the patient remains safe, expresses suicidal feelings to staff, shows hope, uses coping strategies, eats and sleeps adequately and agrees to follow-up.

Nursing importance

  • Most people who die by suicide have a mental disorder, often depression, and many communicate their intent beforehand. A nurse who asks directly, observes closely, restricts means, builds hope and ensures follow-up can prevent suicide.

Conclusion Major depressive disorder is a period of at least 2 weeks of depressed mood or anhedonia with cognitive, biological and psychomotor symptoms, caused by genetic, neurochemical, endocrine, psychological and social factors. Nursing management of the suicidal patient includes direct and thorough risk assessment, a safe environment with appropriate levels of observation, medication safety, a trusting and hopeful relationship, a safety plan instead of no-suicide contracts, meeting basic needs, assisting with antidepressants and ECT, family involvement, care after attempts in line with the MHCA 2017, and close follow-up after discharge.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Mood Disorders
question: (a) Define bipolar affective disorder and describe the clinical features of a manic episode. (5 marks) (b) Explain the treatment of bipolar disorder. (3 marks) (c) Describe the nursing management of a patient with mania. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Mood chart in bipolar disorder
labels: a line showing mood swinging above the baseline (hypomania
with periods of normal mood (euthymia) between episodes; bipolar I with full mania
bipolar II with hypomania and major depression

answer_html:
(a) Definition and clinical features of mania (5 marks) Definition Bipolar affective disorder (BPAD) is a recurrent mood disorder characterised by episodes of mania or hypomania and episodes of depression (or mixed episodes), usually with periods of normal mood in between.

  • Bipolar I disorder – at least one manic or mixed episode (depressive episodes are common).
  • Bipolar II disorder – hypomanic episodes and major depressive episodes, without full mania.
  • Cyclothymia – long-standing mild mood swings.
  • Lifetime prevalence about 1% (more for the bipolar spectrum); onset usually in the late teens or twenties; equal in men and women; strong genetic loading.

Aetiology (in brief) – genetic factors (high heritability), increased dopamine and noradrenaline activity in mania, disturbed circadian rhythms; episodes triggered by sleep loss, stress, substances, antidepressants and childbirth.

Clinical features of a manic episode (lasting at least 1 week, or any duration if hospitalisation is needed)

  1. Mood – elevated, euphoric, expansive or irritable; infectious gaiety that may quickly turn to anger when opposed; labile.
  2. Activity and energy – increased activity, restlessness, starting many tasks without completing them; in severe cases exhaustion.
  3. Speech – pressure of speech (rapid, loud, difficult to interrupt); jokes, puns, rhyming.
  4. Thinking – flight of ideas, distractibility; grandiosity – inflated self-esteem, grandiose delusions (special powers, wealth, important connections); sometimes persecutory delusions.
  5. Sleep – decreased need for sleep (feels rested after 2–3 hours) – often the earliest sign.
  6. Behaviour – disinhibition, overfamiliarity, reckless spending, giving away money, risky driving, increased sexual drive and sexual indiscretion, colourful or bizarre dress and make-up, interfering in others' affairs, aggression when limited.
  7. Appetite – may increase, but the patient may not find time to eat or drink; weight loss and dehydration.
  8. Psychotic symptoms in severe mania – grandiose or persecutory delusions, hallucinations.
  9. Lack of insight and poor judgement. - Mnemonic "DIG FAST" – Distractibility, Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increased, Sleep deficit, Talkativeness. - Hypomania – similar but milder symptoms for at least several days, without marked impairment or psychotic features.

(b) Treatment of bipolar disorder (3 marks)

  • Acute mania – mood stabilisers: lithium (therapeutic serum level about 0.8–1.2 mEq/L in acute mania, lower for maintenance), sodium valproate, carbamazepine; atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole) alone or combined; benzodiazepines (lorazepam) for agitation and sleep.
  • ECT – severe mania, exhaustion, resistance to drugs, pregnancy.
  • Bipolar depression – quetiapine, lamotrigine, lithium; antidepressants only with a mood stabiliser (risk of switching to mania).
  • Maintenance – long-term mood stabilisers to prevent relapse.
  • Psychosocial – psychoeducation, interpersonal and social rhythm therapy (regular sleep and daily routine), family-focused therapy, CBT, early warning sign plans.

(c) Nursing management of a patient with mania (7 marks) Assessment – mood, activity, speech, sleep, food and fluid intake, weight, hygiene, risk of violence and exploitation (financial, sexual), insight, physical health (exhaustion, dehydration, injuries), substance use, family burden; baseline investigations for lithium (renal and thyroid function).

Nursing diagnoses and interventions

  1. Risk for violence and injury related to hyperactivity, irritability and poor judgement
