    • Reduce environmental stimuli – a quiet single room, limited visitors, low lights and noise; avoid crowded areas and television with exciting programmes.
    • Observe closely; remove dangerous objects; adequate staff; recognise early signs of anger; use de-escalation; PRN medication as ordered; restraint only as a last resort, as per law.
  2. Imbalanced nutrition and deficient fluid volume related to hyperactivity and inability to sit to eat
    • Provide high-calorie, high-protein "finger foods" and drinks that can be eaten while moving (sandwiches, bananas, laddoos, milk, juice); small frequent meals; monitor intake, output and weight; ensure fluids, especially for patients on lithium.
  3. Disturbed sleep pattern
    • A quiet, dark room at night; reduce caffeine; avoid stimulating activities in the evening; regular rest periods during the day; medicines as ordered; record hours of sleep.
  4. Impaired social interaction and ineffective impulse control (intrusiveness, manipulation, sexual disinhibition)
    • Set clear, firm, consistent limits on unacceptable behaviour – all staff follow the same approach; explain limits and consequences calmly; avoid arguments and power struggles; do not respond to provocative or flirtatious remarks.
    • Protect the patient from exploitation and embarrassment – supervise contact with others, keep money and valuables safely, prevent sexual involvement.
    • Use brief, simple and direct communication; redirect from one idea to a single task.
  5. Disturbed thought processes (grandiose delusions) – do not argue or reinforce; focus on reality and present activities.
  6. Channel excess energy constructively
    • Non-competitive physical activities – walking, sweeping, folding linen, simple exercises, writing; short tasks that can be completed; avoid competitive games and activities requiring long concentration.
  7. Self-care deficit – assist with bathing, appropriate dress and grooming; give simple step-by-step instructions; praise.
  8. Ineffective health maintenance – medication adherence and lithium safety
    • Give mood stabilisers and antipsychotics as ordered; monitor serum lithium levels (12 hours after the last dose) and signs of toxicity – coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness, slurred speech, unsteadiness, confusion; ensure adequate fluid and normal salt intake; avoid NSAIDs and diuretics; monitor renal and thyroid function; teach the patient and family.
  9. Interrupted family processes
    • Psychoeducation about the illness, the need for long-term treatment and early warning signs of relapse (reduced sleep, overactivity, overspending, irritability); protecting family finances during episodes; reducing stress and conflict.

Evaluation – the patient sleeps 6–8 hours, eats and drinks adequately, harms no one, accepts limits, completes simple tasks, takes medicines regularly and the family recognises relapse signs.

Mixed episodes and rapid cycling

  • Mixed episode – manic and depressive symptoms occur together or alternate rapidly (e.g. overactivity and pressured speech with despair and suicidal thoughts); suicide risk is high and close observation is needed.
  • Rapid cycling – four or more mood episodes in a year; more common in women, with hypothyroidism and with antidepressant use; usually needs a combination of mood stabilisers.

Nursing care in the depressive phase of bipolar disorder

  • The same care as for major depression – suicide risk assessment and precautions, nutrition, sleep and activity – with close watch for a switch into mania, especially if antidepressants are used.

Nursing importance

  • Manic patients are at risk of exhaustion, injury, violence, financial ruin and sexual exploitation. A calm, consistent, low-stimulation approach with firm limits, attention to food, fluids and sleep, and careful lithium monitoring protects the patient while treatment takes effect.

Conclusion Bipolar affective disorder consists of recurrent manic or hypomanic and depressive episodes. Mania presents with elevated or irritable mood, overactivity, pressured speech, flight of ideas, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, disinhibition and reckless behaviour. It is treated with lithium, valproate or atypical antipsychotics, benzodiazepines and ECT when needed, with long-term maintenance and psychoeducation. Nursing care centres on safety and reduced stimulation, nutrition and fluids, sleep, consistent limit setting, protection from exploitation, constructive channelling of energy, self-care, medication adherence with lithium monitoring, and family education.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Mood Disorders
question: Explain dysthymia (persistent depressive disorder) and cyclothymia.
answer_html:
Introduction Dysthymia and cyclothymia are chronic, milder mood disorders lasting for years. Because the symptoms are less dramatic, they are often mistaken for "personality" and remain untreated, yet they cause considerable suffering and impairment.

A. Dysthymia (dysthymic disorder; persistent depressive disorder in DSM-5-TR)

  • Persistent depressed mood for most of the day, on more days than not, for at least 2 years (1 year in children and adolescents).
  • Associated symptoms – poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or excessive sleep, low energy and fatigue, low self-esteem, poor concentration, indecisiveness, hopelessness; the person feels he has "always been like this".
  • Onset is often in childhood, adolescence or early adulthood; course is chronic.
  • A major depressive episode may develop on top of dysthymia ("double depression").
  • Treatment – antidepressants (SSRIs) and psychotherapy (CBT, interpersonal therapy), often long-term; treatment of stressors and associated substance use.

B. Cyclothymia (cyclothymic disorder)

  • A persistent instability of mood for at least 2 years, with numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms that are not severe enough to meet the criteria for a manic or major depressive episode.
  • The person appears moody, unpredictable and erratic; relationships, studies and work may suffer.
  • About a third later develop bipolar disorder.
  • Treatment – psychoeducation, regular sleep and daily routine, mood charting, avoidance of alcohol and drugs, psychotherapy; mood stabilisers in some cases; antidepressants used cautiously.

Nursing management

  • Assessment – mood history (mood diary or life chart), duration, functioning, suicidal ideas, substance use, stressors.
  • Therapeutic relationship – listen, validate the chronic suffering, instil hope that treatment helps.
  • Self-esteem and coping – identify strengths, set small achievable goals, teach problem-solving and stress management; encourage activity and social contact.
  • Medication – adherence and monitoring of side effects; caution about antidepressant-induced hypomania in cyclothymia.
  • Lifestyle – regular sleep–wake schedule, exercise, avoidance of alcohol.
  • Education of patient and family; follow-up and early recognition of a full depressive or manic episode; suicide risk assessment.

Conclusion Dysthymia is chronic low-grade depression lasting 2 years or more, and cyclothymia is chronic mood instability with mild hypomanic and depressive periods for 2 years or more. Both need long-term treatment with psychotherapy and medication where indicated, and nursing care focuses on assessment, hope, self-esteem, coping, regular routine, adherence and monitoring for more severe episodes.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Mood Disorders
question: Explain the perinatal mood disorders – postpartum blues, postpartum depression and postpartum psychosis – and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Pregnancy and the period after childbirth are times of increased vulnerability to mood disorders because of hormonal changes, sleep loss, new responsibilities and psychosocial stress. They affect the mother's health, the baby's growth and development, and the family, and must be detected early.

1. Postpartum blues ("baby blues")

  • Very common – in a large proportion (up to about 50–80%) of new mothers.
  • Begins about day 3–5 after delivery; tearfulness, mood swings, irritability, anxiety, poor sleep.
  • Self-limiting – resolves within about 2 weeks.
  • Care – reassurance, rest, practical help with the baby, emotional support from the family; watch for persistence beyond 2 weeks.

2. Postpartum (perinatal) depression

  • A depressive episode during pregnancy or within the first weeks to months after delivery; it affects roughly 1 in 7 mothers worldwide, and Indian studies report even higher rates.
  • Features – persistent low mood, loss of interest, anxiety about the baby, feelings of inadequacy and guilt as a mother, poor bonding, sleep and appetite disturbance beyond what the baby's care explains, intrusive thoughts of harm to the baby, suicidal thoughts.
  • Risk factors – past history of depression, lack of support, marital conflict and domestic violence, unplanned pregnancy, pressure for a male child, poverty, obstetric complications, a sick or preterm baby.
  • Screening – the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) (10 questions) during pregnancy and after delivery.
  • Treatment – psychological support and therapy (CBT, IPT), family support, antidepressants compatible with breastfeeding (e.g. sertraline); ECT in severe cases.

3. Postpartum psychosis

  • Rare (about 1–2 per 1,000 deliveries), but a psychiatric emergency.
  • Onset usually within the first 2 weeks, often the first few days after delivery.
  • Features – sudden confusion, insomnia, rapidly changing mood (manic, depressive or mixed), delusions involving the baby, hallucinations, disorganised behaviour.
  • Risk – suicide and infanticide; strongly linked to bipolar disorder (personal or family history).
  • Treatment – urgent admission (ideally to a mother–baby unit), antipsychotics, mood stabilisers, ECT; supervised contact with the baby; decisions about breastfeeding based on medicines; long-term follow-up and prevention in later pregnancies.

Role of the nurse

  • Screen all women antenatally and postnatally (EPDS, asking about mood, sleep, support and violence); identify high-risk women (previous episodes, bipolar disorder).
  • Educate the mother and family about baby blues and warning signs of depression and psychosis; involve the husband and family in practical help and night feeds.
  • Promote rest and sleep, nutrition and mother–baby bonding (skin-to-skin contact, breastfeeding support).
  • Ensure safety of mother and baby in severe depression or psychosis – never leave them alone, urgent referral.
  • Support medication adherence and breastfeeding decisions; follow-up during home visits by ANMs and ASHAs; link with Tele-MANAS and psychiatric services.

Conclusion Postpartum blues are common, mild and self-limiting; postpartum depression is a significant depressive episode that affects mother and baby and should be screened for with the EPDS; and postpartum psychosis is a rare emergency with risks of suicide and infanticide. Nurses play a central role in screening, education, support, safety and follow-up.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Mood Disorders
question: Explain the home care, follow-up and rehabilitation of patients with mood disorders.
answer_html:
Introduction Mood disorders are often recurrent – many patients with depression and most with bipolar disorder have further episodes. Continued care after discharge reduces relapse, suicide and disability and helps patients return to normal life.

1. Maintenance treatment and adherence

  • Antidepressants continued for months after recovery (longer for recurrent depression); mood stabilisers long-term in bipolar disorder.
  • Lithium clinic – serum lithium levels regularly (every 3–6 months when stable), renal and thyroid function every 6–12 months, weight and metabolic monitoring with antipsychotics.
  • Education on side effects, toxicity, drug interactions and the danger of stopping suddenly; simple regimens and reminders.

2. Recognition of early warning signs

  • Mania – reduced need for sleep, overactivity, talkativeness, irritability, overspending, overconfidence.
  • Depression – withdrawal, loss of interest, sleep and appetite change, hopelessness, suicidal talk.
  • A written relapse prevention plan – the person's own warning signs and what to do; a mood chart (diary) to track mood, sleep and medicines.

3. Healthy routine (social rhythm)

  • Regular sleep–wake times; avoid sleep deprivation (night shifts, travel, festivals, examinations).
  • Regular meals, exercise and daily activities; stress management and relaxation.
  • Avoid alcohol and drugs; limit caffeine.

4. Family involvement

  • Psychoeducation; reducing criticism and over-involvement; supportive communication.
  • Safeguarding finances during mania (joint accounts, keeping cards safely).
  • Means restriction and watchfulness for suicidal behaviour during depression; a crisis plan with emergency contacts.

5. Rehabilitation

  • Gradual return to work or study; workplace or college adjustments; vocational guidance if needed.
  • Rebuilding relationships and social activities; self-help and peer-support groups.
  • Planning pregnancies with the psychiatrist (especially for women on valproate or lithium).
  • Physical health care – weight, diabetes, BP, thyroid.

6. Follow-up services

  • Regular OPD or DMHP clinic visits; home visits by community nurses; telephone follow-up and Tele-MANAS (14416); early appointments after discharge (a high-risk period for suicide).

Role of the nurse

  • Coordinate follow-up; assess mental state, adherence, side effects, lithium levels and suicide risk at each contact.
  • Teach patients and families about the illness, medicines, warning signs and routine.
  • Support rehabilitation, link with community resources and support groups; document and communicate with the team.

Conclusion Home care and follow-up in mood disorders consist of maintenance treatment with adherence support and lithium monitoring, recognition of early warning signs with a written relapse plan and mood chart, a regular daily rhythm without alcohol or drugs, family psychoeducation and safeguards, rehabilitation to work and social life, and regular follow-up through hospital, DMHP, home visits and Tele-MANAS.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Mood Disorders
question: What is Beck's cognitive triad?
answer_html:
Beck's cognitive triad describes the three patterns of negative thinking typical of depression (Aaron Beck):

  1. Negative view of the self – "I am worthless, a failure."
  2. Negative view of the world (experiences) – "Everything goes wrong; nobody cares about me."
  3. Negative view of the future – "Things will never get better" (hopelessness, which is linked to suicide). These thoughts are maintained by cognitive distortions (overgeneralisation, catastrophising, personalisation). Cognitive behaviour therapy helps the patient identify and challenge these thoughts and replace them with balanced ones.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Mood Disorders
question: What is flight of ideas?
answer_html:
Flight of ideas is a disorder of the stream of thought in which ideas follow each other very rapidly, with abrupt changes of topic, so that the patient never reaches the goal of the conversation.

  • The connections between ideas are understandable – based on chance associations, rhymes, puns (clang associations) or distracting stimuli in the surroundings.
  • It is usually accompanied by pressure of speech and distractibility.
  • It is characteristic of mania.
  • It differs from loosening of associations (in schizophrenia), where the links between ideas are not understandable.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Mood Disorders
question: Differentiate between hypomania and mania.
answer_html:
• Severity – hypomania: milder elevation of mood and activity; mania: severe.
  • Duration – hypomania: at least several days (about 4 days in DSM-5-TR); mania: at least 1 week (or less if hospitalised).
  • Functioning – hypomania: no marked impairment, sometimes increased productivity; mania: marked impairment of social and occupational functioning.
  • Psychotic symptoms – hypomania: absent; mania: may be present (grandiose or persecutory delusions, hallucinations).
  • Hospitalisation – hypomania: usually not needed; mania: often needed for safety.
  • Diagnosis – hypomania with major depression = bipolar II; mania = bipolar I.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Mood Disorders
question: What is the SAD PERSONS scale?
answer_html:
The SAD PERSONS scale (Patterson and colleagues) is a simple tool listing ten risk factors for suicide, one point each:

  • S – Sex (male)
  • A – Age (below 19 or above 45 years)
  • D – Depression
  • P – Previous attempt
  • E – Ethanol (alcohol) abuse
  • R – Rational thinking loss (psychosis)
  • S – Social supports lacking
  • O – Organised plan
  • N – No spouse
  • S – Sickness (chronic illness) A higher score indicates higher risk. It is a memory aid, not a substitute for a full clinical assessment of suicidal intent, plan and means.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Mood Disorders
question: What is learned helplessness?
answer_html:
Learned helplessness is a theory of depression proposed by Martin Seligman. In experiments, animals exposed to unavoidable unpleasant situations stopped trying to escape even when escape became possible – they had learned that their actions had no effect.

  • In humans, repeated experiences of failure or lack of control (abuse, poverty, chronic illness, repeated losses) lead to the belief that one is powerless, producing passivity, hopelessness and depression.
  • Nursing implications – help the patient experience control and success through small achievable tasks, choices in care, problem-solving and praise, which counteract helplessness.

question: (a) Define phobia and explain its aetiology. (4 marks) (b) Describe the clinical features and types of phobia. (4 marks) (c) Explain the management of social phobia (social anxiety disorder), including its nursing management. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: The avoidance cycle that maintains a phobia
labels: trembling) – escape or avoidance – immediate relief (negative reinforcement) – fear grows stronger and avoidance spreads; breaking the cycle through graded exposure until anxiety falls

answer_html:
(a) Definition and aetiology (4 marks) Definition A phobia is a persistent, excessive and irrational fear of a specific object, situation or activity, which is out of proportion to the actual danger, leads to avoidance of the feared stimulus, and causes significant distress or impairment. The person usually recognises that the fear is excessive (insight is present), but cannot control it. Phobias belong to the anxiety or fear-related disorders in ICD-11.

Aetiology

  1. Genetic and temperamental factors – phobias run in families; children with a shy, behaviourally inhibited temperament are at higher risk.
  2. Biological factors – an overactive amygdala (fear centre), altered serotonin, noradrenaline and GABA function; heightened autonomic arousal.
  3. Behavioural (learning) theory
    • Classical conditioning – a neutral object becomes feared after being paired with a frightening experience (Watson's "Little Albert" experiment, in which a child learned to fear a white rat).
    • Mowrer's two-factor theory – fear is acquired by classical conditioning and maintained by operant conditioning, because avoidance brings relief (negative reinforcement), so the fear is never unlearned.
    • Modelling (observational learning) – children learn fears by watching anxious parents (e.g. fear of dogs, cockroaches, injections).
    • Information – frightening stories and media.
  4. Psychoanalytic theory – unconscious anxiety from unresolved conflicts is displaced onto an external object that can be avoided (Freud's case of "Little Hans" and his fear of horses).
  5. Cognitive theory – people with phobias overestimate danger and underestimate their ability to cope; in social phobia, there is a strong fear of negative evaluation and excessive self-focused attention.
  6. Environmental factors – traumatic events, overprotective or critical parenting, bullying, humiliation in childhood.

(b) Clinical features and types (4 marks) Clinical features

  • Intense fear or anxiety on exposure to, or even thinking of, the phobic stimulus – anticipatory anxiety.
  • Autonomic symptoms – palpitations, sweating, trembling, dry mouth, breathlessness, nausea, dizziness, urge to pass urine; it may reach the level of a panic attack.
  • Avoidance of the object or situation, or enduring it with great distress; the avoidance progressively restricts life (school, work, travel, social life).
  • Insight – the person knows the fear is unreasonable.
  • Secondary depression, low self-esteem and use of alcohol to cope may follow.

Types

  1. Specific (simple) phobia – fear of a specific object or situation:
    • Animal type – dogs (cynophobia), snakes (ophidiophobia), spiders (arachnophobia), cockroaches, lizards.
    • Natural environment type – heights (acrophobia), thunder and lightning, water, darkness (nyctophobia).
    • Blood–injection–injury type – sight of blood, injections, injuries; uniquely, may cause fainting (vasovagal response) – important in nursing.
    • Situational type – closed spaces (claustrophobia), lifts, flying, bridges, tunnels.
    • Others – fear of vomiting, choking, illness (nosophobia), dirt (mysophobia), death.
  2. Agoraphobia – fear and avoidance of situations from which escape may be difficult or help unavailable if panic occurs – crowds, markets, public transport, open or closed spaces, leaving home alone; often with panic disorder.
  3. Social phobia (social anxiety disorder) – marked fear of social or performance situations in which the person may be observed and judged – speaking in public, eating, writing or drinking in front of others, meeting strangers, using public toilets – for fear of embarrassment or humiliation.
    • Features – blushing, trembling, sweating, palpitations, dry mouth, stammering, avoidance of eye contact, avoidance of social situations; usually begins in adolescence; may be generalised or limited to performance (e.g. examinations, interviews, stage).

(c) Management of social phobia, including nursing management (7 marks) 1. Psychological treatment (first-line)

  • Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) – the most effective treatment, given individually or in groups:
    • Psychoeducation about anxiety and the avoidance cycle.
    • Cognitive restructuring – identifying and challenging negative predictions ("Everyone will laugh at me", "I will blush and look foolish"), reducing self-focused attention and "safety behaviours" (avoiding eye contact, rehearsing every sentence).
    • Graded exposure – a hierarchy of feared social situations (e.g. greeting a neighbour → asking a question in class → speaking in a small group → giving a short talk), practised step by step until anxiety reduces; role play and video feedback.
    • Behavioural experiments to test feared beliefs.
  • Social skills and assertiveness training – starting conversations, maintaining eye contact, expressing opinions, handling criticism.
  • Relaxation training – slow breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, yoga and mindfulness.

2. Pharmacological treatment

  • SSRIs – sertraline, paroxetine, escitalopram (first-line drugs), or the SNRI venlafaxine; continued for many months after improvement.
  • Beta-blockers (propranolol) – taken before a performance to control trembling and palpitations in performance-only social anxiety.
  • Benzodiazepines (e.g. clonazepam) – short-term only, because of dependence.

3. Nursing management Nursing diagnoses

  • Anxiety related to fear of negative evaluation, as evidenced by blushing, trembling and avoidance of social situations.
  • Social isolation / impaired social interaction related to fear of embarrassment.
  • Situational low self-esteem related to perceived inadequacy in social situations.
  • Ineffective coping (avoidance, possible alcohol use).

Interventions

  • Build a trusting, accepting relationship; listen without criticising; never ridicule or force the patient into feared situations suddenly.
  • Assess the situations feared, level of anxiety, avoidance, impact on studies and work, depression, suicidal ideas and alcohol use.
  • Teach about anxiety – its physical symptoms are uncomfortable but not dangerous; avoidance maintains fear.
  • Teach relaxation and breathing techniques and help the patient practise them before feared situations.
  • Support graded exposure – help build the hierarchy, accompany the patient in early steps, encourage practice of homework, praise every success, and record progress (anxiety ratings before and after exposure).
  • Social skills training in small groups – role play of greetings, conversations, asking for help, presenting in class.
  • Promote self-esteem – focus on strengths, positive self-statements, realistic goals.
  • Medication – give as ordered, explain delayed onset of SSRI benefit, monitor side effects, discourage alcohol as self-medication.
  • Family and teachers – explain the condition, avoid criticism and over-protection, encourage gradual participation; school or workplace accommodations (e.g. gradual oral presentations).
  • Follow-up – continuing exposure practice, relapse prevention, early help if symptoms return.

Evaluation – reduced anxiety ratings, participation in feared situations, improved social and academic or occupational functioning, no alcohol misuse.

Management of other phobias (in brief) – specific phobias respond very well to exposure therapy (systematic desensitisation, in-vivo exposure, flooding, modelling); for blood–injection phobia, applied tension (tensing muscles to raise BP) prevents fainting; agoraphobia is treated with CBT and SSRIs together with treatment of panic disorder.

Nursing importance

  • Phobias often begin in childhood and adolescence and silently restrict education, career and relationships. Nurses who recognise them early, explain the avoidance cycle and support graded exposure can restore normal functioning.

Conclusion A phobia is an excessive, irrational fear leading to avoidance, arising from genetic, biological, conditioning, modelling, psychodynamic and cognitive factors. Phobias are specific (animal, environment, blood–injection–injury, situational), agoraphobic or social. Social phobia – fear of scrutiny and embarrassment – is best treated with CBT (cognitive restructuring, graded exposure, social skills training) and SSRIs, with propranolol for performance anxiety; nursing management builds trust, teaches relaxation, supports graded exposure and social skills, raises self-esteem, ensures medication and involves the family.

question: (a) Define obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and explain its aetiology. (4 marks) (b) Describe its clinical features. (4 marks) (c) Explain the management and nursing care of a patient with OCD. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: The obsessive-compulsive cycle
labels: e.g. "my hands are contaminated") – anxiety and distress – compulsion (washing
counting) – temporary relief – relief reinforces the compulsion – obsession returns more strongly; exposure and response prevention breaks the cycle

answer_html:
(a) Definition and aetiology (4 marks) Definition Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a disorder characterised by persistent obsessions and/or compulsions that are time-consuming (often more than an hour a day) and cause marked distress or impairment of functioning.

  • Obsessions – recurrent, persistent, intrusive and unwanted thoughts, images or urges, recognised by the person as products of his own mind, which he tries to ignore, resist or neutralise, and which cause anxiety.
  • Compulsions – repetitive behaviours or mental acts that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rigid rules, to reduce anxiety or prevent a feared event, though they are not realistically connected with it or are clearly excessive.
  • Lifetime prevalence about 2–3%; onset usually in adolescence or early adulthood (earlier in boys); often chronic; frequently associated with depression and tic disorders.

Aetiology

  1. Genetic – higher rates in first-degree relatives and identical twins.
  2. Neurochemical – serotonin dysfunction (supported by the response to SSRIs and clomipramine); dopamine and glutamate also involved.
  3. Neuroanatomical – overactivity of the cortico–striato–thalamo–cortical circuit – orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate and caudate nucleus.
  4. Immunological – OCD and tics following streptococcal infection in some children (PANDAS).
  5. Psychoanalytic – fixation at the anal stage; defence mechanisms of isolation, undoing and reaction formation used against unacceptable aggressive or sexual impulses.
  6. Learning theory – anxiety becomes attached to neutral thoughts or objects; compulsions reduce anxiety and are therefore reinforced (negative reinforcement), maintaining the cycle.
  7. Cognitive theory – inflated sense of responsibility, thought–action fusion (believing that thinking about something makes it more likely or is as bad as doing it), overestimation of threat, intolerance of uncertainty, perfectionism.
  8. Stress – onset or worsening after life events, childbirth (postpartum OCD) or illness.

(b) Clinical features (4 marks) Common obsessions

  • Contamination – fear of dirt, germs, urine, faeces, impurity (common in India in relation to ritual purity).
  • Pathological doubt – "Did I lock the door? Did I switch off the gas?"
  • Need for symmetry, order and exactness.
  • Intrusive aggressive thoughts – fear of harming others (e.g. a mother fearing she may harm her baby), without any intention to act.
  • Sexual and religious (blasphemous) thoughts, fear of having sinned.
  • Somatic obsessions; obsessional images; obsessional ruminations (endless thinking about abstract questions).

Common compulsions

  • Washing and cleaning – repeated hand washing, bathing for hours, cleaning the house.
  • Checking – locks, switches, gas, documents, repeatedly.
  • Counting, repeating actions a fixed number of times.
  • Ordering and arranging objects symmetrically.
  • Mental rituals – praying, repeating words, reviewing.
  • Reassurance seeking; hoarding (now a related disorder).
  • Obsessional slowness – taking hours to complete daily activities.

Other features

  • The person usually knows the thoughts are excessive (insight good or fair), though insight may be poor in some.
  • Anxiety, guilt, depression, avoidance of triggers; dermatitis of the hands from excessive washing; family members are often drawn into rituals (family accommodation).
  • Severity rated by the Yale–Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS).

(c) Management and nursing care (7 marks) Medical management

  • SSRIs – fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline, paroxetine, escitalopram – often in higher doses and for 10–12 weeks before judging response; clomipramine (tricyclic) is also effective.
  • Augmentation with low-dose antipsychotics (risperidone, aripiprazole) in partial responders.
  • Treatment-resistant OCD – deep transcranial magnetic stimulation, deep brain stimulation and, rarely, neurosurgery.
  • Treatment is usually long-term; relapse is common if medicines are stopped early.

Psychological management

  • Exposure and response prevention (ERP) – the most effective psychological treatment: the patient is exposed gradually to situations that trigger obsessions (e.g. touching a "dirty" object) and prevented from performing the compulsion (not washing), until anxiety falls on its own; repeated until the habit is broken.
  • Cognitive therapy – challenging inflated responsibility and thought–action fusion.
  • Family therapy to reduce accommodation and criticism.

Nursing management Nursing diagnoses

  • Anxiety related to obsessive thoughts, as evidenced by repetitive hand washing.
  • Ineffective coping (rituals) related to underlying anxiety.
  • Self-care deficit and impaired skin integrity related to time spent in rituals and excessive washing.
  • Interrupted family processes related to family involvement in rituals.

Interventions

  1. Accept the patient and the rituals initially – do not ridicule or forbid them abruptly, because preventing rituals suddenly raises anxiety to panic levels.
  2. Allow time for rituals in the beginning while ensuring basic needs; plan the daily schedule so that the patient has enough time for meals, medicines and activities.
  3. Gradually limit the rituals by agreement – reduce the time or number step by step as treatment progresses (e.g. hand washing reduced from 30 to 20 to 10 minutes); praise every reduction.
  4. Support ERP – help construct the exposure hierarchy, stay with the patient during exposure, encourage resisting the compulsion, record anxiety levels, and reinforce homework.
  5. Help the patient recognise and express the anxiety behind the rituals; teach relaxation, slow breathing and distraction.
  6. Structured daily routine with meaningful activities to reduce time available for rituals; involve in occupational and recreational therapy.
  7. Physical care – skin care for chapped hands (moisturiser), nutrition, sleep, hygiene.
  8. Medication – give SSRIs as ordered; explain that benefit is slow; monitor side effects and adherence.
  9. Monitor for depression and suicidal ideas, which are common.
  10. Family education – explain OCD as an illness; avoid criticism and arguments; gradually stop taking part in rituals and giving repeated reassurance (reduce accommodation); support exposure practice at home.

Evaluation – reduced time spent on rituals and lower Y-BOCS score, improved self-care and functioning, ability to manage anxiety without rituals, family no longer involved in rituals.

Obsessive-compulsive related disorders (ICD-11)

  • Body dysmorphic disorder – preoccupation with an imagined or slight defect in appearance, with repeated mirror checking or seeking cosmetic procedures.
  • Hoarding disorder – difficulty discarding possessions, leading to cluttered living spaces.
  • Trichotillomania (hair pulling) and excoriation disorder (skin picking).
  • Hypochondriasis (health anxiety) and olfactory reference disorder (belief of emitting a bad body odour).

Course and prognosis

  • Usually chronic with fluctuations, worsening during stress; about half to two-thirds improve substantially with combined treatment.
  • Better prognosis – good insight, episodic course, early treatment, good social support; worse – early onset, poor insight, hoarding symptoms, comorbid depression or tics, and family accommodation.

Nursing importance

  • OCD is often hidden for years because of shame. The nurse's patient, non-judgemental approach, gradual limit-setting and support for ERP help patients regain control of their time and lives.

Conclusion OCD consists of intrusive, unwanted obsessions and repetitive compulsions performed to reduce anxiety, resulting from genetic, serotonergic, cortico-striatal, psychodynamic, learning and cognitive factors. Common forms are contamination–washing, doubt–checking, symmetry–ordering and intrusive aggressive, sexual or religious thoughts. Treatment combines high-dose SSRIs or clomipramine with exposure and response prevention; nursing care accepts the rituals at first, allows time and then gradually limits them, supports ERP, teaches anxiety management, maintains self-care and skin integrity, monitors depression and educates the family to reduce accommodation.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: Explain generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is characterised by persistent, excessive and uncontrollable worry and anxiety about many everyday matters (health, family, money, work, studies) – or a general sense of apprehension ("free-floating anxiety") – present more days than not for several months (at least 6 months in DSM-5-TR), with physical symptoms and impaired functioning.

Clinical features

  • Psychological – constant worry, apprehension, irritability, poor concentration, feeling "on edge", fear of something terrible happening, difficulty relaxing.
  • Motor tension – restlessness, fidgeting, muscle tension and aches, tension headache, tremor, fatigue.
  • Autonomic overactivity – palpitations, sweating, dry mouth, dizziness, breathlessness, epigastric discomfort, frequent urination.
  • Sleep disturbance – difficulty falling asleep, restless sleep.
  • Often comorbid with depression, panic disorder and alcohol misuse; many patients present to physicians with physical complaints.

Aetiology – genetic predisposition, anxious temperament, GABA and serotonin dysfunction, chronic stress, childhood adversity, cognitive tendency to overestimate threat and poor tolerance of uncertainty.

Rule out – hyperthyroidism, excessive caffeine, drug or alcohol withdrawal, hypoglycaemia, cardiac arrhythmias, medicines (salbutamol, steroids).

Management

  • Psychological – psychoeducation, CBT (worry exposure, cognitive restructuring, problem-solving), applied relaxation, mindfulness and yoga.
  • Pharmacological – SSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline) or SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine), pregabalin, buspirone; benzodiazepines only short-term because of dependence.
  • Lifestyle – regular exercise, sleep hygiene, reduced caffeine, avoidance of alcohol.

Nursing management

  • Nursing diagnosis – Anxiety related to excessive worry about everyday events, as evidenced by restlessness, muscle tension and poor sleep.
  • Establish a calm, trusting relationship; listen to the patient's worries; acknowledge his feelings.
  • Assess the level of anxiety and its physical effects; help him recognise his anxiety and its triggers.
  • Teach relaxation techniques – slow breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery; schedule practice sessions.
  • Help him identify and challenge catastrophic worries; teach problem-solving and "worry time" (postponing worry to a fixed time).
  • Encourage regular physical activity and pleasant activities; teach sleep hygiene; reduce caffeine.
  • Give medicines as ordered; educate about delayed onset of SSRI action and risks of benzodiazepine dependence.
  • Involve the family; teach them not to give repeated reassurance; arrange follow-up.

Conclusion GAD is persistent, excessive worry and apprehension with motor tension, autonomic symptoms and sleep disturbance lasting several months. It is treated with CBT, relaxation, SSRIs or SNRIs, pregabalin or buspirone, with only short-term benzodiazepines. Nursing care focuses on a calm relationship, assessment of anxiety, relaxation training, cognitive and problem-solving strategies, lifestyle changes, medication education and family support.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: Explain panic disorder and the nursing care of a patient during a panic attack.
answer_html:
Definition Panic disorder is characterised by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks, followed by persistent worry about further attacks or their consequences ("I will die", "I will go mad") and/or maladaptive changes in behaviour (avoidance) for at least a month. It is often associated with agoraphobia.

Panic attack – a sudden surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes, with physical and psychological symptoms:

  • Palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness or choking sensation, sweating, trembling, dizziness or light-headedness, nausea, chills or hot flushes, numbness and tingling.
  • Derealisation or depersonalisation; fear of losing control, going mad or dying.
  • Attacks usually last 5–30 minutes; patients often rush to emergency departments believing they are having a heart attack.

Aetiology

  • Genetic predisposition; hypersensitive brain "fear network" (amygdala), noradrenaline and serotonin dysfunction, sensitivity to CO2 and lactate.
  • Cognitive model – catastrophic misinterpretation of normal bodily sensations (a fast heartbeat interpreted as a heart attack) produces more fear, more symptoms and a vicious circle.
  • Stressful life events, caffeine, cannabis and stimulant use as triggers.

Rule out – cardiac disease and arrhythmias, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia, asthma, epilepsy, drug intoxication or withdrawal.

Management

  • CBT – psychoeducation about the panic cycle, cognitive restructuring of catastrophic thoughts, interoceptive exposure (deliberately producing feared sensations, e.g. by spinning or brisk exercise, to learn they are harmless), breathing retraining, and graded exposure to avoided situations (agoraphobia).
  • SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, paroxetine) – first-line drugs; benzodiazepines (clonazepam) short-term for severe symptoms.

Nursing care during a panic attack

  1. Stay with the patient; remain calm and confident – the nurse's calmness reduces the patient's fear.
  2. Move the patient to a quiet, less stimulating place; loosen tight clothing.
  3. Use short, simple sentences: "You are safe. This is a panic attack. It will pass."
  4. Guide slow breathing – breathe in through the nose for a count of four, breathe out slowly through the mouth; breathe along with the patient.
  5. Once medical causes have been excluded, reassure that the symptoms are not dangerous.
  6. Give PRN medication as ordered; record the duration, symptoms and triggers.

Care between attacks

  • Teach about panic and the cycle of fear; help identify triggers and catastrophic thoughts; practise breathing and relaxation daily.
  • Support graded exposure to avoided places; encourage normal activities.
  • Advise avoiding caffeine, alcohol and drugs; ensure medication adherence and follow-up.

Conclusion Panic disorder consists of recurrent unexpected panic attacks – sudden intense fear with palpitations, breathlessness, dizziness and fear of dying – followed by persistent worry and avoidance. It is treated with CBT (including interoceptive exposure and breathing retraining) and SSRIs. During an attack the nurse stays with the patient, reduces stimulation, uses short reassuring statements and guides slow breathing; between attacks she educates and supports exposure.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: Explain post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and its management.
answer_html:
Definition Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) may develop after exposure to an extremely threatening or horrific event – such as war, terrorist attacks, natural disasters, serious accidents, sexual or physical assault, torture, or witnessing a violent death. It is characterised by re-experiencing the trauma, avoidance and a persistent sense of current threat, lasting at least several weeks (more than 1 month in DSM-5-TR) and causing significant impairment.

Clinical features (ICD-11)

  1. Re-experiencing the event in the present – vivid intrusive memories, flashbacks (feeling as if the event is happening again), nightmares, intense fear or distress and physical reactions on reminders.
  2. Avoidance of thoughts, memories, places, people and activities that remind of the trauma.
  3. Persistent perception of heightened current threat – hypervigilance, exaggerated startle reaction, irritability, poor sleep and concentration. - Associated features – emotional numbing, guilt (survivor guilt), shame, depression, substance use, suicidal ideas. - Complex PTSD (ICD-11) – after prolonged or repeated trauma (childhood abuse, domestic violence, captivity): PTSD symptoms plus difficulties in emotional regulation, a negative self-concept (worthless, ashamed) and difficulties in relationships. - Symptoms usually start within months of the trauma, but may be delayed.

Risk factors – severity and duration of trauma, interpersonal trauma (rape, torture), previous trauma or mental illness, lack of social support after the event, female sex, ongoing stress.

Management

  • Early care after trauma – psychological first aid: safety, comfort, basic needs, practical help, connecting with family and services; single-session psychological debriefing is not recommended.
  • Trauma-focused psychological therapies – trauma-focused CBT (cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure) and EMDR (eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing) – first-line.
  • Medication – SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine; prazosin for trauma-related nightmares; treatment of depression and substance use.

Nursing management

  • Trauma-informed care – ensure safety, choice and control; explain procedures; avoid re-traumatising (e.g. unnecessary restraint, insensitive questioning); gender-sensitive care for survivors of sexual violence.
  • Build trust; allow the patient to talk about the trauma at his own pace without forcing.
  • Teach grounding techniques for flashbacks (naming things in the room, feeling the feet on the floor), relaxation and sleep hygiene.
  • Assess and manage suicide risk, depression and substance use.
  • Support the family; link with legal aid, police (for crime survivors), social welfare and support groups; follow-up.

Conclusion PTSD follows extremely threatening events and is marked by re-experiencing (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance and a persistent sense of threat with hyperarousal; complex PTSD adds problems of emotion regulation, self-concept and relationships. Management includes psychological first aid, trauma-focused CBT and EMDR, SSRIs and prazosin, with trauma-informed nursing care.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: Explain acute stress reaction and adjustment disorder.
answer_html:
Introduction Not every reaction to stress is a mental disorder. Some reactions are short and normal; others, though not severe enough to be PTSD or depression, cause distress and impair functioning.

A. Acute stress reaction

  • A transient reaction to an exceptionally stressful event (accident, assault, disaster, sudden death of a close person) in a person without other mental disorder.
  • Onset within minutes to hours of the event; symptoms subside within days (usually within about a week, or a month at most for DSM-5-TR's "acute stress disorder").
  • Features – an initial state of "daze", narrowing of attention, disorientation; then anxiety, fear, anger, despair, overactivity or withdrawal; autonomic signs (palpitations, sweating); sometimes dissociative symptoms and partial amnesia for the event.
  • In ICD-11 it is regarded as a normal reaction to extreme stress (not a mental disorder), but people still need support.
  • Management – psychological first aid: ensure safety and basic needs, calm and comfort, practical help, reunite with family, provide information; brief benzodiazepine for severe insomnia or agitation; observe for development of PTSD or depression.

B. Adjustment disorder

  • A maladaptive reaction to an identifiable psychosocial stressor – divorce, separation, failure in examinations, loss of job, migration, financial loss, serious illness – usually emerging within a month of the stressor.
  • Features – preoccupation with the stressor (excessive worry, recurrent distressing thoughts, rumination) and failure to adapt – difficulty in concentrating, sleep disturbance, low mood, anxiety, irritability, impaired work or social functioning; conduct problems in adolescents.
  • Symptoms do not meet the criteria for another disorder and usually resolve within about 6 months unless the stressor continues.
  • Management – supportive counselling, problem-solving therapy, crisis intervention, strengthening social support, removal or reduction of the stressor; short-term medication for sleep or anxiety; assessment of suicidal risk.

Nursing management

  • Establish rapport; encourage ventilation of feelings; listen actively.
  • Help the person understand the link between the stressor and the symptoms.
  • Teach problem-solving and coping skills – breaking problems into steps, identifying options and resources.
  • Mobilise family and community support; link with social, legal and financial help.
  • Teach relaxation and sleep hygiene; encourage normal routine and activity.
  • Assess suicide risk, especially in adolescents and those with substance use; arrange follow-up.

Conclusion Acute stress reaction is a brief response to an exceptional stressor that settles within days and needs psychological first aid. Adjustment disorder is a maladaptive reaction to an identifiable life stressor with preoccupation and failure to adapt, usually resolving within 6 months; it is managed with supportive counselling, problem-solving, crisis intervention and social support, with nursing care that encourages ventilation, coping, support and monitoring of suicide risk.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: Explain dissociative (conversion) disorders and their nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Dissociative disorders are characterised by an involuntary disruption or loss of the normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, body representation, motor control or behaviour, usually following psychological stress or conflict. When the disturbance appears as neurological symptoms without a neurological cause, it is called conversion disorder (ICD-11: dissociative neurological symptom disorder; DSM-5-TR: functional neurological symptom disorder). The older term was "hysteria".

Types

  1. Dissociative neurological symptom (conversion) disorder
    • Motor – weakness or paralysis of limbs, abnormal gait (astasia–abasia), tremors, non-epileptic (psychogenic) seizures, loss of voice (aphonia), difficulty swallowing.
    • Sensory – numbness (often in a "glove and stocking" pattern not matching nerve supply), blindness, deafness.
    • Symptoms often do not follow anatomical patterns and vary with attention.
  2. Dissociative amnesia – inability to recall important personal information, usually of a stressful nature; may include dissociative fugue (sudden purposeful travel away from home with loss of identity).
  3. Trance and possession trance disorder – involuntary trance states or states in which the person behaves as if possessed by a spirit or deity, outside accepted cultural or religious practice – common in India.
  4. Dissociative identity disorder – two or more distinct personality states.
  5. Depersonalisation–derealisation disorder.

Important concepts

  • Primary gain – reduction of anxiety by converting the conflict into a symptom.
  • Secondary gain – external benefits from the symptom – attention, sympathy, escape from responsibility or an unpleasant situation.
  • La belle indifférence – apparent lack of concern about a serious-looking symptom (seen in some patients; not diagnostic).
  • Patients are not faking (unlike malingering) – the symptoms are involuntary.

Differences between non-epileptic and epileptic seizures – non-epileptic seizures often occur in the presence of others, have a gradual onset, eyes closed and resisting opening, side-to-side head movements, pelvic thrusting, long duration, rare injury or tongue bite, no post-ictal confusion, and a normal EEG during the attack.

Management

  • Exclude organic disease with appropriate examination and investigations (without excessive testing).
  • Explain the diagnosis positively – a real but reversible problem of how the brain functions under stress.
  • Psychotherapy – supportive therapy, CBT, family therapy, stress management; exploring conflicts; suggestion and hypnosis in some cases.
  • Physiotherapy for functional weakness; speech therapy for aphonia.
  • Treat associated depression and anxiety.

Nursing management

  • Accept the symptoms as real for the patient; avoid labelling ("drama", "acting") and avoid arguments.
  • Do not reinforce secondary gain – give attention to the patient's needs and feelings rather than to the symptom; respond matter-of-factly to symptoms; encourage normal activity and self-care.
  • During non-epileptic seizures – ensure safety, remain calm, avoid crowding and excessive attention, observe and record features.
  • Help the patient identify stressors and express feelings verbally; teach problem-solving and assertive communication.
  • Teach relaxation and coping skills; involve the family in reducing conflict and avoiding over-protection.
  • Encourage gradual return to normal roles; follow-up.

Conclusion Dissociative disorders involve disruption of the normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity and motor or sensory function after stress. Conversion (dissociative neurological symptom) disorder produces paralysis, seizures, aphonia or sensory loss without organic cause; amnesia, fugue, trance and possession and dissociative identity disorder are other types. Management excludes organic disease and uses positive explanation, psychotherapy and rehabilitation; nursing care accepts the symptoms, avoids reinforcing secondary gain, focuses on feelings and stressors and promotes normal functioning.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: Explain somatic symptom disorder (bodily distress disorder) and illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis).
answer_html:
Introduction In somatic symptom and related disorders, psychological distress is expressed through bodily symptoms or excessive worry about illness. Such patients are common in general hospitals and primary care in India, often presenting with weakness, burning sensations, aches, "gas" problems or headache, and undergoing many investigations.

A. Somatic symptom disorder (DSM-5-TR) / bodily distress disorder (ICD-11)

  • One or more distressing bodily symptoms (pain, fatigue, gastrointestinal or other complaints) with excessive attention, thoughts, feelings or behaviours related to them – persistent worry, high anxiety about their seriousness, devoting excessive time and energy, repeated consultations and investigations ("doctor shopping").
  • Normal test results and reassurance do not reduce the concern for long.
  • Persistent (usually more than 6 months); causes impairment in daily life.

B. Illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis)

  • Preoccupation with the fear of having, or acquiring, a serious illness (cancer, HIV, heart disease), with few or no actual symptoms.
  • Misinterpretation of normal bodily sensations as signs of disease; repeated checking of the body, searching the internet, seeking reassurance, or avoiding doctors and hospitals.
  • ICD-11 places hypochondriasis among the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.

Aetiology

  • Heightened sensitivity to bodily sensations; anxious and depressive tendencies; childhood experience of illness in the family; learned illness behaviour (secondary gain); difficulty expressing emotions in words; stress; cultural factors that make physical complaints more acceptable than emotional complaints.

Management

  • Exclude physical disease with reasonable investigations; avoid unnecessary repeated tests.
  • One regular doctor and regular scheduled visits (not only when symptoms worsen) – builds trust and reduces doctor shopping.
  • Acknowledge that the symptoms are real and distressing; explain the link between stress, emotions and bodily symptoms.
  • CBT – reducing checking and reassurance seeking, challenging catastrophic interpretations, increasing activity.
  • Antidepressants (SSRIs; low-dose tricyclics for pain) when anxiety or depression is present.

Nursing management

  • Accept the patient's symptoms as real; avoid dismissing remarks ("there is nothing wrong with you").
  • Assess the symptoms once thoroughly; then limit time spent discussing symptoms and redirect conversation to feelings, stressors and daily activities.
  • Do not reinforce the sick role; encourage self-care, exercise, work and social activities; praise healthy behaviour.
  • Teach relaxation, stress management and healthy lifestyle.
  • Educate the family to respond to the person's needs without excessive attention to symptoms.
  • Give medicines as ordered; monitor for depression and suicidal ideas; follow-up with one consistent provider.

Conclusion Somatic symptom (bodily distress) disorder is persistent distressing bodily symptoms with excessive attention and help-seeking, while illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis) is preoccupation with fear of serious illness with few symptoms. Management avoids unnecessary tests, provides one regular doctor and scheduled visits, CBT and antidepressants, and nursing care accepts the symptoms, focuses on feelings and functioning, discourages the sick role and teaches coping.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: Explain the levels of anxiety and the nursing interventions at each level.
answer_html:
Introduction Anxiety is a vague, uneasy feeling of apprehension in response to a real or perceived threat, accompanied by physical and psychological changes. Hildegard Peplau described four levels of anxiety, each with different effects on perception and behaviour, needing different nursing responses.

1. Mild anxiety

  • Features – alert, perceptual field widened, increased motivation and learning ability; restlessness, mild tension, fidgeting.
  • Occurs in everyday life (e.g. before an examination) and can be useful.
  • Interventions – help the person recognise the anxiety and use it constructively; problem-solving and learning; encourage healthy coping (exercise, talking, hobbies).

2. Moderate anxiety

  • Features – perceptual field narrowed; focuses on immediate concerns (selective inattention), but can follow directions; increased pulse and respiration, muscle tension, sweating, rapid speech, difficulty concentrating.
  • Interventions – stay calm; help the person identify and describe the anxiety and its cause; link it to behaviour; encourage ventilation; teach relaxation and problem-solving; give clear instructions; physical activity to discharge tension.

3. Severe anxiety

  • Features – perceptual field greatly reduced; focus on scattered details; cannot learn or solve problems and needs direction; headache, palpitations, hyperventilation, nausea, trembling; feelings of dread; purposeless activity.
  • Interventions – reduce anxiety first: stay with the person; calm, low voice; short, simple sentences; quiet environment with reduced stimuli; guide slow breathing; meet physical needs; direct simple activities (walking); PRN anxiolytic as ordered; explore causes only after the anxiety is reduced.

4. Panic

  • Features – loss of control, disorganised thinking, inability to communicate or function, distorted perception, terror, possible hallucinations; may run, freeze or become violent; exhaustion if prolonged.
  • Interventions – never leave the person alone; ensure safety of patient and others; calm, firm approach; very simple directions; remove to a quiet, safe place; reduce stimuli; physical needs; medication as ordered; once the panic subsides, help the person talk about it and learn coping strategies.

Defence and coping – people use coping mechanisms (talking, exercise, crying, problem-solving) and ego defence mechanisms (repression, denial, displacement, rationalisation); overuse of defences or maladaptive coping (alcohol, avoidance) leads to anxiety disorders.

General principles

  • The nurse's own calmness is essential (anxiety is "contagious").
  • Assess the level of anxiety before choosing the intervention – higher levels need structure and reduction of anxiety, lower levels allow insight, learning and problem-solving.

Conclusion Peplau's four levels of anxiety – mild, moderate, severe and panic – progressively narrow perception and reduce functioning. At mild and moderate levels the nurse helps the patient recognise anxiety and use learning and problem-solving; at severe and panic levels she stays with the patient, ensures safety, reduces stimuli and gives simple direction and medication, exploring causes only after anxiety falls.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: What is a panic attack? List its symptoms.
answer_html:
A panic attack is a sudden, discrete episode of intense fear or discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes, often without warning, and usually lasts 5–30 minutes. Symptoms

  1. Palpitations or racing heart.
  2. Sweating, trembling or shaking.
  3. Breathlessness or feeling of choking.
  4. Chest pain or discomfort.
  5. Nausea or abdominal distress.
  6. Dizziness, light-headedness, feeling faint.
  7. Chills or hot flushes; numbness or tingling.
  8. Derealisation or depersonalisation.
  9. Fear of losing control or "going crazy", and fear of dying. Recurrent unexpected attacks with persistent worry about them constitute panic disorder.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: Differentiate between an obsession and a delusion.
answer_html:
• Nature – obsession: an intrusive, unwanted thought, image or urge; delusion: a false, firm, fixed belief.
  • Recognition – obsession: recognised as one's own thought and as senseless or excessive; delusion: believed to be true.
  • Insight – obsession: usually present; delusion: absent.
  • Resistance – obsession: the person tries to resist it and feels distressed (ego-dystonic); delusion: not resisted (ego-syntonic).
  • Associated behaviour – obsession: compulsions to reduce anxiety; delusion: may act on the belief (e.g. aggression in persecutory delusions).
  • Disorder – obsession: OCD (neurotic); delusion: psychotic disorders (schizophrenia, delusional disorder, mania, psychotic depression).

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: What are primary gain and secondary gain? What is la belle indifférence?
answer_html:
• Primary gain – the internal benefit of a symptom: the reduction of anxiety achieved by converting an unacceptable conflict into a physical symptom (e.g. paralysis of the arm in a person in conflict about striking someone).
  • Secondary gain – the external benefits obtained because of the symptom – attention, sympathy, care, escape from responsibilities or unpleasant situations, financial compensation. Nursing care should avoid reinforcing secondary gain.
  • La belle indifférence – an inappropriate lack of concern or calmness about a serious-looking symptom such as paralysis or blindness, seen in some patients with conversion (dissociative) disorder; it is not a reliable diagnostic sign.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: Define depersonalisation and derealisation.
answer_html:
• Depersonalisation – a feeling of being detached from one's own self, body or thoughts – as if observing oneself from outside, feeling unreal, like a robot or in a dream.
  • Derealisation – a feeling that the surroundings are unreal, distant, foggy, dreamlike or artificial.
  • In both, reality testing remains intact – the person knows the feeling is only a feeling.
  • They occur in anxiety and panic attacks, PTSD, depression, sleep deprivation, substance use and in depersonalisation–derealisation disorder; brief episodes are common in healthy people under stress.

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatisation Disorders
question: What is prolonged grief disorder?
answer_html: Prolonged grief disorder is a new diagnosis in ICD-11 (and DSM-5-TR) for a persistent and pervasive grief response after the death of a person close to the bereaved. Features – persistent longing for, or preoccupation with, the deceased, with intense emotional pain – sadness, guilt, anger, denial, difficulty accepting the death, feeling that a part of oneself has been lost, inability to experience positive mood, emotional numbness, difficulty engaging in social activities. Duration – lasting an atypically long time – at least 6 months after the loss in ICD-11 (12 months in adults in DSM-5-TR) – and clearly exceeding the person's cultural and religious norms, with significant impairment. Treatment – grief-focused CBT and prolonged grief therapy, support groups; assessment of suicide risk.
